title: Lecture 4: Neurons I: Membrane Voltage, Circuits, and Integrate-and-Fire
subtitle: Neurons I: Membrane Voltage, Circuits, and Integrate-and-Fire
text: Neurons I: Membrane Voltage, Circuits, and Integrate-and-Fire Concentration gradient → electrochemical equilibrium → Nernst potential → membrane capacitance / channels → Kirchhoff's law → IF / LIF Build a consistent sign convention from the definitions of force, potential energy, electric potential, and membrane voltage, and explain how a concentration gradient and an electric field jointly determine net ionic flux. Derive the Nernst equation from the electrochemical equilibrium of a single ion, handling the valence z, the inside-to-outside concentration ratio, temperature, and voltage sign correctly. Map the lipid membrane, ion channels, and applied current onto a capacitor, conductance–battery branches, and a current source, then derive the membrane equation from charge conservation. Distinguish the perfect integrate-and-fire model from the leaky integrate-and-fire model, and calculate their slopes, time constants, steady-state voltages, rheobase currents, and first-spike times. State what the equivalent circuit, integrate-and-fire model, and action-potential mechanism each retain and omit, without interpreting model components as literal biological parts. The neural membrane is both a capacitor that separates charge and a conductance network formed by ion-selective channels. Diffusion drives ions down concentration gradients, while the electric field drives charged particles toward lower electric potential energy. Their balance defines each ion's reversal potential. The circuit equivalent is not a decorative analogy: it combines charge conservation, Ohm's law, and channel selectivity into a solvable equation for membrane voltage. Treating an equilibrium potential as the cell's actual instantaneous membrane voltage. Forgetting the sign convention V_m=inside−outside. Applying a cation's sign intuition to Cl−. Conflating current direction, positive-charge motion, and voltage change. Assuming that ions cross the membrane through the capacitor branch; an ideal capacitor represents redistribution of charge on the two sides of the membrane. Treating threshold and reset as an action potential generated naturally by the LIF differential equation. This lecture stops at the LIF equation. Do not fold in Lecture 5's full closed-form LIF solution or HH gating dynamics prematurely, though a clear preview at the end is useful. Membrane-voltage sign convention Vm = \(\varphi _{\mathrm{in}} - \varphi _{\mathrm{out}}\) Inside minus outside Nernst equilibrium potential kB \(T [c]_{\mathrm{out}}\) Ec = ln qc \([c]_{\mathrm{in}}\) Single-ion equilibrium at fixed temperature Definition of capacitance \(Q = CV C\) is approximately constant Capacitive current \(I = C \dot{V}\) \(Q=CV\) Leak current IL = GL (V − EL ) Linear passive conductance Subthreshold LIF equation C V̇ = Ie − GL (V − EL ) Threshold and reset are specified separately F-I slope of the pure IF model Ie \(r= C(VT - VR )\) Constant current, no refractory period, and no leak membrane voltage Electric potential inside the cell minus electric potential outside the cell. diffusion Net random motion driven by a concentration gradient. electric potential energy The energy \(q\phi\) of a charged particle in an electric potential. equilibrium potential The voltage at which the net flux of one ion is zero. reversal potential The voltage at which current through a channel changes direction; in the simplest case, it equals the equilibrium potential. conductance The reciprocal of resistance, \(G=1/R\). capacitance Charge stored per unit voltage, Q/V. Kirchhoff current law The algebraic sum of currents entering and leaving a node is zero. integrate-and-fire model An abstract model that integrates input, emits a spike at threshold, and resets. leaky integrator A state driven by input while exponentially relaxing toward a baseline. If \(V_{m}=-60 \mathrm{mV}\) and \(V_{m}=\phi _{\mathrm{in}}-\phi _{\mathrm{out}}\), which side has the lower electric potential? On which side does a cation have lower electric potential energy? First use the voltage definition to order the electric potentials, then multiply by the sign of the charge to order potential energies. The ordering reverses for anions, so “negative inside” alone cannot determine the direction of every ion. The intracellular electric potential is 60 mV below the extracellular potential. For a cation with \(q>0\), \(U=q\phi\), so its electric potential energy is also lower inside. Intracellular \(K^{+}\) concentration exceeds extracellular \(K^{+}\) concentration, and the Nernst equation uses \(\ln([K]_{\mathrm{out}}/[K]_{\mathrm{in}})\). Is the equilibrium potential positive or negative? The \(K^{+}\) concentration gradient drives efflux. Preventing net efflux requires a negative intracellular potential that attracts \(K^{+}\) inward, so the inside-minus-outside equilibrium potential is negative. Because \(z=+1\) and the concentration ratio is less than 1, the logarithm is negative; therefore \(E_{K}\) is negative. A membrane capacitor has \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\) and receives a constant inward current of 100 pA. Ignoring all ion channels, what is \(dV/dt\)? The \(10^{-12}\) factors in pA/pF cancel to give V/s, whose numerical value equals mV/ms. A constant current therefore produces a linear voltage ramp across an ideal capacitor. \(dV/dt=I/C=0.5 \mathrm{V}/s=0.5 \mathrm{mV}/\mathrm{ms}\). In a leaky integrate-and-fire model, \(E_{L}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), and \(V_{T}=-50 \mathrm{mV}\). What minimum constant current places the subthreshold steady state exactly at threshold? At threshold, \(dV/dt=0\) requires the applied current to exactly balance the leak current. Because \(\mathrm{nS}\cdot \mathrm{mV}=\mathrm{pA}\), any smaller current leaves the steady state below threshold. \(I_{T}=G_{L}(V_{T}-E_{L})=10 \mathrm{nS}\cdot 15 \mathrm{mV}=150 \mathrm{pA}\). If \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) had the same inside-to-outside concentration ratio, why would its equilibrium potential have the opposite sign from that of \(K^{+}\)? In the Nernst equation, signed valence z appears in the denominator. For \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\), \(z=-1\) reverses the sign of the logarithmic term, reflecting the reversal of electric force for a negative charge. This is the distinction tested in Electrochemical potential, membrane voltage, and Nernst equilibrium. Worked example — Calculate the \(K^{+}\) equilibrium potential at body temperature: Use concentrations independent of the illustrative source values: \(T=310 K\), so \(RT/F\approx 26.7 \mathrm{mV}\); for \(K^{+}\), \([K]_{\mathrm{out}}=5 \mathrm{mM}\), \([K]_{\mathrm{in}}=140 \mathrm{mM}\), and \(z=+1\). Calculate \(E_{K}\), then determine how it changes when extracellular \(K^{+}\) rises to 10 mM. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Use concentrations independent of the illustrative source values: \(T=310 K\), so \(RT/F\approx 26.7 \mathrm{mV}\); for \(K^{+}\), \([K]_{\mathrm{out}}=5 \mathrm{mM}\), \([K]_{\mathrm{in}}=140 \mathrm{mM}\), and \(z=+1\). Calculate \(E_{K}\), then determine how it changes when extracellular \(K^{+}\) rises to 10 mM. The initial concentration ratio is \(5/140\approx 0.035714\), and \(\ln(0.035714)\approx -3.332\). \(E_{K}\approx 26.7 \mathrm{mV}\cdot (-3.332)=-88.96 \mathrm{mV}\), or about −89 mV. After extracellular \(K^{+}\) rises, the ratio is \(10/140\approx 0.071429\) and its logarithm is ≈−2.639. The new value is \(E_{K}\approx 26.7\cdot (-2.639)=-70.46 \mathrm{mV}\), about 18.5 mV more positive than before—a depolarizing shift. In both cases \(c_{\mathrm{out}}<c_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(z>0\), so \(E_{K}\) must be negative. Raising the external concentration moves the ratio toward 1 and reduces the magnitude of the potential. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Electrochemical potential, membrane voltage, and Nernst equilibrium”? Membrane voltage arises from a small separation of charge at the membrane surfaces; the bulk intracellular and extracellular solutions remain nearly electroneutral. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Electrochemical potential, membrane voltage, and Nernst equilibrium”? Nernst equilibrium is a zero-net-flux state in which chemical and electrical driving forces cancel. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Electrochemical potential, membrane voltage, and Nernst equilibrium” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Membrane voltage arises from a small separation of charge at the membrane surfaces; the bulk intracellular and extracellular solutions remain nearly electroneutral. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “From the Boltzmann ratio on this lesson to the Nernst equation”? RT has units J/mol and F has units C/mol, so \(RT/F=J/C=V\). The concentration ratio and its logarithm are dimensionless; \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}\) is measured in volts. If \(c_{\mathrm{out}}=c_{\mathrm{in}}\), the logarithm is zero and \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}=0\). Increasing \(c_{\mathrm{out}}/c_{\mathrm{in}}\) for a cation makes \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}\) more positive. The ideal formula tends toward zero voltage as \(T\to 0\), but a physiological model is not valid at absolute zero. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: When an ion moves across a membrane down its concentration gradient, how does charge separation create an opposing electric field, and at what voltage does net flux vanish? The cell membrane separates two conducting saline solutions. Most of the fluid on either side remains nearly electroneutral: membrane voltage requires only a tiny fraction of ions to separate at the membrane surfaces, not a cell interior filled with negative charge. This section introduces the electrical sign convention through \(F=-\nabla U\) and \(\phi =U/q\), then defines \(V_{m}=\phi _{\mathrm{in}}-\phi _{\mathrm{out}}\). A resting value near −60 mV means that the intracellular potential is lower. The same convention governs reversal potentials, channel currents, and action-potential diagrams. A concentration gradient supplies the diffusive drive. Suppose only \(K^{+}\) channels are open and \([K]_{\mathrm{in}}>[K]_{\mathrm{out}}\). Random motion produces net \(K^{+}\) efflux and leaves the inside relatively negative. As charge separation grows, the negative intracellular potential attracts \(K^{+}\) back inward. The chemical drive remains outward while the electrical drive points inward. At equilibrium, their contributions to the electrochemical-potential difference cancel, yielding zero net flux—not an end to microscopic ion exchange. Why does increasing one channel conductance change both the steady-state voltage and the speed of approach? It gives that channel's reversal potential more weight in the steady-state average and increases \(G_{\mathrm{tot}}\), which reduces the membrane time constant \(C/G_{\mathrm{tot}}\); voltage therefore approaches the new steady state faster. This is the distinction tested in The membrane equivalent circuit: capacitance, conductance, batteries, and KCL. Worked example — Instantaneous slope and steady state of a two-branch membrane: Use \(E_{K}=-85 \mathrm{mV}\) as the specified branch parameter for this independent circuit example; it need not equal the −89 mV obtained from a different concentration set above. Let \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), \(E_{L}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\), \(G_{K}=20 \mathrm{nS}\), and \(I_{e}=300 \mathrm{pA}\). Find \(dV/dt\) at \(V=-60 \mathrm{mV}\) and the steady state \(V^{*}\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Use \(E_{K}=-85 \mathrm{mV}\) as the specified branch parameter for this independent circuit example; it need not equal the −89 mV obtained from a different concentration set above. Let \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), \(E_{L}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\), \(G_{K}=20 \mathrm{nS}\), and \(I_{e}=300 \mathrm{pA}\). Find \(dV/dt\) at \(V=-60 \mathrm{mV}\) and the steady state \(V^{*}\). The outward leak current is \(10 \mathrm{nS}\cdot (-60+65)\mathrm{mV}=50 \mathrm{pA}\). The outward K current is \(20 \mathrm{nS}\cdot (-60+85)\mathrm{mV}=500 \mathrm{pA}\), so net inward current is \(300-50-500=-250 \mathrm{pA}\). Thus \(dV/dt=-250 \mathrm{pA}/200 \mathrm{pF}=-1.25 \mathrm{V}/s=-1.25 \mathrm{mV}/\mathrm{ms}\), so voltage is falling at this instant. The steady-state numerator is \(300 \mathrm{pA}+10 \mathrm{nS}\cdot (-65 \mathrm{mV})+20 \mathrm{nS}\cdot (-85 \mathrm{mV})=300-650-1700=-2050 \mathrm{pA}\). Total conductance is 30 nS, so \(V^{*}=-2050/30 \mathrm{mV}\approx -68.33 \mathrm{mV}\) and \(\tau =C/G_{\mathrm{tot}}=200 \mathrm{pF}/30 \mathrm{nS}\approx 6.67 \mathrm{ms}\). The steady state should reflect competition among the two branches after the current-induced shift. Substituting \(V=-68.33 \mathrm{mV}\) makes the total outward branch current approximately 300 pA. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “The membrane equivalent circuit: capacitance, conductance, batteries, and KCL”? The lipid membrane maps to capacitance, ion channels to conductance, and concentration gradients to reversal-potential batteries. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “The membrane equivalent circuit: capacitance, conductance, batteries, and KCL”? \(I_{C}=C dV/dt\) follows from \(Q=CV\) and \(I=dQ/dt\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “The membrane equivalent circuit: capacitance, conductance, batteries, and KCL” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? \(I_{C}=C dV/dt\) follows from \(Q=CV\) and \(I=dQ/dt\). The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Derive the multichannel membrane equation from charge conservation”? C·dV/dt has units \(F\cdot V/s=C/s=A\), and G·(V−E) has units \(S\cdot V=A\), so every term can be added in one KCL equation. If all \(G_{x}=0\), the equation reduces to the ideal capacitor \(C dV/dt=I_{e}\) and has no finite steady state. If one \(G_{k}\) greatly exceeds all other conductances while \(I_{e}\) remains finite, \(V^{*}\) approaches \(E_{k}\). These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does 100 pA eventually produce a spike in perfect IF but never produce one in the LIF model above? Perfect IF has no opposing leak, so positive current continues to charge the capacitor. In LIF, leak grows during depolarization until it exactly balances 100 pA at −55 mV, a steady state below the −50 mV threshold. This is the distinction tested in From perfect integrate-and-fire to leaky integrate-and-fire. Worked example — Compare subthreshold behavior and repetitive firing with the same parameters: Let \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), \(E_{L}=V_{R}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\), and \(V_{T}=-50 \mathrm{mV}\). Apply constant currents of 100 pA and 200 pA. Determine whether each causes spiking; if so, calculate the first-spike time and the rate without a refractory period. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), \(E_{L}=V_{R}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\), and \(V_{T}=-50 \mathrm{mV}\). Apply constant currents of 100 pA and 200 pA. Determine whether each causes spiking; if so, calculate the first-spike time and the rate without a refractory period. The membrane time constant is \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}=200 \mathrm{pF}/10 \mathrm{nS}=20 \mathrm{ms}\), and the rheobase is \(I_{T}=10 \mathrm{nS}\cdot 15 \mathrm{mV}=150 \mathrm{pA}\). At 100 pA, \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=-65 \mathrm{mV}+100 \mathrm{pA}/10 \mathrm{nS}=-55 \mathrm{mV}\), below −50 mV, so the trajectory never crosses threshold. At 200 pA, \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=-65+20=-45 \mathrm{mV}\), above threshold. The threshold-time ratio is \((V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{R})/(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{T})=20/5=4\). Therefore \(t_{sp}=20 \mathrm{ms}\cdot \ln 4\approx 20\cdot 1.3863=27.73 \mathrm{ms}\). Each reset returns to the same voltage under the same input, so every cycle has the same duration. Without a refractory period, \(f=1/0.02773 \mathrm{s}\approx 36.1 \mathrm{Hz}\). Because 200 pA is only slightly above the 150 pA rheobase, the rate should be finite and modest. Ignoring leak, perfect IF gives \(15 \mathrm{mV}/(1 \mathrm{mV}/\mathrm{ms})=15 \mathrm{ms}\), correctly predicting a faster crossing. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “From perfect integrate-and-fire to leaky integrate-and-fire”? Perfect IF ramps linearly under constant current; every positive current eventually produces a spike. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “From perfect integrate-and-fire to leaky integrate-and-fire”? The leak branch introduces \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=E_{L}+I_{e}/G_{L}\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “From perfect integrate-and-fire to leaky integrate-and-fire” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The LIF rheobase current is \(I_{T}=G_{L}(V_{T}-E_{L})\). The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “LIF steady state, rheobase, and first-spike time”? \(C/G_{L}\) has units \(F/S=s\); \(I_{e}/G_{L}\) has units \(A/S=V\); the logarithm contains a dimensionless ratio of voltage differences; \(t_{sp}\) is a time. As \(I_{e}\) approaches \(I_{T}\) from above, \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{T}\to 0\), \(t_{sp}\to \infty\), and firing \(\mathrm{rate}\to 0\). For very large \(I_{e}\), leak matters less during the short ramp and the result approaches the perfect-IF value \(C(V_{T}-V_{R})/I_{e}\). These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Current conservation in the membrane equivalent circuit”? Node conservation divides the applied current into two parts: C \(dV_{m}/dt\) changes the charge stored across the membrane, while \(\sum G_{x}(V_{m}-E_{x})\) flows through ionic branches. \(E_{x}\) sets the zero-current voltage of a branch, and \(G_{x}\) sets how strongly that branch pulls \(V_{m}\) toward \(E_{x}\). Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “membrane voltage” mean in this lecture? membrane voltage: Electric potential inside the cell minus electric potential outside the cell. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “diffusion” mean in this lecture? diffusion: Net random motion driven by a concentration gradient. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “electric potential energy” mean in this lecture? electric potential energy: The energy \(q\phi\) of a charged particle in an electric potential. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “equilibrium potential” mean in this lecture? equilibrium potential: The voltage at which the net flux of one ion is zero. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “reversal potential” mean in this lecture? reversal potential: The voltage at which current through a channel changes direction; in the simplest case, it equals the equilibrium potential. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “conductance” mean in this lecture? conductance: The reciprocal of resistance, \(G=1/R\). This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “capacitance” mean in this lecture? capacitance: Charge stored per unit voltage, Q/V. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “Kirchhoff current law” mean in this lecture? Kirchhoff current law: The algebraic sum of currents entering and leaving a node is zero. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “integrate-and-fire model” mean in this lecture? integrate-and-fire model: An abstract model that integrates input, emits a spike at threshold, and resets. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “Membrane-voltage sign convention” be used? Membrane-voltage sign convention: Vm = \(\varphi _{\mathrm{in}} - \varphi _{\mathrm{out}}\). Inside minus outside This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Nernst equilibrium potential” be used? Nernst equilibrium potential: kB \(T [c]_{\mathrm{out}}\) Ec = ln qc \([c]_{\mathrm{in}}\). Single-ion equilibrium at fixed temperature This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Definition of capacitance” be used? Definition of capacitance: \(Q = CV\). C is approximately constant This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Capacitive current” be used? Capacitive current: \(I = C \dot{V}\). \(Q=CV\) This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Leak current” be used? Leak current: IL = GL (V − EL ). Linear passive conductance This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Subthreshold LIF equation” be used? Subthreshold LIF equation: C V̇ = Ie − GL (V − EL ). Threshold and reset are specified separately This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “F-I slope of the pure IF model” be used? F-I slope of the pure IF model: Ie \(r= C(VT - VR )\). Constant current, no refractory period, and no leak This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written.

title: Lecture 5: Neurons II: LIF Solution and Hodgkin–Huxley
subtitle: Neurons II: LIF Solution and Hodgkin–Huxley
text: Neurons II: LIF Solution and Hodgkin–Huxley LIF ODE → steady state → threshold time → exact F-I relation → HH conductances → gating / refractory period Rewrite the LIF equation in time-constant–steady-state form and explain the exponential trajectory after a current step begins and ends. Derive the exact interspike interval and F–I curve of the LIF model from the threshold condition, and analyze behavior near rheobase and in the strong-input limit. Interpret current direction and maximal conductance in the leak, \(\mathrm{Na}^{+}\), and \(K^{+}\) branches of the Hodgkin–Huxley membrane equation. Derive a gating variable's steady state and time constant from the transition rates of a two-state channel, and explain activation, inactivation, and refractoriness. Explain how area normalization, multicompartment propagation, and cellular diversity extend a point-neuron model without confusing passive subthreshold decay with active action-potential regeneration. An LIF model treats each spike as a threshold-and-reset event, so its threshold-crossing time and firing rate can be derived analytically. The HH model instead explains the spike waveform through feedback among dynamic Na/K conductances. The two models answer different questions: LIF provides a tractable abstraction for networks and coding, whereas HH addresses ionic mechanisms and waveform shape. Membrane time constant, interspike interval, and refractory period must remain distinct. Confusing \(\tau _{m}\), the ISI, and refractory interval \(\delta\). Assuming that \(V_{\infty }=V_{T}\) leads to a threshold crossing in finite time; the voltage only approaches threshold asymptotically. Treating the threshold-linear F-I relation as the exact LIF result. Treating m, h, and n as numbers of ion channels. Forgetting that current=conductance×driving force; increasing a gate does not by itself determine current direction. Treating HH as the unique model of every neuron. Keep membrane time constant, interspike interval, and refractory period separate. Likewise distinguish channel activation probability, conductance, and ionic current. Membrane time constant \(\tau m = C/GL\) Passive linear membrane Steady-state voltage under constant current \(V_{\infty } = E_{L} + I/GL I\) is constant LIF rheobase IT = GL (VT − EL ) \(V_{R}\) does not affect the steady-state crossing criterion Time from reset to threshold \(V_{\infty } - VR\) ∆\(t = \tau m \ln V \infty  - VT\) \(V_{\infty }>V_{T}\) Firing rate with a refractory period r = 1/(δ + ∆t) Periodic response to constant current Conductance-based ionic current \(I_{\mathrm{ion}} = \bar{G}\) popen \((V - E_{\mathrm{rev}} )\) The sign convention and driving force are explicit Two-state gate kinetics \(\dot{n} = \alpha n (1 - n) - \beta n n\) \(0\le n\le 1\) membrane time constant The timescale \(C/G_{L}\) of a passive membrane's exponential response. steady-state voltage The value \(V_{\infty }\) at which the derivative vanishes under constant input. threshold current / rheobase The smallest indefinitely sustained constant current that can elicit a spike. interspike interval, ISI The elapsed time between adjacent spikes. absolute refractory period The minimum interval after a spike during which another spike cannot occur. maximal conductance The conductance scale when all relevant channels are open. activation A gating process in which depolarization increases channel opening. inactivation A process in which sustained depolarization reduces channel availability. cable equation An equation describing how voltage propagates and attenuates through space along a neurite. multicompartment model A representation that discretizes morphology into electrically coupled compartments. For \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\) and \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), what is \(\tau _{m}\)? If C doubles while \(G_{L}\) remains fixed, how does the trajectory change? Current and conductance set the steady state; capacitance appears only in the time constant. Separating steady-state location from approach speed is central to reading a first-order membrane equation. \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}=20 \mathrm{ms}\). Doubling C gives \(\tau _{m}=40 \mathrm{ms}\); the steady state is unchanged, but the trajectory approaches it more slowly. Why does the LIF firing rate rise gradually from zero when \(I_{e}\) barely exceeds \(I_{T}\) instead of jumping to a high value? Although threshold is a discrete event, continuous dynamics before the event determine its waiting time. Critical slowing creates the nonlinear onset of the F–I curve. \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) then lies only slightly above \(V_{T}\). The exponential trajectory moves very slowly as it nears steady state, the logarithmic threshold time diverges, and firing frequency approaches zero. A gating variable obeys \(dn/dt=\alpha (1-n)-\beta n\). What are its steady state and time constant? \(\alpha\) moves closed gates toward the open state, whereas \(\beta\) moves open gates toward the closed state. Their sum sets relaxation speed, and their ratio sets the steady-state open probability. \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}=\alpha /(\alpha +\beta )\) and \(\tau _{n}=1/(\alpha +\beta )\); equivalently, \(\tau _{n} dn/dt=-n+n_{\mathrm{inf}}\). n rises from 0.3 to 0.6 while the K-channel open fraction is \(n^{4}\). By what factor does the open fraction increase? The gating variable itself only doubles, but requiring multiple gates to open together raises the change to the fourth power, producing a steep voltage dependence of conductance. \((0.6/0.3)^{4}=2^{4}=16\). If C and \(G_{L}\) both double, how do \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) and \(\tau _{m}\) change? \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}\) remains unchanged. For the same total current \(I_{e}\), \(I_{e}/G_{L}\) is halved, so \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) moves closer to \(E_{L}\). If input also doubles in proportion to area, the steady-state offset can remain unchanged. This is the distinction tested in LIF time constant, steady state, and current-step response. Worked example — Rise and recovery during a current pulse: Let \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), and \(E_{L}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\). Starting at rest, inject 100 pA for 40 ms, then remove it. Find voltage at 40 ms and again 20 ms later. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), and \(E_{L}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\). Starting at rest, inject 100 pA for 40 ms, then remove it. Find voltage at 40 ms and again 20 ms later. \(\tau _{m}=20 \mathrm{ms}\), and during the pulse \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=-65 \mathrm{mV}+100 \mathrm{pA}/10 \mathrm{nS}=-55 \mathrm{mV}\). Because \(40 \mathrm{ms}=2\tau _{m}\), \(V(40)=-55+(-65+55)e^{-2}=-55-10\cdot 0.1353\approx -56.35 \mathrm{mV}\). After removal, the new steady state is −65 mV and the deviation at removal is 8.65 mV. After another \(20 \mathrm{ms}=1\tau _{m}\), the deviation is \(8.65e^{-1}\approx 3.18 \mathrm{mV}\), so \(V\approx -61.82 \mathrm{mV}\). During the rise, voltage must remain between −65 and −55 mV. During recovery, it must lie between −56.35 and −65 mV. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “LIF time constant, steady state, and current-step response”? \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}\) controls speed, while \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=E_{L}+I_{e}/G_{L}\) sets the steady state under constant current. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “LIF time constant, steady state, and current-step response”? Capacitor voltage is continuous; a current step changes its slope immediately, not its value. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “LIF time constant, steady state, and current-step response” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}\) controls speed, while \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=E_{L}+I_{e}/G_{L}\) sets the steady state under constant current. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Convert the leaky-membrane equation to standard first-order form”? \(C/G_{L}\) has units of seconds, \(I_{e}/G_{L}\) has units of volts, \(t/\tau _{m}\) is dimensionless, and every additive term in the solution is a voltage. As \(G_{L}\to 0\), \(\tau _{m}\to \infty\) and the standard form must reduce to the ideal-capacitor equation. When \(I_{e}=0\), \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=E_{L}\). These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: How do capacitance and leak convert a constant current into an exponential voltage response, and why does voltage return to rest with the same time constant after the step ends? The first two pages rebuild the circuit from an ideal capacitor to a leaky integrate-and-fire membrane. An ideal capacitor obeys \(C dV/dt=I_{e}\) and has no steady state under constant current. Adding leak gives \(C dV/dt=I_{e}-G_{L}(V-E_{L})\). Above \(E_{L}\), outward leak current is positive and opposes further depolarization; below \(E_{L}\), current reverses and drives voltage upward. Thus \(E_{L}\) is the stable point with no input. Define \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=E_{L}+I_{e}/G_{L}\) to write \(\tau _{m} dV/dt=-V+V_{\mathrm{inf}}\). Under constant current, \(V(t)=V_{\mathrm{inf}}+(V_{0}-V_{\mathrm{inf}})e^{-t/\tau _{m}}\). The solution contains its final target \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) and an initial deviation that decays over time. After one \(\tau _{m}\), 36.8% of the deviation remains; after three \(\tau _{m}\), about 5% remains. Why can a complex or negative time returned by the crossing formula when \(I_{e}<I_{T}\) not be interpreted as an unusual form of spiking? The derivation assumes \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}>V_{T}\), making the logarithmic ratio a positive number greater than 1. At a subthreshold steady state, the trajectory never crosses threshold; an expression outside its domain simply signals that the assumption failed. This is the distinction tested in Derive the exact F–I curve from threshold crossings. Worked example — Calculate an F–I point with a refractory period: Let \(\tau _{m}=20 \mathrm{ms}\), \(E_{L}=V_{R}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\), \(V_{T}=-50 \mathrm{mV}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), and \(\delta =2 \mathrm{ms}\). For \(I_{e}=200 \mathrm{pA}\), calculate \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\), charging time, total period, and firing frequency. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(\tau _{m}=20 \mathrm{ms}\), \(E_{L}=V_{R}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\), \(V_{T}=-50 \mathrm{mV}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), and \(\delta =2 \mathrm{ms}\). For \(I_{e}=200 \mathrm{pA}\), calculate \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\), charging time, total period, and firing frequency. \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=-65+200/10=-45 \mathrm{mV}\), and \(I_{T}=150 \mathrm{pA}\), so the neuron can fire. The ratio of voltage differences is \((-45+65)/(-45+50)=20/5=4\). The charging time is \(\Delta t=20 \ln 4\approx 27.73 \mathrm{ms}\). Total period is \(27.73+2=29.73 \mathrm{ms}\), giving frequency \(1000/29.73\approx 33.64 \mathrm{Hz}\). With a refractory period, 33.6 Hz must be below the approximately 36.1 Hz value without one and far below the ceiling \(1/0.002=500 \mathrm{Hz}\). Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Derive the exact F–I curve from threshold crossings”? LIF fires periodically only when \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}>V_{T}\), equivalently \(I_{e}>I_{T}\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Derive the exact F–I curve from threshold crossings”? The exact period contains the natural logarithm of a ratio of voltage differences. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Derive the exact F–I curve from threshold crossings” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The exact period contains the natural logarithm of a ratio of voltage differences. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “LIF period and strong-input limit”? A ratio of voltage differences is dimensionless, as is its logarithm; multiplication by \(\tau _{m}\) gives time, and frequency has units \(s^{-1}=\mathrm{Hz}\). As \(I_{e}\downarrow I_{T}\), \(f\to 0\). As \(I_{e}\to \infty\) with \(\delta =0\), f becomes approximately proportional to \(I_{e}\). With \(\delta >0\), \(f\to 1/\delta\). These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) both double, why does \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}\) remain fixed while \(\tau _{n}\) is halved? Steady state depends only on the ratio \(\alpha /(\alpha +\beta )\), so the common factor cancels. The time constant is the reciprocal of total transition rate; doubling both rates halves the relaxation time. This is the distinction tested in Hodgkin–Huxley gating, area normalization, and spatial propagation. Worked example — Opening of a gating variable after a voltage-clamp step: At a fixed voltage, \(\alpha =0.3 \mathrm{ms}^{-1}\), \(\beta =0.1 \mathrm{ms}^{-1}\), and \(n(0)=0.2\). Find \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}\), \(\tau _{n}\), n after 5 ms, and the change in \(n^{4}\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: At a fixed voltage, \(\alpha =0.3 \mathrm{ms}^{-1}\), \(\beta =0.1 \mathrm{ms}^{-1}\), and \(n(0)=0.2\). Find \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}\), \(\tau _{n}\), n after 5 ms, and the change in \(n^{4}\). \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}=0.3/(0.3+0.1)=0.75\). \(\tau _{n}=1/0.4 \mathrm{ms}^{-1}=2.5 \mathrm{ms}\). \(n(5)=0.75+(0.2-0.75)e^{-5/2.5}=0.75-0.55e^{-2}\approx 0.6756\). Initially \(n^{4}=0.2^{4}=0.0016\); after 5 ms, \(0.6756^{4}\approx 0.2084\), an increase of about 130-fold. \(n(5 \mathrm{ms})\) must lie between initial value 0.2 and steady state 0.75; every gating fraction lies between 0 and 1. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Hodgkin–Huxley gating, area normalization, and spatial propagation”? HH current still equals conductance times driving force; gating variables regulate the instantaneous conductance. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Hodgkin–Huxley gating, area normalization, and spatial propagation”? \(\tau _{n}=1/(\alpha +\beta )\) sets speed, while \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}=\alpha /(\alpha +\beta )\) sets the target at fixed voltage. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Hodgkin–Huxley gating, area normalization, and spatial propagation” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Na activation, Na inactivation, and delayed K activation together generate the action potential and refractory period. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Derive standard gating-variable form from transition rates”? \(dn/dt\) has units 1/time, matching \(\alpha (1-n)\) and \(\beta n\). \(\tau _{n}\) has units of time, while n and \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}\) are dimensionless. If \(\beta =0\), \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}=1\) and the gate eventually opens fully. If \(\alpha =0\), \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}=0\) and it eventually closes fully. Multiplying \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) by the same factor leaves steady state unchanged but speeds the response. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Threshold and refractoriness jointly shape the LIF F–I curve”? When \(I_{e}\le I_{T}\), the subthreshold steady state cannot reach threshold, so firing rate is zero. Above \(I_{T}\), the logarithmic term in the threshold-crossing time shapes the curve, while the absolute refractory period \(\delta\) limits the strong-input rate to \(1/\delta\). Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “membrane time constant” mean in this lecture? membrane time constant: The timescale \(C/G_{L}\) of a passive membrane's exponential response. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “steady-state voltage” mean in this lecture? steady-state voltage: The value \(V_{\infty }\) at which the derivative vanishes under constant input. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “threshold current / rheobase” mean in this lecture? threshold current / rheobase: The smallest indefinitely sustained constant current that can elicit a spike. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “interspike interval, ISI” mean in this lecture? interspike interval, ISI: The elapsed time between adjacent spikes. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “absolute refractory period” mean in this lecture? absolute refractory period: The minimum interval after a spike during which another spike cannot occur. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “maximal conductance” mean in this lecture? maximal conductance: The conductance scale when all relevant channels are open. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “activation” mean in this lecture? activation: A gating process in which depolarization increases channel opening. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “inactivation” mean in this lecture? inactivation: A process in which sustained depolarization reduces channel availability. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “cable equation” mean in this lecture? cable equation: An equation describing how voltage propagates and attenuates through space along a neurite. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “Membrane time constant” be used? Membrane time constant: \(\tau m = C/GL\). Passive linear membrane This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Steady-state voltage under constant current” be used? Steady-state voltage under constant current: \(V_{\infty } = E_{L} + I/GL\). I is constant This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. LIF rheobase: IT = GL (VT − EL ). \(V_{R}\) does not affect the steady-state crossing criterion This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Time from reset to threshold” be used? Time from reset to threshold: \(V_{\infty } - VR\) ∆\(t = \tau m \ln V \infty  - VT\). \(V_{\infty }>V_{T}\) This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Firing rate with a refractory period” be used? Firing rate with a refractory period: r = 1/(δ + ∆t). Periodic response to constant current This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Conductance-based ionic current” be used? Conductance-based ionic current: \(I_{\mathrm{ion}} = \bar{G}\) popen \((V - E_{\mathrm{rev}} )\). The sign convention and driving force are explicit This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Two-state gate kinetics: \(\dot{n} = \alpha n (1 - n) - \beta n n\). \(0\le n\le 1\) This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written.

title: Lecture 6: Neural Coding I: Poisson Spikes and Maximum Likelihood
subtitle: Neural Coding I: Poisson Spikes and Maximum Likelihood
text: Neural Coding I: Poisson Spikes and Maximum Likelihood Stimulus / task → voltage → spikes → raster / PSTH → Poisson variability → encoding \(P(n|s) \to MLE\)/ Fisher information Explain how the analysis moves from the mechanisms that generate action potentials to observable spike sequences, and identify which single-cell details are retained or averaged away in a coding analysis. Interpret the stimulus, MT recording, spike train, raster, and PSTH in a random-dot motion experiment, and calculate firing rates by hand from raw counts. Use the Fano factor and the coefficient of variation of interspike intervals to distinguish count variability from interval variability, and state the statistical object measured by each. Derive the window-count and waiting-time distributions of a homogeneous Poisson process, and explain how a constantly driven LIF neuron differs from Poisson spiking. Write the likelihood, log-likelihood, maximum-likelihood estimate, and Fisher information for a population of independent Poisson neurons, and relate likelihood curvature to estimation uncertainty. Neural encoding requires more than drawing a tuning curve: it specifies the full response distribution conditional on the stimulus. A Poisson model jointly predicts count variance≈mean, exponential ISIs, and independent increments. These are testable assumptions, not universal facts. A population likelihood multiplies the evidence from neurons; the log-likelihood turns that product into a sum, and its curvature connects decoding precision to Fisher information. Treating firing rate as a continuous signal measured directly by the electrode. Treating a raster, a count, a PSTH, and a rate as the same object. Concluding that a spike train is fully Poisson merely because \(\mathrm{Fano}\approx 1\). Ignoring observation window T and thereby confusing the units of rate and count. Reversing \(P(n|s)\) and \(P(s|n)\). Assuming independence in a population likelihood without stating it. Firing rate is not a directly observed continuous signal; it is generally a statistical model quantity or estimate. Neuropixels and head-direction-cell data are useful transfer examples, while MT remains the original example. Expected count in an observation window \(\lambda  = rT\) Homogeneous rate Poisson PMF \(P (K = k) = \lambda _{k} e^{-\lambda } /k\)! Independent increments Fano factor \(F = \operatorname{Var}(K)/E[K]\) Counts across trials under the same condition Poisson ISI density fISI \((t) = re^{-rt}\) Constant rate ISI irregularity CV = SD(ISI)/E[ISI] \(\operatorname{Mean}>0\) Independent-population likelihood \(Y P (k | \theta ) = P (k_{i} | \theta )\) i Conditional independence Maximum-likelihood decoder θb = arg \(\max \ell (\theta )\) A specified encoding model Fisher information \(J = -E[\ell '' (\theta )]\) A regular differentiable model neural encoding A mapping from a stimulus or state to a response distribution. spike train A sequence of discrete spike times. raster plot A visualization of spike times arranged by trial. peri-stimulus time histogram, PSTH An average spike-rate estimate obtained by binning across trials. Fano factor Count variance divided by count mean. point process A probability model for random event times. independent increments Independence of event counts in nonoverlapping time intervals. tuning curve Expected response as a function of a stimulus parameter. likelihood Support for a stimulus or parameter after the response is observed. maximum-likelihood estimate, MLE The parameter or stimulus estimate that maximizes the likelihood. Fisher information Local sensitivity of a probability distribution to a small parameter change. A 20 ms PSTH bin contains a total of 8 spikes across 10 trials. What is the firing rate in that bin? The PSTH denominator includes both the number of trials and the bin width. Dividing only by 20 ms would yield a rate based on the count pooled across trials, not the mean rate per trial. The total observation time is \(10\times 0.020=0.20 \mathrm{s}\), so the rate is \(8/0.20=40 \mathrm{Hz}\). At a fixed stimulus, the count mean is 4 and the variance is 6. What is the Fano factor, and how should it be interpreted relative to a Poisson process? Slow state changes, uncontrolled stimulus variables, correlated inputs, and nonstationary rates can all increase count variance. Distinguishing them requires additional experiments or model comparisons. \(\mathrm{Fano}=6/4=1.5\), which is above the Poisson reference value of 1 and is called overdispersion. This number alone does not identify the underlying mechanism. A homogeneous Poisson process has rate \(r=10 \mathrm{Hz}\). What is the probability of observing zero spikes in \(T=0.2 \mathrm{s}\)? Window counts follow \(a \operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda )\) distribution, where \(\lambda\) must equal rate times time. Exponential waiting times and Poisson window counts are two views of the same process. \(\lambda =rT=2\), so \(P(N=0)=e^{-2}\approx 0.1353\). A deterministic LIF neuron receives constant current and is reset to the same \(V_{R}\) after every spike. Why does it not naturally generate exponentially distributed ISIs? The Poisson assumption is a statistical model of event generation; it does not follow automatically from the use of an integrate-and-fire neuron. Every cycle has the same initial value, input, and dynamics, so threshold is crossed after a fixed time and the ISI is nearly constant. Random ISIs require stochastic input, a fluctuating threshold, or another source of noise. Why does an accurate count model not establish that precise spike timing contains no additional information? It establishes only that counts suffice for the chosen task. To determine whether timing adds predictive information beyond counts, compare the count model with a model that retains timing on independent data. This is the distinction tested in From channel dynamics to coding observables. Worked example — Checking a proposed firing rate against the refractory period: A neuron has an absolute refractory period of at least 2 ms. A model predicts a mean of 80 spikes in a 100 ms window. Use an upper-bound calculation to decide whether the prediction is possible. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: A neuron has an absolute refractory period of at least 2 ms. A model predicts a mean of 80 spikes in a 100 ms window. Use an upper-bound calculation to decide whether the prediction is possible. An absolute refractory period of 2 ms means adjacent spikes must be separated by at least 0.002 s. The idealized maximum sustained rate is \(1/0.002=500 \mathrm{Hz}\). In 100 ms, the neuron can emit at most about \(0.1\times 500=50\) spikes. Conventions about the endpoints of the window can change this by only about one event. A predicted mean of 80 already exceeds the physical maximum, so the model is missing an essential constraint even before it is fit to data. Shortening the window should reduce the maximum event count in direct proportion to its duration. Because 100 ms is one tenth of 1 s, its upper bound is about one tenth of the per-second bound. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “From channel dynamics to coding observables”? Refractoriness and the history of gating variables impose physiological bounds on spike statistics. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “From channel dynamics to coding observables”? The response can be represented by counts, event times, or population vectors; that choice determines which questions can be answered. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “From channel dynamics to coding observables” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Refractoriness and the history of gating variables impose physiological bounds on spike statistics. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. What is the best response to the guiding question: When the question changes from “How are spikes generated?” to “What do spikes represent?”, which mechanisms still constrain the code, and which details can temporarily be compressed? This section reviews Na activation, Na inactivation, K activation, and the refractory period. These mechanisms constrain observable spike sequences: the absolute refractory period imposes a lower bound on adjacent interspike intervals, recovery of gating variables introduces history dependence, and conductances and morphology shape the stimulus-to-spike transformation. Thus, even a coding model that uses only counts cannot permit unbounded firing rates or negative counts. Compressed mechanisms remain present as boundary conditions on the statistical description. This section reviews parameters per unit area, axonal propagation, and cell diversity. Applying the same total current to cells with different areas produces different current densities, while different channel combinations produce tonic, bursting, or adapting response patterns. If multiple cell types are pooled into one “average neuron” category, count variance may reflect differences among cell types rather than intrinsic randomness within a cell. Experimental grouping is therefore a necessary step before specifying a probabilistic model. Why can concatenating all trials into one long spike train before making a histogram conceal important structure? Concatenation discards alignment to each stimulus onset and the identity of each trial. It can no longer separate time-locked changes in the mean, trial-to-trial count variability, and slow state drift, and it may create artificial intervals at concatenation boundaries. This is the distinction tested in Random-dot motion, rasters, PSTHs, and trial-to-trial variability. Worked example — Calculating both a PSTH rate and a count Fano factor: Across 10 trials, one 20 ms bin contains a total of 8 spikes. In a separate analysis of the full 200 ms window, the ten trial counts are \([1,2,3,2,2,1,4,2,1,2]\). Calculate the bin rate, the mean full-window count, the variance defined with 1/K, and the Fano factor. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Across 10 trials, one 20 ms bin contains a total of 8 spikes. In a separate analysis of the full 200 ms window, the ten trial counts are \([1,2,3,2,2,1,4,2,1,2]\). Calculate the bin rate, the mean full-window count, the variance defined with 1/K, and the Fano factor. The bin's total exposure time is \(10\times 0.020=0.20 \mathrm{s}\), so its PSTH rate is \(8/0.20=40 \mathrm{Hz}\). The full-window counts sum to 20, so \(\mu =20/10=2\). The squared deviations from the mean are \([1,0,1,0,0,1,4,0,1,0]\), whose sum is 8. Using 1/K gives variance \(8/10=0.8\). \(\mathrm{Fano}=0.8/2=0.4\), below the Poisson reference. An unbiased sample variance would instead use denominator K−1, so the convention must be reported. An average of 2 spikes over the full 200 ms window corresponds to 10 Hz. This does not conflict with a 40 Hz instantaneous bin because the PSTH can vary over time. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Random-dot motion, rasters, PSTHs, and trial-to-trial variability”? A raster retains individual-trial events; a PSTH estimates the time-varying rate averaged across trials. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Random-dot motion, rasters, PSTHs, and trial-to-trial variability”? The PSTH denominator is trial count times bin duration in seconds, giving a result in Hz. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Random-dot motion, rasters, PSTHs, and trial-to-trial variability” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The PSTH denominator is trial count times bin duration in seconds, giving a result in Hz. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Constructing a PSTH rate estimate from total bin counts”? Counts are dimensionless, so division by \(K\Delta t\) gives \(s^{-1}=\mathrm{Hz}\). The standard-deviation expression also reduces to Hz. As K grows, fluctuations in the estimate shrink as \(1/\sqrt K\). Making \(\Delta t\) too small leaves most bins empty and increases variance, although temporal resolution improves. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does taking the logarithm of a product of likelihood terms leave the location of the maximum-likelihood estimate unchanged? The natural logarithm is strictly increasing on positive numbers, so it preserves the ordering of candidate likelihoods. Taking logs only changes products into sums and improves numerical stability; it does not change the maximizer. This is the distinction tested in Poisson coding, maximum likelihood, and Fisher curvature. Worked example — Estimating a constant Poisson rate from repeated counts: The same condition is presented 5 times. Each trial lasts \(T=0.2 \mathrm{s}\), and the counts are \([1,3,2,0,4]\). Assuming a shared constant Poisson rate r, find its maximum-likelihood estimate and the probability of zero spikes in one 0.2 s window. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: The same condition is presented 5 times. Each trial lasts \(T=0.2 \mathrm{s}\), and the counts are \([1,3,2,0,4]\). Assuming a shared constant Poisson rate r, find its maximum-likelihood estimate and the probability of zero spikes in one 0.2 s window. The total count is \(1+3+2+0+4=10\), and the total exposure is \(5\times 0.2=1.0 \mathrm{s}\). The part of the log-likelihood that depends on r is \(10 \ln r-r\cdot 1.0\), whose first derivative is 10/r−1.0. Setting the derivative to zero gives \(\hat{r}=10 \mathrm{Hz}\). Because the second derivative is \(-10/r^{2}<0\), this is a maximum. For one 0.2 s window, the mean is \(\lambda =\hat{r} T=2\), so \(P(N=0)=e^{-2}\approx 0.1353\). Because the total observation time is exactly 1 second and the total count is 10, the intuitive count rate is 10 Hz. With \(\lambda =2\), the zero-count probability should be less than \(e^{-1}\). Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Poisson coding, maximum likelihood, and Fisher curvature”? A homogeneous Poisson process produces both Poisson window counts and exponential ISIs. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Poisson coding, maximum likelihood, and Fisher curvature”? An encoding model specifies \(P(n|s)\); decoding holds the response fixed and compares likelihoods across s. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Poisson coding, maximum likelihood, and Fisher curvature” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? For an independent population, the log-likelihood is the sum of the evidence contributed by individual neurons. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Fisher information for a population of independent Poisson neurons”? \(T\cdot (\mathrm{Hz}/\theta )^{2}/\mathrm{Hz}=(s\cdot s^{-1})/\theta ^{2}=1/\theta ^{2}\), the required units of information. If every \(f_{i}'(\theta )=0\), mean responses are locally unchanged by the stimulus and \(J=0\). Replicating independent neurons with identical tuning makes J proportional to their number. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Information-compression chain from voltage traces to a PSTH”? Threshold detection first compresses a continuous trace into event times. The raster retains each trial's event structure, whereas the PSTH divides the total spike count in a time bin by \(K\Delta t\), yielding a rate averaged across trials while discarding trial identity. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “neural encoding” mean in this lecture? neural encoding: A mapping from a stimulus or state to a response distribution. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “spike train” mean in this lecture? spike train: A sequence of discrete spike times. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “raster plot” mean in this lecture? raster plot: A visualization of spike times arranged by trial. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “peri-stimulus time histogram, PSTH” mean in this lecture? peri-stimulus time histogram, PSTH: An average spike-rate estimate obtained by binning across trials. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “Fano factor” mean in this lecture? Fano factor: Count variance divided by count mean. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “point process” mean in this lecture? point process: A probability model for random event times. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “independent increments” mean in this lecture? independent increments: Independence of event counts in nonoverlapping time intervals. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “tuning curve” mean in this lecture? tuning curve: Expected response as a function of a stimulus parameter. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “likelihood” mean in this lecture? likelihood: Support for a stimulus or parameter after the response is observed. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “Expected count in an observation window” be used? Expected count in an observation window: \(\lambda  = rT\). Homogeneous rate This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Poisson PMF” be used? Poisson PMF: \(P (K = k) = \lambda _{k} e^{-\lambda } /k\)!. Independent increments This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Fano factor” be used? Fano factor: \(F = \operatorname{Var}(K)/E[K]\). Counts across trials under the same condition This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Poisson ISI density” be used? Poisson ISI density: fISI \((t) = re^{-rt}\). Constant rate This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “ISI irregularity” be used? ISI irregularity: CV = SD(ISI)/E[ISI]. \(\operatorname{Mean}>0\) This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Independent-population likelihood” be used? Independent-population likelihood: \(Y P (k | \theta ) = P (k_{i} | \theta )\) i. Conditional independence This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Maximum-likelihood decoder” be used? Maximum-likelihood decoder: θb = arg \(\max \ell (\theta )\). A specified encoding model This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Fisher information” be used? Fisher information: \(J = -E[\ell '' (\theta )]\). A regular differentiable model This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written.

title: Lecture 7: Neural Coding II: Population Decoding, Fisher Information, and Bayes
subtitle: Neural Coding II: Population Decoding, Fisher Information, and Bayes
text: Neural Coding II: Population Decoding, Fisher Information, and Bayes Population likelihood → Fisher information → CRLB → noise covariance → information limitation → bias–variance tradeoff Explain how a population with diverse preferred directions resolves ambiguities in single-neuron tuning, and write the population Poisson likelihood. Derive Fisher information from the population log-likelihood, distinguishing the contributions of neuron count N, observation time T, and tuning-curve shape. State the assumptions of the Cramér–Rao lower bound and relate perceptual error to neural decoding precision without treating the bound as achieved performance. Calculate the variance of pooled correlated counts, use the inverse covariance matrix to explain harmful noise along the signal direction, and distinguish the existence of correlation from a limitation on information. Derive the bias–variance decomposition and explain how biased or Bayesian decoders can trade prior-induced bias for reduced variance. A single tuning curve often gives similar rates for multiple stimuli, but a population response pattern can resolve the ambiguity. Under ideal assumptions of independent Poisson neurons and uniformly distributed preferred directions, Fisher information grows linearly with N and T. Noise correlations, decoder mismatch, and behavioral constraints can make real-population performance saturate. A Bayesian prior trades a controlled bias for reduced variance. Treating the CRLB as the observed error of every decoder instead of a conditional lower bound. Assuming that positive correlation is always harmful and negative correlation is always beneficial. Conflating three levels: the encoding distribution, the decoding algorithm, and behavior. Automatically attributing saturation of Fisher information to one biological mechanism. Ignoring the modified bound for a biased decoder. Treating a prior as extra data instead of an assumption about stimulus frequency or structure. Keep three levels explicit: the neural encoding distribution, the decoder algorithm, and behavioral performance. The existence of correlation does not establish whether a particular decoder uses or ignores it. Fisher information of an independent Poisson population \(X J =T (f_{i}' )2 /f_{i} i\) Counts are independent Unbiased \(CRLB \operatorname{Var}(\hat{\theta }) \ge  1/J\) Regularity and unbiasedness Noise covariance \(C_{ij} = \operatorname{Cov}(r_{i}, r_{j} )\) Residuals across trials at a fixed stimulus Pearson noise correlation \(\rho i_{j} = C_{ij} /(\sigma _{i} \sigma _{j} )\) Nonzero variances Mahalanobis separation d2M = ∆µT C −1 ∆µ C is positive definite Bias–variance decomposition M \(SE = \operatorname{Var} +b_{2}\) Scalar estimator Bayesian decoding \(P (s|n) \propto  P (n|s)P (s)\) The posterior is properly normalized population code The joint response pattern of multiple neurons. Cramér-Rao lower bound An information-theoretic lower bound on the variance of an unbiased estimator under regularity conditions. noise correlation Correlation of trial residuals at a fixed stimulus. signal correlation Similarity of tuning curves across stimuli. covariance matrix A matrix containing the variance of each dimension and every pairwise covariance. Mahalanobis distance Distance normalized by the noise covariance. information-limiting correlation Shared noise along the stimulus-signal direction that cannot be removed by averaging a larger population. suboptimal decoder A readout that does not use all information available in the encoding distribution. bias The difference between an estimator's mean and the true value. regularization A constraint or prior used to reduce variance or complexity. One neuron has the same mean rate for directions \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). Why might a population still distinguish the two directions? Decoding uses the conditional distribution of the entire response vector; it does not classify each neuron separately and then take a vote. Other neurons with different preferred directions can have different mean response patterns under \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). The resulting joint response vectors have different probabilities, so the population pattern resolves the single-neuron degeneracy. If the number of independent neurons with identical tuning shapes increases from N to 4N while everything else remains fixed, how do Fisher information and asymptotic standard deviation scale? Independent evidence adds, so \(J\propto N\). Error is measured on the standard-deviation scale, the square root of variance, and therefore improves only as \(\sqrt N\). Information increases by a factor of 4, while standard deviation shrinks as \(1/\sqrt J\) to 1/2 of its original value. Why is the statement “The neurons are positively correlated, so coding information must decrease” incorrect? Use \(\mu '^{\mathrm{T}}C^{-1}\mu '\) or an equivalent geometric analysis; the sign of one Pearson correlation coefficient is not enough. Whether a correlation is harmful depends on the alignment of covariance with the direction in which the stimulus changes the mean response. Positive-correlated noise that lies mainly orthogonal to the signal direction can have little effect. An estimator has bias \(b=-0.3\) and variance 0.5. What is its MSE? Bias is squared before it is added to variance. Positive and negative biases contribute equally to MSE, although the direction remains scientifically meaningful. \(MSE=\operatorname{Var}+b^{2}=0.5+0.09=0.59\). Why need a high firing rate at the peak of a tuning curve not contribute the greatest local Fisher information? The Poisson information term is \((f')^{2}/f\). Although f is large at the peak, the slope f' is generally zero, so the mean barely changes under an infinitesimal stimulus change and local information may be zero. This is the distinction tested in Population decoding and the N and T scaling of Fisher information. Worked example — A numerical comparison of information scaling: Suppose the mean shape constant contributed by one uniformly tuned neuron is \(j_{f}=0.8 \mathrm{rad}^{-2}s^{-1}\). For \(N=100\) and \(T=0.5 \mathrm{s}\), calculate J and the asymptotic standard deviation; then increase N to 400. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Suppose the mean shape constant contributed by one uniformly tuned neuron is \(j_{f}=0.8 \mathrm{rad}^{-2}s^{-1}\). For \(N=100\) and \(T=0.5 \mathrm{s}\), calculate J and the asymptotic standard deviation; then increase N to 400. Under the original condition, \(J=NTj_{f}=100\times 0.5\times 0.8=40 \mathrm{rad}^{-2}\). The standard deviation is approximately \(1/\sqrt 40\approx 0.1581 \mathrm{rad}\), or about 9.06°. For \(N=400\), \(J=400\times 0.5\times 0.8=160 \mathrm{rad}^{-2}\). The new standard deviation is \(1/\sqrt 160\approx 0.0791 \mathrm{rad}\approx 4.53\)°, exactly half the original value. Quadrupling neuron count halves standard deviation, consistent with square-root scaling. The units change from \(\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\) for information to rad for error. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Population decoding and the N and T scaling of Fisher information”? A population resolves single-neuron tuning ambiguity through the joint pattern of neurons with different preferred directions. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Population decoding and the N and T scaling of Fisher information”? Independent Poisson information is \(T\sum _i(f_{i}')^{2}/f_{i}\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Population decoding and the N and T scaling of Fisher information” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? A population resolves single-neuron tuning ambiguity through the joint pattern of neurons with different preferred directions. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “From a sum over uniformly spaced preferred directions to a continuous integral”? If \(\theta\) is measured in radians, \(j_{f}\) has units \(\mathrm{Hz}/\mathrm{rad}^{2}\). Multiplication by T seconds and N gives \(1/\mathrm{rad}^{2}\), whose inverse square root has units rad. If tuning is constant, \(f'=0\) and \(j_{f}=0\). When N is small, the integral approximation can depend on direction and the discrete sum must be retained. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: How do neurons with translated tuning curves jointly localize a stimulus, and why do adding neurons and lengthening the observation time increase information in the same way? A single bell-shaped tuning curve can give the same firing rate on either side of its peak, so count \(k_{i}\) may have equal likelihood under directions \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). Neuron i in a population has preferred direction \(\theta _{i}\) and tuning \(f_{i}(\theta )=f(\theta -\theta _{i})\). Although the two stimuli are degenerate for one neuron, they produce different count patterns across other neurons. The joint probability compares the entire pattern, allowing distributed preferences to resolve a single neuron's ambiguity. In a window T, the independent Poisson likelihood is Π_i[(f_i(θ)T)^{k_i}e^{−f_i(θ)T}/k_i!]. Taking the logarithm converts the product to a sum, whose derivative is the score. At the true \(\theta\), the negative expected second derivative contains terms with \(f_{i}''\) that vanish because \(E[k_{i}]=f_{i}T\), leaving \(J(\theta )=T\sum _i[f_{i}'(\theta )]^{2}/f_{i}(\theta )\). Each neuron's local evidence is nonnegative and the contributions add. Why does saturation of performance in a simple left-versus-right pooling model not prove that the Fisher information of the full neural population saturates? Simple pooling uses only one projection of response space and may discard other decodable directions. To determine whether the population itself is information-limited, analyze the full covariance and mean derivative or compare stronger decoders. This is the distinction tested in The CRLB, noise correlations, and information limits. Worked example — Quantifying the pooling floor caused by shared fluctuations: There are \(N=100\) similar neurons, each with count variance \(\sigma ^{2}=4\), and every pair has correlation \(c=0.1\). Calculate the variance of their pool average and compare it with the independent case. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: There are \(N=100\) similar neurons, each with count variance \(\sigma ^{2}=4\), and every pair has correlation \(c=0.1\). Calculate the variance of their pool average and compare it with the independent case. The shared term is \(c\sigma ^{2}=0.1\times 4=0.4\). The averageable term is \((1-c)\sigma ^{2}/N=0.9\times 4/100=0.036\). The total variance is \(0.4+0.036=0.436\). If \(c=0\), the variance is only \(4/100=0.04\). The correlated model is about 10.9 times larger. The result should be less than the single-neuron variance 4 but greater than the independent average 0.04; 0.436 satisfies both checks. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “The CRLB, noise correlations, and information limits”? The CRLB is a variance lower bound under explicit regularity and unbiasedness assumptions, not an automatic equality with observed error. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “The CRLB, noise correlations, and information limits”? The variance of an equicorrelated pool average retains the \(c\sigma ^{2}\) term, so simple pooling can saturate as N grows. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “The CRLB, noise correlations, and information limits” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The variance of an equicorrelated pool average retains the \(c\sigma ^{2}\) term, so simple pooling can saturate as N grows. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Variance of the average of equicorrelated residuals after fixing the stimulus”? \(\epsilon\), k, and R are counts; c is dimensionless, while \(\sigma ^{2}\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(R|s)\) have units of counts squared. When \(c=0\), variance falls as 1/N; when \(N=1\), it reduces to \(\sigma ^{2}\); and with fixed \(c>0\), a floor remains as N becomes large. If different stimuli are pooled before correlation is calculated, the result includes both signal and noise and cannot be substituted into this expression. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does a reasonable Bayesian posterior usually depend less on the prior when data are highly reliable? Reliable data produce a sharp likelihood whose relative variation in the posterior product greatly exceeds that of a smooth prior. After normalization, probability concentrates near the likelihood peak, and the prior makes only a small correction. This is the distinction tested in Biased decoding, bias–variance tradeoffs, and Bayesian priors. Worked example — When does shrinkage reduce MSE?: For an observation X at true \(s_{0}=2\), suppose \(E[X]=2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=1\). Compare the unbiased estimate \(\hat{s}=X\) with the shrinkage estimate \(\widetilde{s}=0.8X\) in terms of bias, variance, and MSE. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: For an observation X at true \(s_{0}=2\), suppose \(E[X]=2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=1\). Compare the unbiased estimate \(\hat{s}=X\) with the shrinkage estimate \(\widetilde{s}=0.8X\) in terms of bias, variance, and MSE. The unbiased estimate has bias 0 and variance 1, so \(MSE=1\). The shrinkage estimate has \(\operatorname{mean} 0.8\times 2=1.6\), bias \(1.6-2=-0.4\), and squared bias 0.16. Scaling by a constant changes the variance to \(0.8^{2}\times 1=0.64\). For the shrinkage estimate, \(MSE=0.64+0.16=0.80\), which is 0.20 lower than 1. If \(s_{0}\) becomes very large, squared bias \((0.2s_{0})^{2}\) grows, so shrinkage need not remain better than the unbiased estimate. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Biased decoding, bias–variance tradeoffs, and Bayesian priors”? \(MSE=\mathrm{variance}+squared\) bias; low variance alone does not imply accurate estimation. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Biased decoding, bias–variance tradeoffs, and Bayesian priors”? The biased CRLB includes the derivative of bias and permits response compression to exchange bias for lower variance. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Biased decoding, bias–variance tradeoffs, and Bayesian priors” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? A Bayesian posterior is likelihood times prior; MAP and posterior mean correspond to different loss choices. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “The bias–variance decomposition”? Variance, MSE, and \(b^{2}\) all have squared stimulus units and can therefore be added. When \(b=0\), the estimator is unbiased and MSE=variance. A constant estimator has zero variance, but unless the constant equals \(s_{0}\), its MSE remains \(b^{2}\). These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Fisher information in an independent Poisson population scales with NT”? For uniform tuning and conditional independence, \(J\approx NTj_{f}\).
