Thus, with tuning shape fixed, doubling either neuron count N or observation time T doubles information, whereas asymptotic error standard deviation shrinks only as \(1/\sqrt{NT}\). Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “population code” mean in this lecture? population code: The joint response pattern of multiple neurons. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “Cramér-Rao lower bound” mean in this lecture? Cramér-Rao lower bound: An information-theoretic lower bound on the variance of an unbiased estimator under regularity conditions. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “noise correlation” mean in this lecture? noise correlation: Correlation of trial residuals at a fixed stimulus. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “signal correlation” mean in this lecture? signal correlation: Similarity of tuning curves across stimuli. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “covariance matrix” mean in this lecture? covariance matrix: A matrix containing the variance of each dimension and every pairwise covariance. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “Mahalanobis distance” mean in this lecture? Mahalanobis distance: Distance normalized by the noise covariance. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “information-limiting correlation” mean in this lecture? information-limiting correlation: Shared noise along the stimulus-signal direction that cannot be removed by averaging a larger population. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “suboptimal decoder” mean in this lecture? suboptimal decoder: A readout that does not use all information available in the encoding distribution. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “bias” mean in this lecture? bias: The difference between an estimator's mean and the true value. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “Fisher information of an independent Poisson population” be used? Fisher information of an independent Poisson population: \(X J =T (f_{i}' )2 /f_{i} i\). Counts are independent This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Unbiased CRLB” be used? Unbiased CRLB: \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\theta }) \ge  1/J\). Regularity and unbiasedness This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Noise covariance” be used? Noise covariance: \(C_{ij} = \operatorname{Cov}(r_{i}, r_{j} )\). Residuals across trials at a fixed stimulus This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Pearson noise correlation” be used? Pearson noise correlation: \(\rho i_{j} = C_{ij} /(\sigma _{i} \sigma _{j} )\). Nonzero variances This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Mahalanobis separation” be used? Mahalanobis separation: d2M = ∆µT C −1 ∆µ. C is positive definite This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Bias–variance decomposition” be used? Bias–variance decomposition: M \(SE = \operatorname{Var} +b_{2}\). Scalar estimator This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Bayesian decoding” be used? Bayesian decoding: \(P (s|n) \propto  P (n|s)P (s)\). The posterior is properly normalized This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written.

title: Lecture 8: Neural Networks I: Spikes, Convolution, and E/I Balance
subtitle: Neural Networks I: Spikes, Convolution, and E/I Balance
text: Neural Networks I: Spikes, Convolution, and E/I Balance Spike-train δ-sum → kernel / convolution → coupled network → \(\operatorname{Poisson} E/I\) input → mean versus variance → failure of 1/N scaling Interpret the direction and shape of recurrent weights \(W_{ij}\) and input weights \(U_{ij}\), and explain their roles in coupled membrane equations. Represent a spike train as a sum of Dirac \(\delta\) functions, then use convolution to turn discrete spikes into synaptic input with a time course. Calculate the mean and variance of the total charge delivered by independent excitatory and inhibitory Poisson inputs within a finite time window. Compare the large-network scalings \(W\sim 1/N\) and \(W\sim 1/\sqrt N\), explaining why the former suppresses fluctuations and why the latter requires strong E/I cancellation. Distinguish excitation-dominated, inhibition-dominated, and balanced fluctuation-driven firing from voltage trajectories, and explain why dynamic balance does not mean that the current is exactly zero at every instant. The Dirac delta makes each spike time an integrable event, and convolution of a synaptic kernel with a spike train produces a continuous current. In the large-N limit, a proposed weight scaling must be checked for both mean and variance. Scaling as 1/N keeps the mean finite but suppresses fluctuations to zero. Balanced \(1/\sqrt N\) scaling lets large excitation and inhibition cancel in the mean while preserving \(O(1)\) fluctuations. Treating \(\delta (t)\) as an ordinary infinite number at \(t=0\). Reversing the time direction of \(K(t-t')\) and \(K(t')\) in a convolution. Forgetting to square the weight when calculating variance. Forgetting that inhibition contributes negatively to the mean but positively to the variance. Checking only mean scaling and not variance scaling. Interpreting E/I balance as exact equality of excitation and inhibition at every instant. The scaling derivations in this lecture are easy to distort by skipping steps. Calculate mean and variance separately and state the independence assumption explicitly. Distributional representation of a spike train ∆\((t) = \delta (t - t_{k} )\) k Defined through integration Synaptic filtering (K ∗ ∆)\((t) = K(t - t' )\)∆\((t' )dt'\) For causal K, depends only on the past Variance of an independent sum ∑ ∑ Var( a i Xi ) = a2i \(\operatorname{Var}(X_{i} )\) The \(X_{i}\) are independent Weak mean-field weights \(W \sim  1/N\) \(\mathrm{Variance}\to 0\) under independence Balanced-network scaling \(W \sim  1/ N E/I\) cancellation is required Balanced net \(\operatorname{mean} E[QE + QI ] = O(1)\) Large signed currents cancel Dirac delta A generalized function, or distribution, that samples a function under integration. convolution An operation that shifts a kernel across the input history, weights it, and sums the result. synaptic kernel The time-dependent response caused by one presynaptic spike. recurrent weight The connection strength from neuron \(j\to i\) within a network. input weight The connection from an external input neuron→recurrent-network neuron. excitation-inhibition balance A state in which large excitatory and inhibitory currents approximately cancel in their means. dynamic balance Balance generated online by recurrent feedback rather than imposed as moment-by-moment equality. order of magnitude The leading scaling as N grows, such as \(O(1)\) or \(O(\sqrt N)\). irregular spiking Spike timing with highly variable ISIs that is approximately Poisson-like. If \(W_{ij}\) denotes \(j\to i\) and the voltage vector of N network neurons is V, does the input to neuron i use row i or column i of W? Fixing receiver i while varying sender index j selects incoming connections. Transposing the convention would mistake outgoing connectivity for incoming connectivity. Neuron i receives input from every j, so it uses row i of W and sums along j. For spike train \(\Delta (t)=\delta (t-1)+\delta (t-3)\), what is the convolution \(K*\Delta\) at \(t=4\)? The sifting property of \(\delta\) converts a convolution integral into a sum over events. If the kernel is causal, future spikes make no contribution. It is \(K(4-1)+K(4-3)=K(3)+K(1)\): every preceding spike contributes the kernel evaluated at its elapsed time. There are N independent Poisson inputs, each with weight W. How do the mean and variance of the total input scale with N and W? Variance depends on squared weight. This is why the 1/N and \(1/\sqrt N\) scalings have different fluctuation limits. The mean scales as NW, the variance as \(NW^{2}\), and the standard deviation as √N|W|. Why do trial-to-trial fluctuations in Poisson input disappear as \(N\to \infty\) when \(W\sim 1/N\)? The downstream neuron receives an almost deterministic mean drive, so this limit is not ideal for producing Poisson-like irregular spiking. The total variance is \(NW^{2}\sim N/N^{2}=1/N\to 0\), even though the total mean remains finite because \(NW\sim 1\). Why should \(\delta (t_{k})\) not be treated as an infinite number that must be stored directly in code? \(\delta\) is defined by how it acts under integration. Numerical implementations usually store event indices and add a discrete kernel afterward, or approximate the event with area 1 in a finite bin. Storing infinity directly would break units and arithmetic. This is the distinction tested in Coupled networks, \(\delta\) spike trains, and synaptic convolution. Worked example — Superposition of exponential kernels from two spikes: Spikes occur at 1 ms and 3 ms. This example calculates only the kernel shape, using the dimensionless, peak-normalized causal kernel \(K(u)=e^{-u/2 ms}H(u)\); an external weight supplies the physical current amplitude. Find the dimensionless total kernel response at \(t=2 \mathrm{ms}\) and 4 ms. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Spikes occur at 1 ms and 3 ms. This example calculates only the kernel shape, using the dimensionless, peak-normalized causal kernel \(K(u)=e^{-u/2 ms}H(u)\); an external weight supplies the physical current amplitude. Find the dimensionless total kernel response at \(t=2 \mathrm{ms}\) and 4 ms. At \(t=2 \mathrm{ms}\), the delay from the 1 ms spike is 1 ms, contributing \(e^{-1/2}\approx 0.6065\). The 3 ms spike has not yet occurred and contributes 0. Thus the total response at \(t=2 \mathrm{ms}\) is approximately 0.6065. At \(t=4 \mathrm{ms}\), the two delays are 3 ms and 1 ms, contributing \(e^{-3/2}\approx 0.2231\) and \(e^{-1/2}\approx 0.6065\). Adding them gives \(0.2231+0.6065=0.8296\). After the second spike, the total response can rise; each individual exponential contribution is at most 1, its value at the event. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Coupled networks, \(\delta\) spike trains, and synaptic convolution”? The first index of \(W_{ij}\) is receiver i; the second is sender j. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Coupled networks, \(\delta\) spike trains, and synaptic convolution”? A \(\delta\) spike train is an event distribution that becomes an ordinary time process after convolution with a kernel. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Coupled networks, \(\delta\) spike trains, and synaptic convolution” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The first index of \(W_{ij}\) is receiver i; the second is sender j. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Using the sifting property of \(\delta\) to reduce a convolution to a sum of kernels”? \(\Delta\) has units 1/s, while the convolution integral contributes dt' with units s, so \(K_{s}*\Delta\) has the same units as \(K_{s}\). Multiplication by W must then produce the current units required by the membrane equation. With no spikes, the sum is empty and the response is zero. As the kernel approaches \(\delta\), the convolution approaches the unsmoothed spike train. Responses add in amplitude when identical spikes coincide. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: How can a consistent index and convolution notation incorporate the complete spike history of every neuron into N coupled membrane equations? The network contains N interconnected neurons and M external inputs. \(W_{ij}\) is the recurrent weight \(j\to i\), and \(U_{ij}\) is the weight from external input j→network neuron i. For each i, the membrane equation contains leak, every network sender, and every external sender. Whether diagonal entries of W allow self-connections is a modeling choice. A network is recurrent when W contains feedback paths, not because of where nodes happen to be drawn. The spike train of neuron j is \(\Delta _{j}(t)=\sum _k\delta (t-t_{k}^{(j)})\). The area of \(\delta\) is 1, so for any smooth g, \(\int \delta (t-t_{k})g(t)dt=g(t_{k})\). Event times \(t_{k}\) are preserved while waveform details are omitted. If time is measured in seconds, \(\Delta\) has units \(s^{-1}\) and cannot be sampled directly as a finite current value. Why does inhibition enter the mean with a negative sign but still enter the independent variance with a positive sign? Variance measures squared deviations from the mean. Multiplication by −W only reverses the direction of a fluctuation; its squared magnitude remains \(W^{2}\), so independent uncertainty from both excitation and inhibition increases total variance. This is the distinction tested in Mean, variance, and the failure of 1/N scaling for stochastic E/I input. Worked example — Fluctuations under 1/N scaling with ten thousand inputs: Let \(N_{E}=N_{I}=10000\), \(r_{E}=r_{I}=10 \mathrm{Hz}\), \(\Delta t=1 \mathrm{ms}\), and \(W_{E}=W_{I}=1/N\) in arbitrary units. Calculate each population's mean magnitude, the net mean, total variance, and standard deviation. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(N_{E}=N_{I}=10000\), \(r_{E}=r_{I}=10 \mathrm{Hz}\), \(\Delta t=1 \mathrm{ms}\), and \(W_{E}=W_{I}=1/N\) in arbitrary units. Calculate each population's mean magnitude, the net mean, total variance, and standard deviation. \(W=1/10000=10^{-4}\). The mean of either population is NWr\(\Delta t=10000\cdot 10^{-4}\cdot 10\cdot 0.001=0.01\). E/I symmetry makes the net \(\operatorname{mean} 0.01-0.01=0\). The variance of either population is \(N W^{2}\) \(r\Delta t=10000\cdot 10^{-8}\cdot 10\cdot 0.001=10^{-6}\). Total variance is \(2\times 10^{-6}\), and standard deviation is \(\operatorname{sqrt}(2\times 10^{-6})\approx 0.001414\). Variance must remain positive even when E/I means cancel exactly. The standard deviation is about 14% of the single-population \(\operatorname{mean} 0.01\). Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Mean, variance, and the failure of 1/N scaling for stochastic E/I input”? The E/I mean is a signed difference, whereas independent variances add through squared weights. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Mean, variance, and the failure of 1/N scaling for stochastic E/I input”? With \(W\sim 1/N\), the mean is \(O(1)\) and the variance is \(O(1/N)\), so stochastic fluctuations vanish at large N. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Mean, variance, and the failure of 1/N scaling for stochastic E/I input” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? With \(W\sim 1/N\), the mean is \(O(1)\) and the variance is \(O(1/N)\), so stochastic fluctuations vanish at large N. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Mean and variance of convergent Poisson input”? If W is charge per spike, Q is charge. Because \(r\Delta t\) is dimensionless, the mean has units of charge and the variance has units of charge squared. When \(N_{E}=N_{I}\), \(W_{E}=W_{I}\), and \(r_{E}=r_{I}\), the mean is zero but the variance is the sum of two positive population contributions. As \(N\to \infty\) with \(W\sim 1/N\), this variance approaches zero. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why is a net input mean near zero insufficient evidence that the network is in a strongly balanced state? Weak inputs can also give zero net mean. Strong balance additionally requires large separate E and I means that cancel at leading order, finite net variance, and the predicted scaling as connectivity changes. This is the distinction tested in Strong \(1/\sqrt N\) coupling, E/I balance, and irregular spiking. Worked example — Balancing the same ten thousand inputs under \(1/\sqrt N\) scaling: Continue with \(N_{E}=N_{I}=10000\), \(r=10 \mathrm{Hz}\), and \(\Delta t=1 \mathrm{ms}\), but set \(W=1/\sqrt N=0.01\). The E/I means are exactly equal. Calculate each population mean, net mean, total variance, and standard deviation. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Continue with \(N_{E}=N_{I}=10000\), \(r=10 \mathrm{Hz}\), and \(\Delta t=1 \mathrm{ms}\), but set \(W=1/\sqrt N=0.01\). The E/I means are exactly equal. Calculate each population mean, net mean, total variance, and standard deviation. The mean of either population is \(10000\cdot 0.01\cdot 10\cdot 0.001=1\). By symmetry the net mean is \(1-1=0\), but each term is 100 times larger than its value 0.01 under 1/N scaling. The variance of either population is \(10000\cdot 0.01^{2}\cdot 10\cdot 0.001=0.01\). Total variance is 0.02, and standard deviation is \(\operatorname{sqrt}(0.02)\approx 0.1414\), remaining finite to leading order as N changes. Changing from 1/N to \(1/\sqrt N\) makes a single weight 100 times larger and variance 10000 times larger, from \(2\times 10^{-6}\) to 0.02. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Strong \(1/\sqrt N\) coupling, E/I balance, and irregular spiking”? \(W\sim 1/\sqrt N\) keeps variance \(O(1)\) but makes the separate E and I means \(O(\sqrt N)\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Strong \(1/\sqrt N\) coupling, E/I balance, and irregular spiking”? Balance cancels the leading-order mean while retaining instantaneous fluctuations; it is not zero current at every moment. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Strong \(1/\sqrt N\) coupling, E/I balance, and irregular spiking” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Recurrent feedback can dynamically adjust E/I rates and place a strongly coupled network in an irregular balanced state. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Finite variance and the balance condition under \(1/\sqrt N\) scaling”? a and N are dimensionless; \(w/\sqrt N\) inherits the units of a single-synapse weight. Mean and variance units are as in the preceding module. If the balance difference is a fixed nonzero constant, the net mean diverges as \(\sqrt N\). If the weights are changed to 1/N, the variance again approaches zero. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “A strongly coupled network retains finite fluctuations after balance”? Under \(W\sim 1/\sqrt N\), the conditional means of excitatory and inhibitory input are each \(O(\sqrt N)\) and must cancel at leading order. Their instantaneous difference remains \(O(1)\), so net input is not zero at every instant and can continue to drive irregular spiking. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “Dirac delta” mean in this lecture? Dirac delta: A generalized function, or distribution, that samples a function under integration. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “convolution” mean in this lecture? convolution: An operation that shifts a kernel across the input history, weights it, and sums the result. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “synaptic kernel” mean in this lecture? synaptic kernel: The time-dependent response caused by one presynaptic spike. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “recurrent weight” mean in this lecture? recurrent weight: The connection strength from neuron \(j\to i\) within a network. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “input weight” mean in this lecture? input weight: The connection from an external input neuron→recurrent-network neuron. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “excitation-inhibition balance” mean in this lecture? excitation-inhibition balance: A state in which large excitatory and inhibitory currents approximately cancel in their means. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “dynamic balance” mean in this lecture? dynamic balance: Balance generated online by recurrent feedback rather than imposed as moment-by-moment equality. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “order of magnitude” mean in this lecture? order of magnitude: The leading scaling as N grows, such as \(O(1)\) or \(O(\sqrt N)\). This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “irregular spiking” mean in this lecture? irregular spiking: Spike timing with highly variable ISIs that is approximately Poisson-like. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “Distributional representation of a spike train” be used? Distributional representation of a spike train: ∆\((t) = \delta (t - t_{k} )\) k. Defined through integration This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Synaptic filtering” be used? Synaptic filtering: (K ∗ ∆)\((t) = K(t - t' )\)∆\((t' )dt'\). For causal K, depends only on the past This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Variance of an independent sum” be used? Variance of an independent sum: ∑ ∑ Var( a i Xi ) = a2i \(\operatorname{Var}(X_{i} )\). The \(X_{i}\) are independent This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Weak mean-field weights” be used? Weak mean-field weights: \(W \sim  1/N\). \(\mathrm{Variance}\to 0\) under independence This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Balanced-network scaling” be used? Balanced-network scaling: \(W \sim  1/ N\). E/I cancellation is required This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Balanced net mean” be used? Balanced net mean: \(E[QE + QI ] = O(1)\). Large signed currents cancel This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written.

title: Lecture 9: Neural Networks II: Synaptic Dynamics and Rate Models
subtitle: Neural Networks II: Synaptic Dynamics and Rate Models
text: Neural Networks II: Synaptic Dynamics and Rate Models Integrating factor → causal exponential kernel → synaptic-current ODE → spike averaging → F-I nonlinearity → rate dynamics Use an integrating factor to derive the causal solution of \(\tau dx/dt=-x+I(t)\), and recognize it as the convolution of the input with an exponential kernel. Explain the area, time constant, and causality of a normalized exponential kernel, and calculate its response to a step or impulse input. Rewrite convolution with an exponential synapse as a first-order synaptic-current ODE, and count the 2N continuous states and discrete events in a network of N neurons. Approximate spike trains by firing rates through Poisson averaging, and distinguish the dynamical assumptions and relevant timescales of three rate models. Write the feedforward layer \(h^{(\ell )}=F(U^{(\ell )}h^{(\ell -1)})\), check weight shapes, and explain why nonlinearity prevents a multilayer composition from collapsing to one linear map. The solution of a first-order linear ODE is the causal exponential convolution of its past input; conversely, exponential convolution can be implemented by an ODE with one additional state variable. This equivalence turns a spiking network into a coupled voltage-and-current system and, under temporal averaging and timescale separation, produces rate models. Different rate-model forms make different assumptions about which variables are fast or slow and cannot be interchanged merely because they look similar. Omitting the \(1/\tau\) normalization of the exponential kernel. Conflating membrane \(\tau\), synaptic \(\tau _{s}\), and rate-response \(\tau _{r}\). Automatically equating a statistical firing-rate estimate with a dynamical rate variable. Making a fast-variable approximation without writing the derivative that is set to zero. Ignoring the biological problem of negative rates when using a tanh or linear F-I function. Conflating feedforward architecture with backpropagation training. Distinguish a statistical description of spike rate from a dynamical firing-rate variable. They are related, but they are not automatically the same object. Causal exponential kernel \(K\tau  (t) = e^{-t/\tau } H(t)/\tau \) \(\tau >0\) Linear low-pass solution \(x = K\tau  \ast  I\) The transient has been handled Exponential-synapse ODE \(\tau s\) I˙ = \(-I + u(t)\) Single-exponential kernel Instantaneous F-I approximation \(h = F(I)\) Rate response is fast Dynamic rate response \(\tau r\) \(\dot{h} = -h + F(I)\) Smooth population rate Feedforward layer h(ℓ) = F(W (ℓ) h(ℓ−1) ) Shape-compatible weights integrating factor A function that turns the left side of a first-order linear ODE into a product derivative. causal kernel A filter that is zero at negative times and depends only on past input. synaptic time constant The timescale of synaptic-current integration or decay. firing-rate response time The timescale on which a population rate approaches \(F(I)\). time-scale separation A regime in which one variable is much faster than another and can be approximately eliminated. F-I function A nonlinearity mapping input current to steady firing rate. threshold-linear Zero below threshold and increasing linearly above threshold. \(\operatorname{sigmoid} A\) smooth S-shaped function with lower and upper saturation. feedforward network An architecture in which information moves in one direction across layers without a recurrent loop. What is the integral of \(K_\tau (t)=\tau ^{-1}e^{-t/\tau }H(t)\), and what does it imply for a constant input? Under the area-normalized, unit-DC-gain convention used in this lecture, omitting \(1/\tau\) changes the kernel area from 1 to \(\tau\) and alters both weight units and steady-state gain. Peak normalization is not inherently wrong, but it requires a simultaneous redefinition of the weights. Its integral from 0 to \(\infty\) is 1. The long-run convolution output for a constant input equals the input amplitude and does not acquire an extra factor of \(\tau\). How many continuous ODE states are in a network with N membrane voltages \(V_{i}\) and N exponential synaptic currents \(I_{i}\)? The spike train is not an additional continuous state. Voltage-threshold crossings generate it, and its impulses change synaptic currents. There are 2N continuous states, plus discrete events such as thresholds, resets, and spike arrivals. If \(\tau _{s}\ll \tau _{h}\), why can the synaptic current I be approximated by its instantaneous steady state? This is a timescale-separation approximation that must be checked against parameters and trajectories; it is not license to delete a derivative under all conditions. I relaxes rapidly before h changes appreciably, making \(\tau _{s} dI/dt\) relatively small. Setting \(0=-I+Wh+Ux\) approximately gives \(I\approx Wh+Ux\). Both layers are linear, with no bias or nonlinearity: \(h=U_{1}x\) and \(y=U_{2}h\). Why does depth add no expressive power? Componentwise nonlinearities prevent this complete collapse by making different input regions experience different effective linear relations. Because \(y=U_{2}U_{1}x\), the matrix product can be defined as a single \(U_{\mathrm{eff}}\) and the entire network is still one linear map. If the kernel is incorrectly written \(e^{-t/\tau }H(t)\), omitting \(1/\tau\), what happens to the long-run response to a constant input? If the weight units from this lecture's area-normalized convention are retained, the kernel area changes from 1 to \(\tau\) and the steady-state response becomes \(\tau I_{0}\). If peak normalization is intentional, weights must instead be interpreted as amplitudes and their units checked again. This is the distinction tested in Integrating factors, causal integrals, and exponential convolution. Worked example — A step response at three times: Let \(\tau =10 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(x(0)=0\), with \(I(t)=6\) for \(t\ge 0\). Calculate \(x(10 \mathrm{ms})\), \(x(20 \mathrm{ms})\), and \(x(30 \mathrm{ms})\), and identify the long-run value. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(\tau =10 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(x(0)=0\), with \(I(t)=6\) for \(t\ge 0\). Calculate \(x(10 \mathrm{ms})\), \(x(20 \mathrm{ms})\), and \(x(30 \mathrm{ms})\), and identify the long-run value. The step response is \(x(t)=6(1-e^{-t/10 ms})\). At \(t=10 \mathrm{ms}\), \(x=6(1-e^{-1})\approx 6\times 0.6321=3.793\). At \(t=20 \mathrm{ms}\), \(x=6(1-e^{-2})\approx 5.188\); at \(t=30 \mathrm{ms}\), \(x\approx 6(1-e^{-3})=5.701\). As \(t\to \infty\), the exponential vanishes and \(x\to 6\), consistent with gain 1 for a unit-area kernel under constant input. The response should rise monotonically from 0 and remain below 6. After each \(\tau\), the remaining error is multiplied by \(e^{-1}\). Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Integrating factors, causal integrals, and exponential convolution”? An integrating factor converts the left side of a first-order linear equation into the exact derivative of a product. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Integrating factors, causal integrals, and exponential convolution”? The solution consists of an initial transient plus the causal convolution of past input. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Integrating factors, causal integrals, and exponential convolution” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? An integrating factor converts the left side of a first-order linear equation into the exact derivative of a product. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Integrating-factor solution of a first-order system with arbitrary input”? \(K_\tau\) has units 1/time, so \(K_\tau I\) dt' has the same units as I. The equation requires x and I to share units, and \(t/\tau\) is dimensionless. When \(I=0\), only exponential decay of the initial condition remains. Under a constant input, \(x\to I\) in the long run. As \(\tau \to 0\), \(x(t)\to I(t)\) when the input is sufficiently smooth. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: How does an arbitrary time-varying input leave a gradually decaying memory in a first-order linear system, and why can that memory be written as a normalized causal convolution? Consider \(\tau dx/dt=-x+I(t)\). Moving terms and dividing by \(\tau\) gives \(dx/dt+x/\tau =I(t)/\tau\). After multiplication by \(e^{t/\tau }\), the left side becomes \(d[xe^{t/\tau }]/dt\) by the product rule. Integrating from initial time \(t_{0}\) to the present t retains both an initial-condition term and a forced integral. If the system is assumed to have been stable since the distant past and the initial transient has vanished, the lower limit can instead be written as \(-\infty\). The general solution is \(x(t)=x(t_{0})e^{-(t-t_{0})/\tau }+\int _{t_{0}}^{t}\tau ^{-1}e^{-(t-t')/\tau }I(t')dt'\). The first term is memory of the initial state, and the second is the input history. Older inputs have larger elapsed time t−t' and receive exponentially smaller weight. Future times \(t'>t\) are excluded from the integration interval, so the response is causal. Why is an event-driven implementation less sensitive to dt than approximating \(\delta\) as a single bin of fixed height? An event-driven implementation applies the jump derived by integration and preserves impulse area. Unless fixed height is scaled by 1/dt, changing the time step changes both the area and total input. This is the distinction tested in ODE representation of an exponential synapse and a network with 2N states. Worked example — Synaptic jump and decay after one impulse: Let \(\tau _{s}=5 \mathrm{ms}\), the event term be \(q\delta (t)\), \(q=50 \mathrm{pA}\cdot \mathrm{ms}\), and \(I(0^{-})=0\) just before the event. Find \(I(0^{+})\) and the current at 5 ms and 10 ms. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(\tau _{s}=5 \mathrm{ms}\), the event term be \(q\delta (t)\), \(q=50 \mathrm{pA}\cdot \mathrm{ms}\), and \(I(0^{-})=0\) just before the event. Find \(I(0^{+})\) and the current at 5 ms and 10 ms. Integrate \(\tau _{s} dI/dt=-I+q\delta\) across the event. As event width approaches zero, the integral of the finite −I term vanishes, leaving \(\tau _{s}[I(0^{+})-I(0^{-})]=q\). The jump is \(q/\tau _{s}=50 \mathrm{pA}\cdot \mathrm{ms}/5 \mathrm{ms}=10 \mathrm{pA}\), so \(I(0^{+})=10 \mathrm{pA}\). With no new input after the event, \(I(t)=10e^{-t/5 ms}\) pA. \(I(5 \mathrm{ms})=10e^{-1}\approx 3.679 \mathrm{pA}\); \(I(10 \mathrm{ms})=10e^{-2}\approx 1.353 \mathrm{pA}\). After each \(\tau _{s}\), amplitude is multiplied by \(e^{-1}\). The response area \(10 \mathrm{pA}\times 5 \mathrm{ms}=50 \mathrm{pA}\cdot \mathrm{ms}\) equals q. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “ODE representation of an exponential synapse and a network with 2N states”? Convolution with a normalized exponential is equivalent to a first-order synaptic-state ODE. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “ODE representation of an exponential synapse and a network with 2N states”? N membrane voltages plus N synaptic currents give 2N continuous states, in addition to threshold events. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “ODE representation of an exponential synapse and a network with 2N states” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? N membrane voltages plus N synaptic currents give 2N continuous states, in addition to threshold events. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Proving that exponential convolution satisfies a first-order synaptic ODE”? If I is a current, S must also have units of current. When \(S=q\delta\), q has units current×time because \(\delta\) has units 1/time. When \(S=0\), I decays exponentially. Under sustained constant \(S_{0}\), \(I\to S_{0}\). When \(\tau _{s}\) is very small, I follows sufficiently smooth S rapidly. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why is \(\tau _{s}\ll \tau _{h} a\) mathematical justification for deleting the synaptic derivative, whereas “the model should be simpler” is not? The timescale ratio supplies a testable small parameter and an expected error: the fast variable relaxes before the slow variable changes. Without timescale separation, deleting the derivative changes delay, stability, and transients and must be tested against data. This is the distinction tested in From spike averaging to rate dynamics and feedforward layers. Worked example — Calculating a two-layer threshold-linear feedforward network by hand: Input \(x=(1,2)^{\mathrm{T}}\), first-layer \(U^{1}=[[1,-1],[0.5,1]]\), and \(F(z)=\max(0,z)\) applied componentwise. Second-layer weight \(U^{2}=[2,-1]\), with a linear output layer. Find the hidden layer and output, and verify all shapes. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Input \(x=(1,2)^{\mathrm{T}}\), first-layer \(U^{1}=[[1,-1],[0.5,1]]\), and \(F(z)=\max(0,z)\) applied componentwise. Second-layer weight \(U^{2}=[2,-1]\), with a linear output layer. Find the hidden layer and output, and verify all shapes. \(U^{1}\) has shape \(2\times 2\) and multiplies a \(2\times 1\) input to give a \(2\times 1\) vector: \(z^{1}=(1\cdot 1-1\cdot 2,0.5\cdot 1+1\cdot 2)^{\mathrm{T}}=(-1,2.5)^{\mathrm{T}}\). Componentwise threshold-linear activation gives \(h^{1}=(0,2.5)^{\mathrm{T}}\). \(U^{2}\) has shape \(1\times 2\) and can multiply the \(2\times 1\) hidden vector, giving scalar \(y=2\cdot 0-1\cdot 2.5=-2.5\). If the second layer also used a nonnegative threshold-linear activation, the final output would be \(\max(0,-2.5)=0\). The output nonlinearity must be stated explicitly. The inner dimensions match in every matrix multiplication. The first hidden unit's negative preactivation is clipped to zero, while the second retains 2.5. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “From spike averaging to rate dynamics and feedforward layers”? Spike-to-rate averaging gives conditional-mean dynamics and discards single-trial event fluctuations. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “From spike averaging to rate dynamics and feedforward layers”? The three rate models respectively assume fast rate, retain both timescales, or assume fast synapses. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “From spike averaging to rate dynamics and feedforward layers” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? A feedforward steady-state layer is \(h=F(Ux)\), and weight shape is determined by the widths of adjacent layers. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Deriving the common single-state form from a two-timescale rate model”? h has units Hz. If F maps current to Hz, W h and U x must have units of current; \(\tau _{h} dh/dt\) and h both have units Hz. If \(\tau _{s}\) is not sufficiently small, the quasi-steady approximation introduces phase and amplitude errors. \(W=0\) at steady state gives a feedforward layer. If F is the identity, stacked layers remain linear. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “The synaptic time constant determines how long one spike is retained”? For a peak-normalized exponential response, larger \(\tau _{s}\) makes the effect of a spike decay more slowly and preserves a longer memory. Under the area-normalized kernel \(K_{s}=\tau _{s}^{-1}e^{-t/\tau _{s}}\), the peak also changes as \(1/\tau _{s}\), so the normalization convention must be checked before curves are compared. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “integrating factor” mean in this lecture? integrating factor: A function that turns the left side of a first-order linear ODE into a product derivative. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “causal kernel” mean in this lecture? causal kernel: A filter that is zero at negative times and depends only on past input. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “synaptic time constant” mean in this lecture? synaptic time constant: The timescale of synaptic-current integration or decay. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “firing-rate response time” mean in this lecture? firing-rate response time: The timescale on which a population rate approaches \(F(I)\). This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “time-scale separation” mean in this lecture? time-scale separation: A regime in which one variable is much faster than another and can be approximately eliminated. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “F-I function” mean in this lecture? F-I function: A nonlinearity mapping input current to steady firing rate. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “threshold-linear” mean in this lecture? threshold-linear: Zero below threshold and increasing linearly above threshold. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “sigmoid” mean in this lecture? sigmoid: A smooth S-shaped function with lower and upper saturation. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “feedforward network” mean in this lecture? feedforward network: An architecture in which information moves in one direction across layers without a recurrent loop. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “Causal exponential kernel” be used? Causal exponential kernel: \(K\tau  (t) = e^{-t/\tau } H(t)/\tau \). \(\tau >0\) This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Linear low-pass solution” be used? Linear low-pass solution: \(x = K\tau  \ast  I\). The transient has been handled This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Exponential-synapse ODE” be used? Exponential-synapse ODE: \(\tau s\) I˙ = \(-I + u(t)\). Single-exponential kernel This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Instantaneous F-I approximation” be used? Instantaneous F-I approximation: \(h = F(I)\). Rate response is fast This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Dynamic rate response” be used? Dynamic rate response: \(\tau r\) \(\dot{h} = -h + F(I)\). Smooth population rate This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Feedforward layer” be used? Feedforward layer: h(ℓ) = F(W (ℓ) h(ℓ−1) ). Shape-compatible weights This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written.

title: Lecture 10: Synaptic Plasticity
subtitle: Synaptic Plasticity
text: Synaptic Plasticity \(LTP/LTD/STDP \to NMDA-\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\)→ Hebbian/covariance rule → covariance eigenmodes → positive feedback → Oja/BCM stabilization Connect Hebb's hypothesis, LTP/LTD, the STDP timing window, and the NMDA–Ca2+–AMPA mechanism into a conditional explanatory sequence, distinguishing empirical regularities from proposed mechanisms. Derive the expected weight dynamics \(E[dw/dt]=Cw\) from a centered firing-rate Hebbian rule, explaining vector orientation, matrix shape, and why mean subtraction permits depression. Use a quadratic form to prove that a covariance matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite, then use an eigenbasis to explain why the direction of greatest variance grows fastest. Compare how synaptic scaling, Oja's rule, and the BCM sliding threshold regulate overall magnitude, local normalization, and the boundary between LTP and LTD. Distinguish unsupervised, supervised, and reward-based learning, and explain how an error, reward, or reward-prediction error can gate plasticity as a third factor. This lecture joins three levels of synaptic plasticity: experimental phenomena (LTP/LTD/STDP), proposed molecular mechanisms (NMDA-dependent \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) signaling and AMPA trafficking), and abstract learning rules. A basic Hebbian rule amplifies high-variance eigenmodes of input covariance but also creates positive feedback and unbounded growth. Synaptic scaling, Oja's rule, and BCM stabilize the system through global normalization, local weight-dependent decay, and a dynamic threshold, respectively. Equating LTP/LTD with one \(NMDA/\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) pathway even though mechanisms vary across synapses and contexts. Using only coincident high activity in basic Hebbian learning and overlooking centered covariance and depression. Treating an eigenvector as a particular neuron. Claiming that covariance “must be positive” without writing a quadratic-form proof of PSD. Confusing directional selection with stabilization of the norm. Equating Hebbian learning with PCA without stating its assumptions. Assuming dopamine is the third factor in every form of reward learning. The Hebbian-learning/PCA relationship holds only under particular linear, statistical, and stabilizing assumptions; “Hebbian = PCA” is not a universal identity. STDP timing rule ∆\(w = f (t_{\mathrm{post}} - t_{\mathrm{pre}} )\) Pair-based approximation Basic rate Hebbian rule \(\tau w\) ẇi = hxi With nonnegative activity, it only potentiates Expected dynamics of centered Hebbian learning \(\tau w\) \(E[\dot{w}] = Cw\) Linear neuron with stationary inputs Positive semidefiniteness of covariance vT Cv ≥ 0 Finite second moments Hebbian eigenmode growth \(\dot{a}k = (\lambda _{k} /\tau w )\)ak Fixed C Oja's rule \(\dot{w}i \propto  hxi - h_{2}\) wi Online approximation to PCA BCM sign switch ẇi ∝ hxi (h − θ) Dynamic threshold long-term potentiation, LTP A lasting increase in synaptic efficacy. long-term depression, LTD A lasting decrease in synaptic efficacy. spike-timing-dependent plasticity, STDP An empirical rule in which weight change depends on relative pre/post spike timing. Hebbian learning A class of rules in which coordinated activity drives changes in connectivity. covariance rule A plasticity rule driven by centered pre- and postsynaptic fluctuations. principal eigenvector The direction associated with the largest covariance eigenvalue. synaptic scaling Global rescaling that maintains an overall activity or weight range. Oja rule A Hebbian PCA rule with a local normalization term. BCM rule A rule that uses a sliding postsynaptic threshold to control LTP and LTD. three-factor rule An update determined jointly by presynaptic activity, postsynaptic activity, and a third modulatory or teaching signal. Under the standard pair-based STDP convention \(\Delta t=t_{\mathrm{post}}-t_{\mathrm{pre}}\), what are the sign of \(\Delta t\) and the usual direction of weight change when the presynaptic spike precedes the postsynaptic spike? Pre-before-post timing makes glutamate release more likely to overlap with postsynaptic depolarization, promoting NMDA current and a Ca2+ signal. Bursts, neuromodulators, dendritic location, and membrane-voltage state can all reshape the window, so its sign is not a universal law. \(\Delta t>0\), and the classical window commonly assigns potentiation, so \(\Delta w>0\); this is nevertheless an empirical pattern for particular synapses, states, and paired-stimulation protocols. If h and \(x_{i}\) are always nonnegative, why can the basic Hebbian rule \(dw_{i}/dt\propto hx_{i}\) not generate LTD? Which centered quantity can become negative? If the input is above its mean while the output is below its mean, or vice versa, the two deviations have opposite signs and their product lowers the weight. A centered rule learns shared fluctuations rather than shared absolute activity. Because \(hx_{i}\ge 0\), the update can only vanish or increase the weight; the centered product \((h-E[h])(x_{i}-E[x_{i}])\) can be negative. Given a covariance matrix C and an arbitrary vector v, why can \(v^\mathrm{T} C\) v never be less than zero? Each sample is first projected onto v to produce a real number. Its square is nonnegative, and the expectation of nonnegative values is also nonnegative. The same argument shows that theoretical covariance eigenvalues are nonnegative. Because \(v^\mathrm{T} C\) \(v=E[(v^\mathrm{T}(x-\mu ))^2]\), the mean squared scalar projection. For \(C=\operatorname{diag}(4,1)\), starting the basic expected Hebbian dynamics at \(w(0)=(1,1)^\mathrm{T}\), which component becomes dominant? Does the weight norm stabilize on its own? Hebbian dynamics can select the principal covariance direction but supplies no negative feedback on magnitude. Direction selection and norm stabilization are separate problems; the latter requires scaling, Oja-like, or BCM-like mechanisms. The first component grows as \(e^{4t/\tau }\), faster than the second component's \(e^{t/\tau }\); the direction therefore approaches the first axis, while the norm remains unbounded. Why is a classical STDP window not interchangeable with a firing-rate covariance rule? STDP preserves millisecond relative timing between pre- and postsynaptic spikes, whereas a covariance rule averages activity fluctuations over a longer window. They can be related under specific statistical and timescale assumptions, but they use different state variables, experimental protocols, and levels of mechanistic interpretation. This is the distinction tested in From Synaptic Timing and Receptor Mechanisms to a Firing-Rate Hebbian Rule. Worked example — How Two Activity States Produce Potentiation or Depression: An input has \(\operatorname{mean} 5 \mathrm{Hz}\) and the postsynaptic output has \(\operatorname{mean} 10 \mathrm{Hz}\). Compare state A, \(x_{i}=8\),\(h=14\), with state B, \(x_{i}=8\),\(h=7\), taking one update to be proportional to the product of deviations. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: An input has \(\operatorname{mean} 5 \mathrm{Hz}\) and the postsynaptic output has \(\operatorname{mean} 10 \mathrm{Hz}\). Compare state A, \(x_{i}=8\),\(h=14\), with state B, \(x_{i}=8\),\(h=7\), taking one update to be proportional to the product of deviations. In state A, the deviations are +3 and +4; their product is +12, so this sample drives potentiation. In state B, the deviations are +3 and -3; their product is -9, so this sample drives depression. With the basic product \(hx_{i}\) instead, the two states give 112 and 56. Both are positive, so the rule cannot distinguish joint elevation from one variable being high and the other low. When \(x_{i}\) equals its mean exactly, its deviation is zero. No matter how large h is, that sample contributes nothing to the covariance estimate for this synapse. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “From Synaptic Timing and Receptor Mechanisms to a Firing-Rate Hebbian Rule”? LTP and LTD are experimentally observed lasting changes in efficacy; an STDP window summarizes an empirical result for a particular timing protocol. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “From Synaptic Timing and Receptor Mechanisms to a Firing-Rate Hebbian Rule”? NMDA coincidence detection requires glutamate together with postsynaptic depolarization, after which Ca2+ can influence AMPA trafficking. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “From Synaptic Timing and Receptor Mechanisms to a Firing-Rate Hebbian Rule” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? LTP and LTD are experimentally observed lasting changes in efficacy; an STDP window summarizes an empirical result for a particular timing protocol. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “From a Doubly Centered Local Update to Covariance Learning”? If both x and h are measured in Hz, the right-hand side of the unscaled rule has units \(\mathrm{Hz}^2\). A proportionality coefficient or \(\tau _{w}\) must absorb the required units so that \(dw/dt\) has units weight/time. Course equations commonly suppress this biological scale factor. If the input covariance is zero, the expected update is zero. If all activities remain positive and are not centered, the rule reduces to pure growth and cannot represent anticorrelation or LTD below baseline. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: How can a local synapse convert the timing relation between pre- and postsynaptic activity into a lasting weight change, and how can that phenomenon be abstracted into a computable rate rule? Hebb's original proposal links coincident activity to stronger connectivity. Experimentally, high-frequency stimulation of the CA3-to-CA1 pathway can induce long-term potentiation (LTP), whereas a low-frequency protocol can induce long-term depression (LTD). Both describe persistent changes in synaptic efficacy after induction. Neither is the same as transient facilitation, and a single response curve cannot establish one unique molecular mechanism. Spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) makes relative timing part of the update. Let \(\Delta t=t_{\mathrm{post}}-t_{\mathrm{pre}}\). A classical pair-based window is often written as \(\Delta w=A_{+}e^{-\Delta t/\tau _{+}}\) for \(\Delta t>0\) and \(\Delta w=-A_{-}e^{\Delta t/\tau _{-}}\) for \(\Delta t<0\). The exponential terms encode weaker local coincidence at longer intervals. A_± and τ_± depend on the experimental protocol; they are not constants shared by every brain region. Why does a negative off-diagonal covariance entry not violate positive semidefiniteness? Positive semidefiniteness constrains the variance \(v^\mathrm{T}Cv\) along every complete direction, not each matrix entry separately. Two variables can be anticorrelated, giving \(C_{ij}<0\), while every linear combination still has a variance equal to an expected square. This is the distinction tested in Covariance Geometry, the PSD Proof, and Hebbian Eigenmode Blow-Up. Worked example — Growth Rates and Direction for a Two-Dimensional Covariance: Let \(C=\operatorname{diag}(4,1)\), \(\tau _{w}=1 \mathrm{s}\), and \(w(0)=(1,1)^\mathrm{T}\). Compute the two components and their ratio at \(t=1 \mathrm{s}\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(C=\operatorname{diag}(4,1)\), \(\tau _{w}=1 \mathrm{s}\), and \(w(0)=(1,1)^\mathrm{T}\). Compute the two components and their ratio at \(t=1 \mathrm{s}\). The eigenvectors are the coordinate axes \(e_{1}\),\(e_{2}\), with eigenvalues 4 and 1, respectively. \(w_{1}(1)=e^4\approx 54.60\) and \(w_{2}(1)=e\approx 2.72\). The ratio \(w_{1}/w_{2}=e^3\approx 20.09\), so the direction is already close to the first axis; yet the norm is about 54.67, far above its initial value \(\sqrt 2\). If C is replaced by the zero matrix, both components remain 1. If its diagonal entries are exchanged, the ultimately dominant axis is exchanged as well. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Covariance Geometry, the PSD Proof, and Hebbian Eigenmode Blow-Up”? The central evidence that covariance is symmetric PSD is \(v^\mathrm{T}Cv=E[(v^\mathrm{T}(x-\mu ))^2]\ge 0\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Covariance Geometry, the PSD Proof, and Hebbian Eigenmode Blow-Up”? The eigenbasis decomposes coupled weight dynamics into independent exponential modes, with \(\lambda _{k}\) setting each mode's growth rate. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Covariance Geometry, the PSD Proof, and Hebbian Eigenmode Blow-Up” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The eigenbasis decomposes coupled weight dynamics into independent exponential modes, with \(\lambda _{k}\) setting each mode's growth rate. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “PSD, Nonnegative Eigenvalues, and the Eigenmode Solution”? The exponent \(\lambda _{k}t/\tau _{w}\) must be dimensionless. If \(\lambda\) has units \(\mathrm{input}^2\), the learning-rate coefficient in the complete model must have units reciprocal \(\mathrm{input}^2\). For \(\lambda _{k}=0\), that mode's coefficient remains at its initial value. If the two largest eigenvalues are equal, there is no unique principal direction; the outcome depends on initialization and noise. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why is it inadequate to reduce a reward-based three-factor rule to “Hebbian learning multiplied by dopamine”? The third factor may encode reward, reward-prediction error, an error signal, context, or another neuromodulatory gate. Its timing, receptors, eligibility trace, and specificity for the target weight all affect learning, so dopamine is only one candidate implementation in some systems. This is the distinction tested in Stabilizing Rules and Third-Factor Learning. Worked example — How the BCM Threshold Reverses the Sign of Change at One Synapse: Let \(x_{i}=2\) and use \(x_{i}\) \(h(h-\theta )\) as the core update. Set \(\theta =5\), compare \(h=3\) with \(h=8\), and then explain how sustained high activity changes \(\theta\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(x_{i}=2\) and use \(x_{i}\) \(h(h-\theta )\) as the core update. Set \(\theta =5\), compare \(h=3\) with \(h=8\), and then explain how sustained high activity changes \(\theta\). For \(h=3\), \(2\times 3\times (3-5)=-12\), so the update is depressive. For \(h=8\), \(2\times 8\times (8-5)=48\), so the update is potentiating. If \(h^2\) remains high over time, the sliding-threshold dynamics raise \(\theta\), making the same future h less likely to cross the potentiation threshold. The instantaneous update is zero when \(h=\theta\) or \(x_{i}=0\); changing presynaptic activity alone cannot substitute for crossing the postsynaptic threshold. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Stabilizing Rules and Third-Factor Learning”? Scaling rescales synapses globally; Oja's rule combines a Hebbian term with local weight-dependent decay; BCM uses a dynamic postsynaptic threshold. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Stabilizing Rules and Third-Factor Learning”? The connection between Oja's rule and PCA requires centered, linear, stationary input and a suitable learning rate. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Stabilizing Rules and Third-Factor Learning” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Three-factor learning supplements pre/post coactivity with an error, reward, or contextual gate. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “How an Oja Fixed Point Selects Direction and Controls Norm”? The terms \(h^2w\) and hx must have the same units. A biological rule requires proportionality constants or normalized variables to make them match; the abstract equation usually absorbs those scales into \(\eta\). If \(\lambda _{k}=0\), that direction has no statistical drive. If the input is nonstationary, conclusions based on a fixed C and a fixed principal component no longer apply. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Oja's Rule Selects the Principal Statistical Direction While Bounding Weight Norm”? For centered linear input, the Oja update combines the Hebbian term h x and weight-dependent decay \(-h^{2}w\) in one local rule. The first rotates w toward high-variance directions of the input covariance, while the second strengthens as output grows, allowing the direction to approach the principal eigenvector without unbounded norm growth. This conclusion assumes stationary input, a suitably small learning rate, and a nondegenerate largest eigenvalue. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “long-term potentiation, LTP” mean in this lecture? long-term potentiation, LTP: A lasting increase in synaptic efficacy. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “long-term depression, LTD” mean in this lecture? long-term depression, LTD: A lasting decrease in synaptic efficacy. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “spike-timing-dependent plasticity, STDP” mean in this lecture? spike-timing-dependent plasticity, STDP: An empirical rule in which weight change depends on relative pre/post spike timing. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “Hebbian learning” mean in this lecture? Hebbian learning: A class of rules in which coordinated activity drives changes in connectivity. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “covariance rule” mean in this lecture? covariance rule: A plasticity rule driven by centered pre- and postsynaptic fluctuations. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “principal eigenvector” mean in this lecture? principal eigenvector: The direction associated with the largest covariance eigenvalue. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “synaptic scaling” mean in this lecture? synaptic scaling: Global rescaling that maintains an overall activity or weight range. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “Oja rule” mean in this lecture? Oja rule: A Hebbian PCA rule with a local normalization term. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “BCM rule” mean in this lecture? BCM rule: A rule that uses a sliding postsynaptic threshold to control LTP and LTD. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “STDP timing rule” be used? STDP timing rule: ∆\(w = f (t_{\mathrm{post}} - t_{\mathrm{pre}} )\). Pair-based approximation This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Basic rate Hebbian rule” be used? Basic rate Hebbian rule: \(\tau w\) ẇi = hxi. With nonnegative activity, it only potentiates This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Expected dynamics of centered Hebbian learning” be used? Expected dynamics of centered Hebbian learning: \(\tau w\) \(E[\dot{w}] = Cw\). Linear neuron with stationary inputs This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Positive semidefiniteness of covariance” be used? Positive semidefiniteness of covariance: vT Cv ≥ 0. Finite second moments This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Hebbian eigenmode growth” be used? Hebbian eigenmode growth: \(\dot{a}k = (\lambda _{k} /\tau w )\)ak. Fixed C This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Oja's rule” be used? Oja's rule: \(\dot{w}i \propto  hxi - h_{2}\) wi. Online approximation to PCA This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “BCM sign switch” be used? BCM sign switch: ẇi ∝ hxi (h − θ).
