title: Lecture 11: Machine Learning: Regression, Gradient Descent, and Backpropagation
subtitle: Machine Learning: Regression, Gradient Descent, and Backpropagation
text:
Machine Learning: Regression, Gradient Descent, and Backpropagation Dataset (x,y) → architecture → loss → gradient descent → linear regression → closed form Define a supervised-learning problem in terms of its dataset, architecture, loss, and learning rule, and distinguish the target support of classification from that of regression. Use a first-order Taylor expansion to explain why the gradient is the locally steepest ascent direction and why a step along the negative gradient reduces squared loss. Derive the linear-regression gradient, its Hebbian-like and stabilizing components, and the normal equation step by step, including how to handle a singular design matrix. Explain why a deep linear network has a linear input-output map even though its multilayer factorization produces nonlinear and generally nonconvex optimization dynamics. Derive the backpropagated error recurrence and each layer's weight gradient by tracking shapes, while treating backpropagation as a training algorithm rather than an established neurobiological mechanism. A machine-learning problem must specify its representation or architecture, objective or loss, and optimization or learning rule. Linear regression is the transparent example: the squared-error gradient decomposes into a data-dependent Hebbian-like term and a weight-dependent stabilizing term and admits a normal-equation closed form. In a deep network, backpropagation repeatedly applies the chain rule, carrying output error through transposed weights and local activation derivatives to each layer. Conflating architecture, loss, and optimizer. Forgetting that the gradient points uphill and the update needs a negative sign. Omitting matrix shapes and therefore misplacing transposes in matrix calculus. Attempting a direct inverse for a singular design matrix. Assuming optimization of a deep linear network is itself linear or convex. Treating backpropagation as an established biological synaptic mechanism. Reading an informal historical aside in a this lesson as a rigorous technical conclusion. Do not describe backpropagation as a biological mechanism in which error is directly sent back to neurons. Label it as a training algorithm and distinguish its formal resemblance to three-factor plasticity from its mechanistic differences. Gradient descent ∆\(w = -\eta 
abla w L\) \(\eta >0\) and a local step Linear-regression loss 1 \(L= \Vert y - X T w\Vert 2 2P\) Source orientation X:N×P Least-squares gradient \(
abla w\) \(L = -X(y - X T w)/P\) Differentiable squared loss Closed-form solution ŵ = (XX T )−1 Xy Invertible \(XX^\mathrm{T}\) Backpropagated-error recurrence \(\delta  (\ell ) = (W (\ell +1)T \delta  (\ell +1) ) \odot  \varphi '\) Compatible shapes Layer weight gradient \(\partial L/\partial W (\ell ) = \delta  (\ell )\) \(z (\ell -1)T\) One example; average over the batch afterward supervised learning Learning a predictor from input-target pairs. classification Prediction of a discrete label. regression Prediction of a continuous target. architecture The connectivity and computations defining a model. loss function An objective quantifying disagreement between prediction and target. gradient The vector of parameter derivatives pointing in the direction of fastest local increase. learning rate The scale of each gradient step. normal equation The linear equation satisfied by a least-squares optimum. backpropagation An algorithm for efficiently computing multilayer chain-rule gradients. local derivative The derivative of one computational node's output with respect to its input. What must a supervised-learning algorithm specify separately, and why is “use a neural network” not a complete specification? The architecture determines which mappings can be represented, the loss defines error, and the learning rule determines how parameters change. The same architecture can be trained with different losses, and the same loss can be optimized in different ways. It must specify the architecture or representation, the loss or objective, the optimization or learning rule, and the dataset's input-target pairing. If \(
abla L=(3,4)^\mathrm{T}\) and a local step is limited to length 0.1, which direction minimizes the linear term in the Taylor expansion? The gradient norm is 5. For a fixed step length, the dot product is smallest at an angle of 180°, so use the unit negative gradient. Standard gradient descent instead lets \(\eta ||
abla L||\) determine the step length. Choose \(\Delta w=-0.1(3,4)^\mathrm{T}/5=(-0.06,-0.08)^\mathrm{T}\). With \(X\in \mathbb{R}^{N	imes P}\) and \(w\in \mathbb{R}^{N	imes 1}\), what are the shapes of the least-squares prediction, residual, and gradient? The factor 2 comes from differentiating the square. Left-multiplying the residual by X aggregates the errors from P samples back into N feature coordinates. When only direction matters, one may write that the gradient is proportional to -Xr; with an equality sign, however, 2/P cannot be omitted. Both the prediction \(X^\mathrm{T}w\) and residual \(y-X^\mathrm{T}w\) are P×1. Under this lecture's convention \(L=||y-X^\mathrm{T}w||^{2}/P\), the gradient is \(-(2/P)X(y-X^\mathrm{T}w)\), with shape N×1. The factor 2 disappears only if the loss includes 1/2. Let \(W^1\in \mathbb{R}^{4	imes 3}\), \(W^2\in \mathbb{R}^{2	imes 4}\), and \(x\in \mathbb{R}^{3	imes 1}\). If output error \(\delta ^2\in \mathbb{R}^{2	imes 1}\), what are the shapes of the hidden error and \(\partial L/\partial W^1\)? The transposed weight matrix maps error from output space back into hidden coordinates. An outer product then combines postsynaptic error with presynaptic activation to produce the gradient for every connection. \(\delta ^1=(W^2)^\mathrm{T}\delta ^2\odot \phi '\) is \(4	imes 1\), and \(\partial L/\partial W^1=\delta ^1x^\mathrm{T}\) is \(4	imes 3\). Why is the statement “the gradient points toward the minimum” inaccurate? The gradient points in the locally steepest ascent direction at the current point; its negative is the local descent direction. It uses only first-order information at that location and does not directly identify a distant global minimum. This is the distinction tested in The Components of Supervised Learning and Gradient Descent. Worked example — A Gradient Step Computed by Hand: Let \(x=(1,2)^\mathrm{T}\), \(y=5\), \(w=(0,0)^\mathrm{T}\), \(L=1/2(y-w^\mathrm{T}x)^2\), and \(\eta =0.1\). Compute the update and the new loss. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(x=(1,2)^\mathrm{T}\), \(y=5\), \(w=(0,0)^\mathrm{T}\), \(L=1/2(y-w^\mathrm{T}x)^2\), and \(\eta =0.1\). Compute the update and the new loss. Initially the prediction is 0 and residual \(e=5\), so \(\mathrm{gradient}=-ex=(-5,-10)^\mathrm{T}\). The update gives \(w_{\mathrm{new}}=w-\eta \mathrm{gradient}=(0.5,1.0)^\mathrm{T}\). The new prediction is \(0.5+2=2.5\), and the new loss is \(1/2(5-2.5)^2=3.125\); the initial loss was 12.5. Both the gradient and w are \(2	imes 1\). If the update's negative sign is mistakenly removed, w becomes (-0.5,-1), \(\mathrm{prediction}=-2.5\), and the loss increases to 28.125. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “The Components of Supervised Learning and Gradient Descent”? The dataset supplies the evidence defining the problem, the architecture defines the hypothesis class, the loss defines error, and the optimizer defines the search path. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “The Components of Supervised Learning and Gradient Descent”? A gradient has the same shape as its parameter and points in the locally steepest ascent direction; gradient descent applies the negative sign. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “The Components of Supervised Learning and Gradient Descent” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The dataset supplies the evidence defining the problem, the architecture defines the hypothesis class, the loss defines error, and the optimizer defines the search path. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Deriving Gradient Descent from a Taylor Expansion and Computing a Single-Sample Linear Gradient”? If y and ŷ are measured in deg/s while x is dimensionless, the gradient has units \((\mathrm{deg}/s)^2\) per weight; \(\eta\) must convert the update back to weight units. The gradient vanishes when the residual \(e=0\) or \(x=0\). If \(\eta\) is too large, the neglected second-order term can cause the loss to increase. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: How is a prediction task formulated as an optimizable mathematical problem, and how does local loss geometry imply a parameter update? Supervised learning supplies input-target pairs. In handwritten-digit recognition, x is an image and y is a discrete digit label, making the task classification. In optic-flow estimation, x may be two adjacent frames and y a continuous motion vector at each location, making it regression. Both require a clear account of how training examples are sampled and whether test examples follow the same distribution. The architecture specifies the prediction function. A multilayer network can be written \(z^{(0)}=x\), \(h^{(\ell )}=W^{(\ell -1)}z^{(\ell -1)}\), \(z^{(\ell )}=\phi (h^{(\ell )})\), and finally \(\hat{y}=g(W^{(L)}z^{(L)})\). If layer ℓ contains \(N_\ell\) units, then \(W^{(\ell -1)}\in \mathbb{R}^{N_\ell 	imes N_{\ell -1}}\). Writing every shape exposes most transpose errors before the derivation begins. Why can training every layer of a deep linear network not be treated as ordinary convex linear regression, even though the overall mapping is linear? The product \(W^L\cdots W^0\) defines a linear mapping, but it is a multilinear product of the component layer parameters. Scale and factorization are nonunique, and updates to different layers depend on one another, so optimization in parameter space is generally nonconvex. This is the distinction tested in Linear Regression: Gradient Decomposition, the Normal Equation, and Deep Linear Factorization. Worked example — A Closed-Form Fit with Two Features and Two Samples: Let \(X=[[1,0],[0,2]]\), so its columns are \((1,0)^\mathrm{T}\) and \((0,2)^\mathrm{T}\), and let targets \(y=(3,4)^\mathrm{T}\). Find \(\hat{w}\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(X=[[1,0],[0,2]]\), so its columns are \((1,0)^\mathrm{T}\) and \((0,2)^\mathrm{T}\), and let targets \(y=(3,4)^\mathrm{T}\). Find \(\hat{w}\). \(XX^\mathrm{T}=\operatorname{diag}(1,4)\), and \(Xy=(3,8)^\mathrm{T}\). \((XX^\mathrm{T})^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(1,1/4)\), hence \(\hat{w}=(3,2)^\mathrm{T}\). The predictions \(X^\mathrm{T}\hat{w}=(3,4)^\mathrm{T}\) exactly match the targets, so the residual is zero. In this example, incorrectly using \(X^\mathrm{T}X\) also happens to give a diagonal matrix and can conceal an orientation bug. With a general nonsquare X, the shapes reveal the error immediately. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Linear Regression: Gradient Decomposition, the Normal Equation, and Deep Linear Factorization”? A least-squares update decomposes into input-target correlation and weight-dependent covariance stabilization. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Linear Regression: Gradient Decomposition, the Normal Equation, and Deep Linear Factorization”? A closed form requires a stated orientation for X and invertibility; use a pseudoinverse or regularization when the system is singular. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Linear Regression: Gradient Decomposition, the Normal Equation, and Deep Linear Factorization” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? A closed form requires a stated orientation for X and invertibility; use a pseudoinverse or regularization when the system is singular. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “The Batch Least-Squares Gradient and Normal Equation”? The quantities \(XX^\mathrm{T}w\) and Xy have matching feature×target scales. Large differences among feature units worsen conditioning and sensitivity to the learning rate, so standardization is often needed. When \(XX^\mathrm{T}\) is singular, the inverse does not exist. Gradient descent may still reach an interpolating solution, but initialization, optimizer, and regularization determine which one it selects. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does the backpropagated error recurrence use the transpose of the downstream weight matrix? The forward map W carries hidden coordinates into downstream coordinates. The chain rule must aggregate downstream scalar sensitivities back into each hidden coordinate, which is exactly the reverse Jacobian product \(W^\mathrm{T}\delta\); its shape also returns from the downstream dimension to the hidden dimension. This is the distinction tested in Backpropagation: Layerwise Chain Rules, Error Coordinates, and Weight Gradients. Worked example — Tracing One Backpropagation Path by Shape: Take \(x=(1,2)^\mathrm{T}\), \(W^0=[[1,0],[0,1]]\), identity \(\phi\), \(W^1=(1,-1)\), target \(y=0\), and loss=\(1/2(\hat{y}-y)^2\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Take \(x=(1,2)^\mathrm{T}\), \(W^0=[[1,0],[0,1]]\), identity \(\phi\), \(W^1=(1,-1)\), target \(y=0\), and loss=\(1/2(\hat{y}-y)^2\). The hidden activation is \(z^1=W^0x=(1,2)^\mathrm{T}\), and prediction \(\hat{y}=(1,-1)\cdot (1,2)=-1\). \(\delta ^2=\hat{y}-y=-1\), and \(\delta ^1=(W^1)^\mathrm{T}\delta ^2=(-1,1)^\mathrm{T}\). \(\partial L/\partial W^1=\delta ^2(z^1)^\mathrm{T}=(-1,-2)\), while \(\partial L/\partial W^0=\delta ^1x^\mathrm{T}=[[-1,-2],[1,2]]\). A small increase in \(W^1_1\) raises ŷ. The current residual is -1, so raising ŷ moves it toward target 0; accordingly, the gradient with respect to \(W^1_1\) is negative and the negative-gradient update increases that weight. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Backpropagation: Layerwise Chain Rules, Error Coordinates, and Weight Gradients”? \(\delta\) denotes the derivative of loss with respect to a preactivation, not a directly observed biological firing error. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Backpropagation: Layerwise Chain Rules, Error Coordinates, and Weight Gradients”? The hidden-error recurrence contains the transpose of the downstream weights and the derivative of the local activation. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Backpropagation: Layerwise Chain Rules, Error Coordinates, and Weight Gradients” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? A weight gradient is the outer product of postsynaptic sensitivity and presynaptic activation. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Backpropagation Recurrence in a Two-Layer Network”? The units of \(\delta\) are loss/preactivation. Multiplication by a presynaptic activation gives loss/weight, as required by the definition of a gradient. If \(\phi '=0\) for a hidden unit, that unit transmits no gradient to upstream weights for the current sample. This does not mean the unit is permanently useless, although sustained inactivity blocks learning. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “The Negative Gradient Descends the Local Loss Slope”? At the current parameter, the gradient points in the locally fastest direction of increasing loss, so update \(\Delta w=-\eta 
abla L\) moves in the opposite direction. The markers show only normalized iteration order, not experimental observations. They illustrate that an appropriate step can approach the minimum successively, whereas the Taylor approximation does not guarantee descent with an excessively large learning rate. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “supervised learning” mean in this lecture? supervised learning: Learning a predictor from input-target pairs. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “classification” mean in this lecture? classification: Prediction of a discrete label. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “regression” mean in this lecture? regression: Prediction of a continuous target. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “architecture” mean in this lecture? architecture: The connectivity and computations defining a model. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “loss function” mean in this lecture? loss function: An objective quantifying disagreement between prediction and target. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “gradient” mean in this lecture? gradient: The vector of parameter derivatives pointing in the direction of fastest local increase. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “learning rate” mean in this lecture? learning rate: The scale of each gradient step. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “normal equation” mean in this lecture? normal equation: The linear equation satisfied by a least-squares optimum. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “backpropagation” mean in this lecture? backpropagation: An algorithm for efficiently computing multilayer chain-rule gradients. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “Gradient descent” be used? Gradient descent: ∆\(w = -\eta 
abla w L\). \(\eta >0\) and a local step This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Linear-regression loss” be used? Linear-regression loss: 1 \(L= \Vert y - X T w\Vert 2 2P\). Source orientation X:N×P This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Least-squares gradient” be used? Least-squares gradient: \(
abla w\) \(L = -X(y - X T w)/P\). Differentiable squared loss This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Closed-form solution” be used? Closed-form solution: ŵ = (XX T )−1 Xy. Invertible \(XX^\mathrm{T}\) This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Backpropagated-error recurrence” be used? Backpropagated-error recurrence: \(\delta  (\ell ) = (W (\ell +1)T \delta  (\ell +1) ) \odot  \varphi '\). Compatible shapes This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Layer weight gradient” be used? Layer weight gradient: \(\partial L/\partial W (\ell ) = \delta  (\ell )\) \(z (\ell -1)T\).
