title: Lecture 12: Introduction to Vision: Hierarchy, Receptive Fields, and LNP Models
subtitle: Introduction to Vision: Hierarchy, Receptive Fields, and LNP Models
text: Introduction to Vision: Hierarchy, Receptive Fields, and LNP Models Retina→V1→streams → contrast → LNP → DoG center-surround → rectified feature maps → Gabor orientation Use the course-level photoreceptor–RGC–V1–MT/IT/LIP diagram to explain the visual hierarchy while separating anatomical pathways, receptive-field computations, and functional labels. Explain every stage of the LNP model—linear filter, static nonlinearity, and conditional Poisson output—and why early vision is commonly modeled in terms of contrast rather than raw luminance. Construct ON and OFF Difference-of-Gaussians receptive fields through spatial convolution and predict the response signs for a uniform field, a center spot, and surround illumination. Decompose a Gabor kernel into its Gaussian envelope, carrier frequency, orientation, and phase; then explain how the subsequent static nonlinearity introduces thresholding and saturation in V1 simple-cell orientation tuning. Extend receptive fields into space-time, distinguish separable from nonseparable kernels, and infer direction selectivity from slope in an x-t diagram. The visual hierarchy is not merely an anatomical list but a computational organization in which receptive-field size, feature complexity, history dependence, and invariance change by stage. LNP first projects a stimulus onto a linear receptive field, maps the drive through a nonlinearity to a rate, and uses a Poisson process to describe spikes. DoG, Gabor, and nonseparable spatiotemporal kernels summarize center-surround, orientation, and motion selectivity. Treating a receptive field only as a geometric region in visual space. Using raw luminance and contrast interchangeably. Leaving the sign or flip convention of a convolution kernel unstated. Assuming a feature map is a copy of the original image rather than a map of filter responses. Confusing Gabor orientation, phase, and spatial frequency. Assuming a separable spatiotemporal receptive field is automatically direction-selective. Equating an anatomical hierarchy with one purely feedforward computation. Do not describe a receptive field only as a screen “location”; it is a stimulus-response relationship. Distinguish a linear receptive field, classical receptive field, and experimental definition. Sparse-noise receptive-field mapping provides a useful transfer example. Visual contrast \(s = (I - I_{0} )/I_{0}\) \(I_{0}>0\) Linear receptive-field drive \(L=K \ast s\) Linear shift-invariant approximation Static nonlinearity \(r = F(L)\) A nonnegative or saturating rate, as specified LNP spike generation \(n \sim  \operatorname{Poisson}(rT )\) Conditional Poisson process Center-surround receptive field KDoG = Gcenter − Gsurround A wider surround Simple-cell orientation filter KGabor = G(x′, y ′ ) cos(kx′ + ϕ) Localized sinusoid Separable receptive field \(K(x, y, t) = Ks\) Kt Rank-1 space-time structure receptive field A local or functional relation between a stimulus pattern and a response, not merely a screen location. feature selectivity A preferential response to a class of stimulus structures. dorsal stream A broad visual pathway associated with motion- and action-related processing. ventral stream A broad visual pathway associated with processing related to object identity. linear-nonlinear-Poisson model, \(\ln P A\) cascade of a linear filter, nonlinearity, and Poisson spike-count variability. center-surround A receptive-field organization with opposite signs in the center and periphery. feature map The rectified response of one filter at every location. Gabor kernel A Gaussian-windowed sinusoid. separable Having space and time components that can be written as a product. direction selectivity A preferential response to one direction of motion. For \(I_{0}=100\) and local \(I=120\), what is the contrast? If \(I_{0}=200\) and local \(I=220\), how does contrast change even though the raw increment is the same? Contrast measures relative change. The same 20-unit luminance increment is proportionally smaller on the brighter background, so an early-vision model should not compare raw differences alone. The first contrast is 0.2; the second is 0.1. If an ON-center kernel has zero total integral, what should its linear response be when uniform positive contrast covers both center and surround? A zero-integral center-surround filter removes the common luminance component while preserving spatial differences. A real cell may deviate from exactly zero because of imperfect balance, nonlinearity, and adaptation. Approximately zero, because the positive center contribution cancels the negative surround contribution. If k increases in a Gabor kernel while the Gaussian envelope stays fixed, which aspect of tuning changes? k determines phase change per unit distance along x', \(\theta\) determines the carrier coordinate's direction, and \(\phi\) translates the light and dark lobes. The carrier's spatial frequency increases and its ON/OFF lobes become more closely spaced; rotation \(\theta\) sets the preferred orientation. Why can a fully separable kernel \(K(x,t)=K_{x}(x)K_{t}(t)\) generally not distinguish two moving edges with equal speeds and opposite directions using only its linear response? Direction selectivity requires coupling spatial position to temporal delay. In a nonseparable kernel the preferred position changes with lag, matching a trajectory in one direction while rejecting the reverse trajectory. Its spatial preference has the same shape and position at every time lag, so it contains no tilted x-t structure encoding the order of locations. Why is “ON cells prefer light and OFF cells prefer dark” an incomplete account of a center-surround receptive field? The response depends on contrast location and surround context. A bright spot in an ON center can excite, whereas a bright surround can cancel it. A balanced kernel may not respond to the same global luminance, so both polarity and spatial pattern must be specified. This is the distinction tested in Visual Hierarchy, the LNP Model, and Center-Surround Computation. Worked example — Predicting Signs in a Discrete Three-Position Center-Surround Filter: Use \(K=(-0.5,1,-0.5)\) for the left surround, center, and right surround. Compare stimuli \(s_{A}=(0,1,0)\) and \(s_{B}=(1,1,1)\), then rectify. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Use \(K=(-0.5,1,-0.5)\) for the left surround, center, and right surround. Compare stimuli \(s_{A}=(0,1,0)\) and \(s_{B}=(1,1,1)\), then rectify. \(L_{A}=(-0.5)0+1\times 1+(-0.5)0=1\), so \([L_{A}]_{+}=1\) after rectification. \(L_{B}=-0.5+1-0.5=0\); the balanced kernel cancels uniform contrast. With the OFF-center kernel -K, stimulus A gives -1 and therefore 0 after [L]_+. A zero sum of kernel weights is exactly the discrete condition for uniform cancellation. A nonzero sum leaves a residual response to a uniform field. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Visual Hierarchy, the LNP Model, and Center-Surround Computation”? The visual hierarchy mixes anatomy with computational abstraction; a region label is not an exclusive function. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Visual Hierarchy, the LNP Model, and Center-Surround Computation”? An LNP linear drive may have either sign, the nonlinearity makes rate nonnegative, and a conditional distribution then generates spike count. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Visual Hierarchy, the LNP Model, and Center-Surround Computation” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The visual hierarchy mixes anatomy with computational abstraction; a region label is not an exclusive function. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “From Contrast and Convolution to an ON-Center DoG”? Contrast is dimensionless. If x,y are measured in degrees of visual angle, a normalized Gaussian has units degree^{-2}, and integration leaves L with the drive units of A and B. If \(\sigma _{s}=\sigma _{c}\) and \(A=B\), the entire kernel is zero. If the surround is broad but B is not scaled for its area, comparing peak heights misrepresents total inhibitory strength. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: How does the visual system turn a luminance image into local contrast features and connect a receptive field to spikes through a minimal probabilistic model? This lesson place photoreceptors, retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), V1, MT, IT, and LIP on a hierarchy diagram. The retina first encodes local contrast; V1 emphasizes local structure such as orientation; MT and the dorsal stream are associated with motion and action-relevant variables; IT and the ventral stream with object features; and LIP often with decision-related representations. This course-level computational map does not imply exclusively one-way feedforward information flow. Along the hierarchy, classical receptive fields generally become larger, the selected features more complex, and history dependence and context stronger. Higher-level cells may also become more invariant to position, phase, or local detail. Feature selectivity asks which stimulus pattern changes the response; a receptive field additionally asks which positions and time lags matter. A single heat-map color cannot capture both questions. Why does changing Gabor phase \(\phi\) not change preferred orientation \(\theta\)? \(\phi\) translates positive and negative lobes along a fixed carrier axis and determines whether a bright or dark edge aligns with the filter. \(\theta\) rotates the coordinate system and determines which edge or grating direction aligns with the elongated lobes. This is the distinction tested in Feature Maps, Gabor Simple Cells, and Orientation Tuning. Worked example — Simple-Cell Responses at One Orientation and Different Phases: Idealize the linear drive to a matching grating as \(L=A \cos(\phi _{s}-\phi _{K})\), with \(A=10\). Compare phase differences 0, \(\pi /2\), and \(\pi\) using \(r=[L]_{+}\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Idealize the linear drive to a matching grating as \(L=A \cos(\phi _{s}-\phi _{K})\), with \(A=10\). Compare phase differences 0, \(\pi /2\), and \(\pi\) using \(r=[L]_{+}\). At difference 0, \(L=10cos0=10\) and \(r=10\). At difference \(\pi /2\), \(L=10\cos(\pi /2)=0\) and \(r=0\). At difference \(\pi\), \(L=10\cos\pi =-10\) and rectification gives \(r=0\). Without rectification, the response at phase \(\pi\) is -10 rather than no response; nonnegativity of firing rate comes from the nonlinear stage. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Feature Maps, Gabor Simple Cells, and Orientation Tuning”? Each location in a feature map stores a filter response, not a copy of the input image. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Feature Maps, Gabor Simple Cells, and Orientation Tuning”? For a Gabor filter, the envelope sets localization, \(\theta\) sets orientation, k sets frequency, and \(\phi\) sets phase. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Feature Maps, Gabor Simple Cells, and Orientation Tuning” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? For a Gabor filter, the envelope sets localization, \(\theta\) sets orientation, k sets frequency, and \(\phi\) sets phase. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “How a Rotated Gabor Filter Produces Orientation-Selective Drive”? Both kx' and \(\phi\) must be dimensionless, so k has units inverse distance. The exponential argument \(x'^2/\sigma _{x}^2\) is dimensionless as well. As \(\sigma _{x}\),\(\sigma _{y}\to \infty\), localization is lost. As \(k\to 0\), the carrier approaches a constant and the kernel resembles a Gaussian blob rather than an oriented alternating filter. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does a biphasic temporal kernel not automatically guarantee direction selectivity? If the kernel still factors into a fixed spatial profile and a temporal waveform, it only reweights one spatial feature over time and never pairs distinct locations with particular lags. Direction selectivity requires space-time nonseparability or an equivalent multichannel nonlinear computation. This is the distinction tested in Spatiotemporal Receptive Fields and Motion as Space-Time Orientation. Worked example — Matching a Discrete Three-Frame Trajectory: Across frames at times t-2,t-1,t, a rightward edge occupies positions 0,1,2. Put the receptive field's positive positions at 0,1,2 for the corresponding lags. Award +1 for a match and 0 otherwise; compare this sequence with leftward positions 2,1,0. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Across frames at times t-2,t-1,t, a rightward edge occupies positions 0,1,2. Put the receptive field's positive positions at 0,1,2 for the corresponding lags. Award +1 for a match and 0 otherwise; compare this sequence with leftward positions 2,1,0. The rightward sequence matches at all three lags, giving total linear drive \(1+1+1=3\). The leftward sequence matches only at middle position 1; the other two frames mismatch, so total drive is 1. With threshold 2, the rightward response passes and the leftward response is clipped to 0. If the three frames are averaged without order, both sequences contain positions \({0,1,2}\), and the distinction disappears. Temporal order is therefore indispensable. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Spatiotemporal Receptive Fields and Motion as Space-Time Orientation”? Spatiotemporal convolution uses past stimulus history, so the orientation of the time-lag axis must be explicit. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Spatiotemporal Receptive Fields and Motion as Space-Time Orientation”? A separable kernel's spatial profile does not move with lag; a tilted nonseparable kernel can encode the sign of velocity. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Spatiotemporal Receptive Fields and Motion as Space-Time Orientation” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Motion is an orientation in the x-t plane, and velocity corresponds to trajectory slope. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “The Matching Condition for a Moving Edge and a Tilted Receptive Field”? \(v\tau\) has distance units and can be added to x. The spatiotemporal integral also includes dx \(d\tau\), so kernel normalization must preserve the drive units. At \(v=0\) the ridge is untilted and selects a static feature. With an extremely short temporal window, opposite-direction trajectories have not separated enough and direction discrimination weakens. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “From ON/OFF Local-Contrast Channels to an Oriented Gabor-Like Receptive Field”? ON/OFF center-surround filters first recode absolute luminance as local contrast. Arranging several polarity-specific subfields along one axis makes signed contributions add for the matching direction and cancel for an orthogonal direction, creating an elongated, orientation-selective Gabor-like linear receptive field. The diagram distinguishes local DoG contrast computation from the later subfield arrangement that creates orientation tuning. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “receptive field” mean in this lecture? receptive field: A local or functional relation between a stimulus pattern and a response, not merely a screen location. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “feature selectivity” mean in this lecture? feature selectivity: A preferential response to a class of stimulus structures. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “dorsal stream” mean in this lecture? dorsal stream: A broad visual pathway associated with motion- and action-related processing. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “ventral stream” mean in this lecture? ventral stream: A broad visual pathway associated with processing related to object identity. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “linear-nonlinear-Poisson model, LNP” mean in this lecture? linear-nonlinear-Poisson model, LNP: A cascade of a linear filter, nonlinearity, and Poisson spike-count variability. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “center-surround” mean in this lecture? center-surround: A receptive-field organization with opposite signs in the center and periphery. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “feature map” mean in this lecture? feature map: The rectified response of one filter at every location. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “Gabor kernel” mean in this lecture? Gabor kernel: A Gaussian-windowed sinusoid. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “separable” mean in this lecture? separable: Having space and time components that can be written as a product. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “Visual contrast” be used? Visual contrast: \(s = (I - I_{0} )/I_{0}\). \(I_{0}>0\) This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Linear receptive-field drive” be used? Linear receptive-field drive: \(L=K \ast s\). Linear shift-invariant approximation This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Static nonlinearity” be used? Static nonlinearity: \(r = F(L)\). A nonnegative or saturating rate, as specified This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “LNP spike generation” be used? LNP spike generation: \(n \sim  \operatorname{Poisson}(rT )\). Conditional Poisson process This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Center-surround receptive field” be used? Center-surround receptive field: KDoG = Gcenter − Gsurround. A wider surround This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Simple-cell orientation filter” be used? Simple-cell orientation filter: KGabor = G(x′, y ′ ) cos(kx′ + ϕ). Localized sinusoid This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Separable receptive field” be used? Separable receptive field: \(K(x, y, t) = Ks\) Kt. Rank-1 space-time structure This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written.

title: Lecture 13: Spike-Triggered Average and White-Noise System Identification
subtitle: Spike-Triggered Average and White-Noise System Identification
text: Spike-Triggered Average and White-Noise System Identification White-noise stimulus → spike-triggered ensemble → matrix notation → least squares/Hessian → white covariance → STA proportionality Organize white-noise stimuli, spike trains, and the spike-triggered ensemble into a system-identification workflow, distinguishing a descriptive STA, a filter estimator, and a complete LNP component. Move among continuous convolution, pixel-index summation, and matrix notation while tracking the shapes of S, K, L, and the count vector and the orientation of the time-lag axis. Derive the normal equation and Hessian from mean-squared loss for a linear neuron, and explain circular versus elongated loss contours through stimulus covariance. Starting from \(SS^\mathrm{T}\approx T\sigma _{s}^2I\), derive the proportionality between \(\hat{K}\) and the STA while retaining the scaling by spike count, bin width, and stimulus variance. Recover a static nonlinearity with the small-bin Poisson approximation and diagnose STA failure caused by multiple features, an even nonlinearity, colored stimuli, or insufficient data. STA is both a descriptive average and, under a linear model, Gaussian white stimulation, and a suitable nonlinearity, a filter estimator. Matrix least squares reveals why: white stimulation makes the design covariance approximately a scalar identity, reducing the normal equation to a stimulus-response correlation. Recovering the nonlinearity yields an LNP model that can predict new stimuli, but multiple relevant dimensions, even-symmetric nonlinearities, or correlated stimulation can make the STA zero or biased. Treating the STA only as an image average without specifying time-lag alignment. Leaving matrix orientation unstated and confusing \(S^\mathrm{T}K\) with KS. Omitting the large-sample and equal-variance assumptions behind white covariance. Equating STA amplitude unconditionally with physical filter gain. Concluding from \(STA=0\) that a neuron has no receptive field. Forgetting to divide by bin width when recovering F. Evaluating a model on its training fit instead of held-out prediction. Distinguish the STA as a descriptive average, linear-filter estimator, and LNP-model component. They are related under particular assumptions, not unconditionally equivalent. Pixelized linear drive \(L = ST K S\):P×T Least-squares filter K̂ = (SS T )−1 Sh Invertible \(SS^\mathrm{T}\) Loss Hessian \(H = SS T /T\) Linear squared loss White-noise covariance SS \(T \approx  T \sigma s_{2} I\) Large T with independent equal-variance pixels Spike-triggered average 1 X \(ST A = st\) nsp t∈spikes Aligned stimulus histories STA/filter relation \(\hat{K} \propto  ST A\) White Gaussian single-filter assumptions Small-bin nonlinearity estimate P (spike|L) ≈ ∆\(tF (L)\) \(\Delta t\) rate≪1 system identification Inferring a system model from input-output data. white noise An ideal random stimulus with uncorrelated dimensions or time bins and uniform power. spike-triggered ensemble The collection of stimulus histories preceding all spikes. spike-triggered average, STA The mean of the spike-triggered ensemble. design matrix A matrix organizing stimulus vectors by examples or time bins. Hessian The matrix of second derivatives of loss with respect to parameters. isotropic Having equal curvature or variance in every direction. whitening Removing covariance correlations to obtain variables near unit covariance. correlated stimulus A stimulus whose dimensions have nonzero covariance. relevant dimension A stimulus-projection direction on which the response depends. What does column t of \(S\in \mathbb{R}^{P\times T}\) represent, and why is K^TS_{:t} a scalar? Each time bin is one high-dimensional regression example. Placing time in rows while retaining the original formulas misaligns the orientations of K, S, and the response. It is the stimulus history preceding time t, flattened in a fixed lag order. K and that column are both P-dimensional, so their inner product is one linear drive. What experimental problem is indicated by a small eigenvalue of the least-squares Hessian \(H=SS^\mathrm{T}/T\)? Many K values displaced along that direction give almost identical predictions, leaving the estimate dominated by measurement noise or regularization. Identifiability improves only by adding stimulus variation in that direction. The stimulus varies little along that eigenvector direction, so loss curvature is weak and the data constrain that filter component poorly. Why are loss contours nearly circular, rather than tilted ellipses, for large-sample equal-variance white noise? The identity matrix favors no coordinate direction. Finite samples still create off-diagonal fluctuations, so circularity is an approximation rather than exact geometry in every experiment. Because \(H\approx \sigma _{s}^2I\), all orthogonal filter directions have equal curvature and cross-terms are nearly zero. A neuron fires strongly when \(|K^\mathrm{T}s|\) is large and responds identically to positive and negative projections. Why can its linear STA be nearly zero? A zero first moment does not imply an absence of stimulus dependence. Spike-triggered covariance can reveal increased variance along K, and an energy model can represent this even response. Stimuli resembling +K and -K both precede spikes, and the two groups cancel in their vector average. Why must each member of the spike-triggered ensemble contain a stimulus history rather than only the frame in which the spike occurs? Neural responses have latency and may depend on multiple past lags. Using only the current frame discards temporal filtering and attaches the causal feature to the wrong spike time. A history vector permits simultaneous estimation of spatial and temporal receptive-field structure. This is the distinction tested in White-Noise System Identification in Three Notations. Worked example — Matrix Prediction with Two Pixels and Four Time Bins: Let \(S=[[1,-1,1,-1],[1,1,-1,-1]]\) and \(K=(2,1)^\mathrm{T}\). Compute \(L=S^\mathrm{T}K\) and interpret each entry. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(S=[[1,-1,1,-1],[1,1,-1,-1]]\) and \(K=(2,1)^\mathrm{T}\). Compute \(L=S^\mathrm{T}K\) and interpret each entry. At t1 the stimulus is (1,1), so \(L_{1}=2\times 1+1\times 1=3\); at t2 it is (-1,1), so \(L_{2}=-2+1=-1\). At t3 the stimulus is (1,-1), so \(L_{3}=2-1=1\); at t4 it is (-1,-1), so \(L_{4}=-2-1=-3\). Therefore \(L=(3,-1,1,-3)^\mathrm{T}\). The first pixel has the larger weight, so changing its coordinate affects the drive more strongly. S is \(2\times 4\) and \(S^\mathrm{T}\) is \(4\times 2\); multiplication by \(2\times 1\) K must yield \(4\times 1\). A 2-dimensional result signals that the orientation has been reversed. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “White-Noise System Identification in Three Notations”? An STA requires identical stimulus-history alignment at every spike; averaging only the spike frame is insufficient. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “White-Noise System Identification in Three Notations”? Continuous convolution, a pixel sum, and \(S^\mathrm{T}K\) are alternative representations of the same calculation. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “White-Noise System Identification in Three Notations” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? An STA requires identical stimulus-history alignment at every spike; averaging only the spike frame is insufficient. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Discretizing Spatiotemporal Convolution as \(S^\mathrm{T}K\)”? If continuous K has units drive/(contrast·area·time), multiplying by contrast and dx dy \(d\tau\) gives drive. If discrete K absorbs grid volume, its numerical units depend on binning. A frame rate that is too low aliases fast temporal structure. A history window that is too short truncates the kernel; one that is too long increases P and reduces statistical power per dimension. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: Given a complete stimulus movie and spike times, how can the stimulus history before each spike be converted into a dataset for estimating a filter? System identification reverses forward prediction. A forward LNP model predicts spikes from known K and F; the experiment supplies stimulus s and spikes k and seeks K and F. The standard protocol in this lesson presents random checkerboard white noise, records neural spikes, looks backward from every spike over the same time lags, and averages those stimulus histories. Stimulus coordinates, frame duration, and neural latency must be defined first. The spike-triggered ensemble contains every stimulus vector that preceded a spike, and its mean is the STA. For an ON-center RGC, the most recent lag may show a bright center and dark surround, while an earlier lag may differ in sign or shape, producing a biphasic temporal kernel. Every history must be aligned to its spike; otherwise alignment error artificially smears the filter in addition to true latency variation. Why does an elongated loss contour indicate that some filter combinations are estimated unreliably? Moving along the ellipse's long axis raises loss only slightly. This is a small-eigenvalue direction of the Hessian, where many different K values make similar predictions on the sampled stimuli, allowing finite noise to shift the minimum substantially. This is the distinction tested in Least Squares, the Hessian, and White-Noise Isotropy. Worked example — Recovering a Known Filter from a White Design: Continue with \(S=[[1,-1,1,-1],[1,1,-1,-1]]\), true \(K=(2,1)^\mathrm{T}\), and \(h=S^\mathrm{T}K=(3,-1,1,-3)^\mathrm{T}\). Recover K by least squares. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Continue with \(S=[[1,-1,1,-1],[1,1,-1,-1]]\), true \(K=(2,1)^\mathrm{T}\), and \(h=S^\mathrm{T}K=(3,-1,1,-3)^\mathrm{T}\). Recover K by least squares. \(SS^\mathrm{T}=[[4,0],[0,4]]=4I\), showing that the two stimulus dimensions have isotropic sample covariance. \(Sh=(8,4)^\mathrm{T}\); for example, its first entry is \(1\times 3+(-1)\times (-1)+1\times 1+(-1)\times (-3)=8\). \(\hat{K}=(4I)^{-1}(8,4)^\mathrm{T}=(2,1)^\mathrm{T}\), exactly recovering the true filter. If the second stimulus row is replaced by a copy of the first, \(SS^\mathrm{T}\) has \(\operatorname{rank} 1\). Only the sum of the two filter weights affects prediction, so the weights cannot be identified separately. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Least Squares, the Hessian, and White-Noise Isotropy”? The normal equation expresses filter estimation as inverse covariance applied to stimulus-response correlation. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Least Squares, the Hessian, and White-Noise Isotropy”? A Hessian eigenvalue measures both loss curvature and identifiability along its filter direction. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Least Squares, the Hessian, and White-Noise Isotropy” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? A Hessian eigenvalue measures both loss curvature and identifiability along its filter direction. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “The Normal Equation and an Isotropic Hessian”? \(SS^\mathrm{T}\) has units stimulus^2 and Sh has units stimulus×response. The resulting estimate therefore has units response/stimulus, as required for linear-filter gain. If \(T\le P\) or stimulus dimensions are linearly dependent, \(SS^\mathrm{T}\) may be singular and the inverse expression cannot be used directly. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why is a smooth increasing \(\hat{F}(L)\) curve on the training data insufficient evidence that an LNP model predicts? Both K and F were estimated from the same data, and binning plus a flexible curve can absorb noise. Generalization must be tested by computing projections on held-out stimuli and predicting conditional rates or spikes there. This is the distinction tested in From the Kernel Estimate to the STA, Nonlinearity, and Failure Diagnostics. Worked example — How an Even Nonlinearity Makes the STA Vanish: A one-dimensional stimulus s takes -1, 0, or +1 with equal prior probability. The neuron spikes with probability 0.4 at \(s=\pm 1\) and 0.1 at \(s=0\). Compute the spike-triggered mean and second moment and compare them with the original stimulus variance. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: A one-dimensional stimulus s takes -1, 0, or +1 with equal prior probability. The neuron spikes with probability 0.4 at \(s=\pm 1\) and 0.1 at \(s=0\). Compute the spike-triggered mean and second moment and compare them with the original stimulus variance. The total spike probability is \((0.4+0.1+0.4)/3=0.3\). Bayes' rule gives \(P(s=-1|\mathrm{spike})=4/9\), \(P(s=0|\mathrm{spike})=1/9\), and \(P(s=+1|\mathrm{spike})=4/9\). The positive and negative endpoints have equal conditional weight, so \(STA=E[s|\mathrm{spike}]=(-1)(4/9)+0+(+1)(4/9)=0\). The spike-triggered second moment is \(E[s^2|\mathrm{spike}]=(4/9)+(4/9)=8/9\). Because the conditional mean is zero, this is also the spike-triggered variance. The original stimulus has zero mean and variance \(E[s^2]=2/3\). Spike-triggered variance increases by \(8/9-2/3=2/9\), revealing a preference for large |s|. The three conditional probabilities sum to 1. If the spike probabilities at ±1 are changed to equal that at \(s=0\), the spike-triggered distribution returns to the prior and the variance difference becomes zero. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “From the Kernel Estimate to the STA, Nonlinearity, and Failure Diagnostics”? The proportionality between \(\hat{K}\) and STA contains \(n_{sp}\), T, \(\sigma _{s}^2\), and \(\Delta t\); their directional relation is more robust than raw amplitude. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “From the Kernel Estimate to the STA, Nonlinearity, and Failure Diagnostics”? Estimate the nonlinearity by dividing projection-conditioned spike probability by bin width. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “From the Kernel Estimate to the STA, Nonlinearity, and Failure Diagnostics” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? An even response, multiple relevant dimensions, and colored stimulation can bias an STA or make it zero. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “STA Proportionality with All Scale Factors Retained”? \(n_{sp}/(T\Delta t)\) has units 1/time; dividing by \(\sigma _{s}^2\) and multiplying by stimulus gives rate/stimulus, as required for a linear rate filter. If bins are too wide, \(k_{t}\) can exceed 1 and the Bernoulli simplification fails. With too few spikes, STA variance is large even when the expectation relation holds. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Forward LNP Prediction and Reverse STA Estimation Form One Validation Workflow”? A forward LNP model projects stimulus history onto \(L=k^{\mathrm{T}}s\), transforms it through \(F(L)\) into a conditional firing rate, and generates spikes. Reverse analysis aligns and averages the stimulus history before each spike. For zero-mean white Gaussian input, one relevant dimension, and sufficient data, STA points along k. Colored input, an even nonlinearity, or multiple relevant dimensions breaks this simple relation. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “system identification” mean in this lecture? system identification: Inferring a system model from input-output data. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “white noise” mean in this lecture? white noise: An ideal random stimulus with uncorrelated dimensions or time bins and uniform power. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “spike-triggered ensemble” mean in this lecture? spike-triggered ensemble: The collection of stimulus histories preceding all spikes. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “spike-triggered average, STA” mean in this lecture? spike-triggered average, STA: The mean of the spike-triggered ensemble. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “design matrix” mean in this lecture? design matrix: A matrix organizing stimulus vectors by examples or time bins. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “Hessian” mean in this lecture? Hessian: The matrix of second derivatives of loss with respect to parameters. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “isotropic” mean in this lecture? isotropic: Having equal curvature or variance in every direction. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “whitening” mean in this lecture? whitening: Removing covariance correlations to obtain variables near unit covariance. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “correlated stimulus” mean in this lecture? correlated stimulus: A stimulus whose dimensions have nonzero covariance. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “Pixelized linear drive” be used? Pixelized linear drive: \(L = ST K\). S:P×T This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Least-squares filter” be used? Least-squares filter: K̂ = (SS T )−1 Sh. Invertible \(SS^\mathrm{T}\) This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Loss Hessian” be used? Loss Hessian: \(H = SS T /T\). Linear squared loss This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “White-noise covariance” be used? White-noise covariance: SS \(T \approx  T \sigma s_{2} I\). Large T with independent equal-variance pixels This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Spike-triggered average” be used? Spike-triggered average: 1 X \(ST A = st\) nsp t∈spikes. Aligned stimulus histories This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “STA/filter relation” be used? STA/filter relation: \(\hat{K} \propto  ST A\). White Gaussian single-filter assumptions This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Small-bin nonlinearity estimate” be used? Small-bin nonlinearity estimate: P (spike|L) ≈ ∆\(tF (L)\). \(\Delta t\) rate≪1 This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written.

title: Lecture 14: Spike-Triggered Covariance and Generalized Linear Models
subtitle: Spike-Triggered Covariance and Generalized Linear Models
text: Spike-Triggered Covariance and Generalized Linear Models Multiple features → STC eigenspace → stimulus correction → GLM distribution → linear predictor → link Explain why one STA cannot describe an H1-like or complex-cell-like response driven by multiple features, and use spike-triggered covariance eigenvectors to find stimulus directions whose variance changes. Define the response distribution, linear predictor, and link function of a GLM, including the relation between the canonical parameter and the mean. Write the log likelihoods for Gaussian, Poisson, and Bernoulli probability models and explain the supports enforced by identity, log, and logit links. Strictly separate Poisson counts, small-bin Bernoulli spike/no-spike observations, and logistic classification so their likelihoods and interpretations are not conflated. Reconstruct the stimulus, self-history, and coupling filters of a retinal population GLM, and explain why fitted coupling provides conditional prediction rather than proof of a direct synapse. STC compares spike-triggered covariance with raw stimulus covariance to find directions in which pre-spike variance expands or contracts; colored stimulation requires whitening or correction. A GLM unifies several regressions through a response distribution, linear predictor, and link. A retinal population GLM can fit stimulus filters, self-history, and cross-neuron coupling together, but remains a statistical model: a coupling filter is not automatically a direct synapse. Concluding from \(STA=0\) that there is no relevant feature. Applying ordinary eigendecomposition directly to \(\Delta C\) under colored stimulation. Interpreting “linear” in GLM as requiring a linear response mean. Using an identity link for Poisson data and thereby allowing a negative rate. Conflating Bernoulli logistic classification with a Poisson small-count model. Treating fitted coupling filters as direct anatomical synapses. Ignoring history dependence and thereby biasing the apparent stimulus filter. Do not read “linear” in GLM as a requirement that the response mean be linear. The predictor is linear; the link determines its relation to the mean. STC covariance change ∆C = Cspike − Cstim Centered ensembles GLM linear predictor \(\eta  = X\beta \) Shape-compatible design Link function \(g(E[y|x]) = \eta \) Chosen response family Inverse Poisson log link \(\lambda  = e\eta \) Positive mean Inverse logistic link \(q = (1 + e^{-\eta } )-1\) \(0<q<1\) Poisson log likelihood ℓP ois = (yη − eη − log y!) Conditionally independent bins or counts Logistic loss −ℓBern = cross-entropy Bernoulli outcomes spike-triggered covariance, STC Analysis of covariance in the spike-triggered ensemble. relevant subspace The response-sensitive subspace spanned by several stimulus filters. exponential family A family of distributions expressible in a specified canonical statistic-parameter form. linear predictor \(\eta =X\beta\). link function The mapping between a conditional mean and \(\eta\). Poisson regression A log-link GLM for a count or rate. logistic regression A logit-link GLM for a Bernoulli outcome. log odds \(\log[q/(1-q)]\). history filter The linear effect of past spikes on the current conditional response. coupling filter A predictive filter applied to the histories of other units. If \(C_{\mathrm{stim}}=I\) and \(C_{\mathrm{spike}}=\operatorname{diag}(4,0.25)\), what are the two eigenvalues of \(\Delta C\), and what does each mean? STC measures conditional covariance relative to raw stimulus covariance. Both positive and negative changes may reveal relevant dimensions, so keeping only the largest positive eigenvalue is unjustified. The eigenvalues are 3 and -0.75. Variance before spikes increases in the first direction and decreases in the second. Which part of a GLM is linear? Is the mean response of \(a \operatorname{Poisson} GLM\) linear? The distribution and link determine mean support and curvature. Treating a GLM as ordinary linear regression would incorrectly permit a negative mean count. The predictor \(\eta =X\beta\) is linear. Through the inverse log link, the Poisson mean is \(\lambda =e^\eta\) and is nonlinear in the predictor. What mean count does \(a \operatorname{Poisson} GLM\) predict for \(\eta =\log 2\)? What probability does a Bernoulli-logit model predict for \(\eta =0\)? The two inverse links map any real \(\eta\) into a positive real mean and a probability in (0,1), respectively. Enforcing this support is central to link selection. The Poisson mean is \(\lambda =e^{\log 2}=2\); the Bernoulli probability is \(q=1/(1+e^0)=0.5\). If the coupling filter from neuron j to neuron i has a positive coefficient in a retinal GLM, does that prove a direct excitatory connection from j to i? Shared input, unobserved cells, stimulus-model mismatch, and common network state can all produce fitted coupling. Establishing a causal synapse requires perturbation or a stronger identification design. No. It says only that, conditional on the included covariates, past spikes of j improve the prediction of i's conditional rate. Why cannot the sign of an STC eigenvector say whether a stimulus is excitatory or inhibitory? Covariance describes an unoriented axis. v and -v have identical squared projections and covariance. To learn how projection sign affects rate, fit or inspect the nonlinearity along that axis. This is the distinction tested in Multiple Relevant Features and Spike-Triggered Covariance. Worked example — Positive and Negative Directions in Two-Dimensional STC: Let \(C_{\mathrm{stim}}=I\) and \(C_{\mathrm{spike}}=\operatorname{diag}(4,0.25)\). Find \(\Delta C\) and its eigenvectors, then interpret them. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(C_{\mathrm{stim}}=I\) and \(C_{\mathrm{spike}}=\operatorname{diag}(4,0.25)\). Find \(\Delta C\) and its eigenvectors, then interpret them. \(\Delta C=\operatorname{diag}(3,-0.75)\). It is already diagonal, with eigenvectors \(e_{1}=(1,0)^\mathrm{T}\) and \(e_{2}=(0,1)^\mathrm{T}\). Along \(e_{1}\), spike-conditioned variance rises from 1 to 4, a change of +3, suggesting that large \(|s_{1}|\) is associated with spiking. Along \(e_{2}\), variance falls from 1 to 0.25, a change of -0.75, suggesting that spiking favors \(s_{2}\) within a narrow range. \(\operatorname{trace} \Delta C=2.25\) is the total variance change, but the trace alone erases the axis-specific combination of one positive and one negative change. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Multiple Relevant Features and Spike-Triggered Covariance”? STC finds spike-conditioned changes in variance and can reveal dimensions that symmetry hides from the STA. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Multiple Relevant Features and Spike-Triggered Covariance”? Both positive and negative covariance changes are informative; an eigenvector's sign is not an excitation sign. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Multiple Relevant Features and Spike-Triggered Covariance” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? STC finds spike-conditioned changes in variance and can reveal dimensions that symmetry hides from the STA. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “From a Covariance Difference to Relevant Axes”? Covariance and \(\Delta C\) have units stimulus^2, as do their eigenvalues. In normalized or whitened space they can be interpreted as dimensionless relative changes. If \(C_{\mathrm{spike}}=C_{\mathrm{stim}}\), the second moment does not change and STC reveals no feature; the neuron may still depend on higher-order statistics. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: When a neuron responds to both signs of a projection or to several directions, how can features be recovered from the shape, rather than the mean, of the pre-spike stimulus distribution? This lesson use the blowfly H1 neuron, whose stimulus \(s(t)=v(t)\) is image velocity rather than a two-dimensional light pattern. The response may depend on projections through several temporal filters \(K_{1}\cdots K_{n}\) followed by a multidimensional nonlinearity F. Thus stimulus-vector coordinates are defined by the question: they may be pixels, velocity history, past spikes, or other measured covariates. If the nonlinearity is symmetric for +K and -K, the spike-triggered mean cancels. If the response depends on several relevant filters, one STA supplies at most one mean direction. It may consistently point toward one linear combination but cannot recover the full relevant subspace. Symmetry cancellation and dimensional limitation are distinct and should not both be dismissed as a noisy or unstable average. STC computes \(C_{\mathrm{spike}}\) and compares it with \(C_{\mathrm{stim}}\). Eigenvectors of \(\Delta C\) give directions of altered variance, and eigenvalue signs show whether variance grew or shrank. Why is the identity link \(\lambda =\eta\) structurally unsuitable for \(a \operatorname{Poisson} GLM\)? The linear predictor \(\eta\) may be any real number, so an identity link permits negative expected counts. The log link \(\lambda =e^\eta\) maps the whole real line to positive means and yields the convenient residual gradient of the canonical Poisson likelihood. This is the distinction tested in The Three GLM Components and Gaussian and Poisson Likelihoods. Worked example — The Direction of a One-Coefficient Poisson Update: For one observation \(x=2\) and \(\beta =0\), \(\eta =0\) and \(\lambda =1\); the observed count is \(y=3\). Find this observation's contribution to the log-likelihood gradient with respect to \(\beta\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: For one observation \(x=2\) and \(\beta =0\), \(\eta =0\) and \(\lambda =1\); the observed count is \(y=3\). Find this observation's contribution to the log-likelihood gradient with respect to \(\beta\). \(\eta =x\beta =0\), and the inverse log link gives \(\lambda =e^0=1\). The count residual \(y-\lambda =2\). The gradient contribution is \(x(y-\lambda )=2\times 2=4\), which is positive; gradient ascent raises \(\beta\) and therefore the predicted count. If \(y=0\), the same sample gives gradient \(2(0-1)=-2\), lowering \(\beta\) and \(\lambda\) while the prediction remains positive. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “The Three GLM Components and Gaussian and Poisson Likelihoods”? The linear component of a GLM is the predictor; the inverse link may make the mean nonlinear. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “The Three GLM Components and Gaussian and Poisson Likelihoods”? A Gaussian identity link corresponds to squared error, while a Poisson log link enforces a positive count mean. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “The Three GLM Components and Gaussian and Poisson Likelihoods” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? A Gaussian identity link corresponds to squared error, while a Poisson log link enforces a positive count mean. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Deriving the Poisson Log Likelihood and Gradient from the Probability Mass”? Both \(\eta\) and log\(\lambda\) must be dimensionless. An expected event count is dimensionless; a continuous-time rate enters the Poisson mean only after multiplication by \(\Delta t\). If data variance greatly exceeds its mean, the Poisson model may be overdispersed; a negative-binomial or latent-state model may fit better. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does fitting stimulus and coupling filters jointly still not justify interpreting a coupling coefficient as a causal synapse? The model controls only measured covariates. Unobserved common input, global state, model mismatch, and indirect network paths can still create conditional dependence. Establishing a causal synapse additionally requires intervention, anatomy, or stronger identifiability assumptions. This is the distinction tested in Retinal Population Filters, Bernoulli Logit, and Conditional Dependence. Worked example — Combining History Filters into a Conditional Spike Probability: A bin's predictor consists of bias -2, stimulus contribution +1.5, refractory self-history -3, and coupling from another neuron +0.5. Compute \(\eta\) and q, then remove the refractory term and compare. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: A bin's predictor consists of bias -2, stimulus contribution +1.5, refractory self-history -3, and coupling from another neuron +0.5. Compute \(\eta\) and q, then remove the refractory term and compare. With every term, \(\eta =-2+1.5-3+0.5=-3\) and \(q=1/(1+e^3)\approx 0.047\). Without the refractory term, \(\eta =0\) and \(q=0.5\). Thus a strong negative filter from the neuron's recent spike can suppress immediate spike probability even in the presence of stimulus and coupling drive. Contributions add in log-odds space, not as probabilities. Directly adding probabilities can exceed 1. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Retinal Population Filters, Bernoulli Logit, and Conditional Dependence”? A population predictor may include stimulus, self-history, cross-neuron history, and a bias simultaneously. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Retinal Population Filters, Bernoulli Logit, and Conditional Dependence”? A coupling filter is a conditional statistical coefficient, not automatically a direct excitatory or inhibitory synapse. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Retinal Population Filters, Bernoulli Logit, and Conditional Dependence” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The Bernoulli logit maps to probability; the small-bin Poisson approximation requires a very small expected count. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “From Bernoulli Likelihood to the Sigmoid and Cross-Entropy”? \(\eta\) and log odds are dimensionless. A covariate with physical units therefore needs a reciprocal-unit coefficient so \(x_{j}\beta _{j}\) is dimensionless. As q approaches 0 or 1, sigmoid slope \(q(1-q)\) becomes small. Complete separation can make unregularized logistic coefficients diverge. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “A Population GLM Places Stimulus, Self-History, and Coupling in One Conditional Predictor”? A population GLM adds a stimulus filter, self-history filter, and cross-neuron coupling filters in predictor \(\eta _{i}(t)\), then uses a log or logit inverse link to produce a nonnegative rate or binary spike probability. Simultaneous fitting reduces omitted-covariate confounding, but a coupling coefficient still denotes predictive dependence conditional on the included variables, not an anatomical synapse. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “spike-triggered covariance, STC” mean in this lecture? spike-triggered covariance, STC: Analysis of covariance in the spike-triggered ensemble. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “relevant subspace” mean in this lecture? relevant subspace: The response-sensitive subspace spanned by several stimulus filters. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “exponential family” mean in this lecture? exponential family: A family of distributions expressible in a specified canonical statistic-parameter form. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “linear predictor” mean in this lecture? linear predictor: \(\eta =X\beta\). This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “link function” mean in this lecture? link function: The mapping between a conditional mean and \(\eta\). This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “Poisson regression” mean in this lecture? Poisson regression: A log-link GLM for a count or rate. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “logistic regression” mean in this lecture? logistic regression: A logit-link GLM for a Bernoulli outcome. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “log odds” mean in this lecture? log odds: \(\log[q/(1-q)]\). This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “history filter” mean in this lecture? history filter: The linear effect of past spikes on the current conditional response. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “STC covariance change” be used? STC covariance change: ∆C = Cspike − Cstim. Centered ensembles This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “GLM linear predictor” be used? GLM linear predictor: \(\eta  = X\beta \). Shape-compatible design This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Link function” be used? Link function: \(g(E[y|x]) = \eta \). Chosen response family This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Inverse Poisson log link” be used? Inverse Poisson log link: \(\lambda  = e\eta \). Positive mean This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Inverse logistic link” be used? Inverse logistic link: \(q = (1 + e^{-\eta } )-1\). \(0<q<1\) This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Poisson log likelihood” be used? Poisson log likelihood: ℓP ois = (yη − eη − log y!). Conditionally independent bins or counts This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Logistic loss” be used? Logistic loss: −ℓBern = cross-entropy. Bernoulli outcomes This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written.

title: Lecture 15: Efficient Coding and Information Theory
subtitle: Efficient Coding and Information Theory
text: Efficient Coding and Information Theory Barlow hypotheses → surprise \(-\log p\)→ entropy → mutual information → Gaussian channel → redundancy/capacity Distinguish Barlow's three hypotheses accurately and present efficient coding as a normative proposal constrained by noise and resources. Explain surprise=\(-\log p\) from the additivity of information for independent events, and compute entropy, conditional entropy, and mutual information. Derive the joint-distribution form of mutual information, show that \(I=0\) under independence, and explain why differential entropy can be negative and depends on coordinate units. Starting from \(x=s+\eta _{x}\) and \(y=Ax+\eta _{y}\), derive input and output covariance while distinguishing signal, input noise, and output noise by their locations in the encoder. Explain the Gaussian-MI determinant formula, fixed-information constraints, channel capacity, decorrelation, and orthogonal nonuniqueness, and show how added symmetries can select center-surround filters. Barlow's efficient coding is a normative hypothesis: under resource and noise constraints, a sensory system should reduce predictable redundancy while retaining useful information. Information theory quantifies predictability and transmission through surprise, entropy, and mutual information. Atick and Redlich model the retina as a noisy linear encoder and decoder that lowers redundancy under fixed-information and output-capacity constraints. Decorrelation is nonunique; rotational symmetry together with locality and related constraints can select a center-surround form. Treating efficient coding as a uniquely established mechanism rather than a normative hypothesis. Equating entropy unconditionally with useful information. Calling a negative differential entropy an error. Assuming \(MI=0\) means only zero linear correlation; when well-defined, it means independence. Optimizing only decorrelation while ignoring noise and output capacity. Assuming that the whitening solution is unique. Presenting the normative center-surround prediction as singular causal evidence. Distinguish entropy, differential entropy, mutual information, redundancy, and channel capacity. Avoid unconditional claims such as “more entropy is better.” Surprise \(S(x) = - \log p(x)\) Chosen logarithm base Entropy \(H(X) = E[- \log p(X)]\) Discrete distribution Mutual information \(I(X; Y ) = H(X) - H(X|Y )\) Known joint distribution Dependence form of MI \(\sum  p(x, y)\) \(I= p(x, y)\) \(\log p(x)p(y)\) Support handled correctly Linear Gaussian covariance propagation Cy = ACx \(AT + \sigma y_{2}\) I Independent additive output noise Gaussian-MI determinant form 1 det Cy \(I(X; Y ) = \log 2 \det Cy|x\) Jointly Gaussian variables Decorrelation objective Cout ≈ diagonal Second-order redundancy efficient coding A normative principle for optimizing an information representation under resource and noise constraints. redundancy Structure that is predictable from other components and transmitted repeatedly. surprise The −log probability of an event. entropy Average surprise or uncertainty. conditional entropy Residual uncertainty after another variable is given. mutual information The reduction in uncertainty about one variable supplied by another. differential entropy An entropy-like quantity for a continuous density that can be negative and depends on units. channel capacity The maximum mutual information attainable under input constraints. decorrelation Making off-diagonal covariance entries approach zero. normative model A model of what a system should optimize rather than a direct specification of mechanism. With logarithms base 2, what is the surprise of an outcome with probability 1/8? Three independent fair binary choices are required to reduce the probability to 1/8, so observing the outcome conveys 3 bits. Changing the logarithm base changes the numerical unit. \(-\log_{2}(1/8)=3\) bits. Let X be fair Bernoulli and \(Y=X\). What are \(H(X)\), \(H(X|Y)\), and \(I(X;Y)\)? Once Y is known, X is known exactly and conditional uncertainty is zero. High entropy in Y does not imply low redundancy between the two variables. \(H(X)=1\) bit, \(H(X|Y)=0\), and \(I(X;Y)=1\) bit. Let \(x=s+\eta _{x}\) and \(y=Ax+\eta _{y}\), with every term zero-mean and the noises independent. How should \(C_{y}\) be written? Signal and input noise both pass through A, whereas output noise is added afterward. The two noise sources therefore cannot be placed at the same point in the model. \(C_{y}=A(C_{s}+C_{\eta _{x}})A^\mathrm{T}+C_{\eta _{y}}\); for isotropic noise, \(C_{y}=A(C_{s}+\sigma _{x}^2I)A^\mathrm{T}+\sigma _{y}^2I\). After whitening makes covariance I, why does left multiplication by any orthogonal U leave output covariance equal to I? Second-order decorrelation requires normalized orthogonal axes but does not uniquely specify their spatial form. Center-surround filters require translation or rotation symmetry, locality, or other constraints. Because \(U I U^\mathrm{T}=UU^\mathrm{T}=I\). Why does negative differential entropy not mean probability theory has failed? A continuous density is not the probability of one outcome; it may exceed 1, and its entropy contains the coordinate bin size or units. Rescaling a variable adds a log-scale term. Shared scale contributions cancel in MI, which remains nonnegative and retains its dependence interpretation. This is the distinction tested in Barlow's Hypotheses and the Foundations of Information Theory. Worked example — Binary Entropy and Predictability: Compute the entropy of \(\operatorname{Bernoulli} p=0.5\) and \(p=0.9\) using \(\log 2\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Compute the entropy of \(\operatorname{Bernoulli} p=0.5\) and \(p=0.9\) using \(\log 2\). \(H(0.5)=-0.5log2(0.5)-0.5log2(0.5)=1\) bit. \(H(0.9)=-0.9log2(0.9)-0.1log2(0.1)\approx 0.137+0.332=0.469\) bit. At \(p=0.9\) the outcome is more predictable, so expected surprise is lower. This has nothing to do with the numerical mean of the random variable. As \(p\to 1\), \(H\to 0\). Exchanging p with 1-p leaves entropy unchanged because it merely swaps outcome labels. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Barlow's Hypotheses and the Foundations of Information Theory”? Efficient coding is constrained optimization, not the unique mechanism behind every sensory feature. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Barlow's Hypotheses and the Foundations of Information Theory”? The logarithmic form of surprise follows because independent probabilities multiply while their information adds. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Barlow's Hypotheses and the Foundations of Information Theory” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Efficient coding is constrained optimization, not the unique mechanism behind every sensory feature. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Equivalent Forms of Mutual Information and Independence”? Probabilities and their ratios are dimensionless, making the logarithm valid. A differential density has reciprocal units, which is why a standalone differential entropy depends on coordinate units. A deterministic continuous relation can yield infinite MI in the ideal zero-noise limit. Finite measurement noise and discretization alter the numerical estimate. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: How can the idea that a sensory system should not waste spikes on predictable content be converted into quantitative measures of uncertainty and dependence? This lesson retain three ideas from Barlow: detect “passwords” of critical significance, filter signals for other nervous-system regions, and recode sensory messages to reduce redundancy. This lecture focuses on the third. Efficient coding explains why a code is advantageous under specified input statistics, noise, and cost. It is a normative hypothesis; the same receptive field may also have developmental, biophysical, or task-specific explanations. Surprise for one outcome should increase as its probability decreases, and surprises for independent events should add. Because their joint probability is pq, the continuous monotone solution of \(S(pq)=S(p)+S(q)\) is \(S(p)=-\log_{bp}\). Base 2 gives bits and base e gives nats; an event of probability 1 has zero surprise. Why does moving input and output noise into one term before A change the optimization? A reshapes input noise, so increasing gain at one frequency also amplifies its input noise. Output noise does not pass through A, and increasing gain can improve signal relative to output noise. Their effects on the gain tradeoff differ and cannot be merged. This is the distinction tested in The Noisy Retina of Atick and Redlich and Covariance Propagation. Worked example — Transforming Signal and Noise Together in a Two-Dimensional Encoder: Let \(C_{s}=\operatorname{diag}(9,1)\), input noise \(C_\eta x=I\), \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,2)\), and output noise \(C_\eta y=0.25I\). Find \(C_{y}\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(C_{s}=\operatorname{diag}(9,1)\), input noise \(C_\eta x=I\), \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,2)\), and output noise \(C_\eta y=0.25I\). Find \(C_{y}\). \(C_{x}=C_{s}+I=\operatorname{diag}(10,2)\). \(AC_{x}A^\mathrm{T}=\operatorname{diag}((1/2)^2\times 10,2^2\times 2)=\operatorname{diag}(2.5,8)\). \(C_{y}=\operatorname{diag}(2.5,8)+\operatorname{diag}(0.25,0.25)=\operatorname{diag}(2.75,8.25)\). For \(A=0\), only 0.25I remains in \(C_{y}\). The output appears decorrelated but contains no s, showing that decorrelation alone is not a valid objective. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “The Noisy Retina of Atick and Redlich and Covariance Propagation”? Input noise is added before encoder A and is filtered; output noise is added afterward. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “The Noisy Retina of Atick and Redlich and Covariance Propagation”? Covariance propagates as \(ACA^\mathrm{T}\), and independent additive noises enter at their respective stages. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “The Noisy Retina of Atick and Redlich and Covariance Propagation” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Covariance propagates as \(ACA^\mathrm{T}\), and independent additive noises enter at their respective stages. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Deriving Output Covariance Step by Step”? If s and x are dimensionless contrast and A has units output/contrast, then \(AC_{x}A^\mathrm{T}\) has \(\mathrm{output}^2\) units and can be added to \(C_{\eta _{y}}\). When \(\eta _{x}\) correlates with s or noise depends on the stimulus, cross-terms do not vanish and the simple independent additive model fails. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What crucial conditions are missing from the statement “decorrelation produces center-surround filters”? Decorrelation requires only a diagonal or whitened output covariance, and any subsequent orthogonal rotation satisfies it equally well. Translation and rotation symmetry, locality, wiring, noise, or cost constraints are needed to select center-surround filters from the equivalent solutions. This is the distinction tested in Gaussian Information, Nonunique Decorrelation, and the Selection of Center-Surround Filters. Worked example — Rotation Ambiguity in Two-Dimensional Whitening: Let \(C_{x}=\operatorname{diag}(4,1)\), \(V=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1)\), and 45° rotation \(U=(1/\sqrt 2)[[1,-1],[1,1]]\). Compare the pre-output-noise code covariances of V and UV, then state when MI is also invariant. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(C_{x}=\operatorname{diag}(4,1)\), \(V=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1)\), and 45° rotation \(U=(1/\sqrt 2)[[1,-1],[1,1]]\). Compare the pre-output-noise code covariances of V and UV, then state when MI is also invariant. \(VC_{x}V^\mathrm{T}=\operatorname{diag}((1/2)^2\times 4,1)=I\). With \(A'=UV\), \(A'C_{x}A'^\mathrm{T}=U I U^\mathrm{T}=I\). The outputs of V align with the original axes, whereas those of UV are 45° mixtures of the two whitened coordinates. Before output noise, both have decorrelated unit variance. If subsequent noise is \(\sigma _{y}^{2}I\), adding it also contributes the same \(\sigma _{y}^{2}\) on both output axes. If U is not orthogonal—for example, if its first row is multiplied by 2—the pre-noise covariance is no longer I. If output-noise covariance is anisotropic, orthogonal U alone also does not imply invariant MI. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Gaussian Information, Nonunique Decorrelation, and the Selection of Center-Surround Filters”? The determinant ratio in Gaussian MI compares total output covariance with conditional noise covariance. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Gaussian Information, Nonunique Decorrelation, and the Selection of Center-Surround Filters”? Whitening and decorrelation are nonunique under orthogonal rotations. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Gaussian Information, Nonunique Decorrelation, and the Selection of Center-Surround Filters” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? A unique center-surround form requires symmetry, locality, or other additional constraints; redundancy reduction alone does not imply it. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “From Gaussian Entropy to an Information Constraint and Rotation Ambiguity”? \(\det C_{y}\) and \(\det C_{y|s}\) share units output-units^{2d}, so their ratio and its logarithm are dimensionless. Whitening usually standardizes outputs to unit variance; retaining physical units requires an additional scale matrix. For singular covariance, restrict the log determinant to the supported subspace or regularize it. Non-Gaussian components can remain dependent even when covariance is I, allowing higher-order objectives to break the rotational degeneracy. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Redundancy Reduction in a Noisy Sensory Channel Must Respect Fidelity and Output-Cost Constraints”? Encoder A transforms signal and input noise together, whereas output noise enters after A. A diagonal output covariance alone therefore does not guarantee useful coding. In the Atick–Redlich framework, redundancy is reduced subject to retained-information and output-power or dynamic-range constraints. Whitening removes second-order correlations, but any orthogonal rotation preserves whitened covariance; localized center-surround filters require additional assumptions such as symmetry and locality. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “efficient coding” mean in this lecture? efficient coding: A normative principle for optimizing an information representation under resource and noise constraints. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “redundancy” mean in this lecture? redundancy: Structure that is predictable from other components and transmitted repeatedly. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “surprise” mean in this lecture? surprise: The −log probability of an event. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “entropy” mean in this lecture? entropy: Average surprise or uncertainty. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “conditional entropy” mean in this lecture? conditional entropy: Residual uncertainty after another variable is given. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “mutual information” mean in this lecture? mutual information: The reduction in uncertainty about one variable supplied by another. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “differential entropy” mean in this lecture? differential entropy: An entropy-like quantity for a continuous density that can be negative and depends on units. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “channel capacity” mean in this lecture? channel capacity: The maximum mutual information attainable under input constraints. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “decorrelation” mean in this lecture? decorrelation: Making off-diagonal covariance entries approach zero. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “Surprise” be used? Surprise: \(S(x) = - \log p(x)\). title: Lecture 16: Adaptation, Natural Scene Statistics, and Fourier Analysis
subtitle: Adaptation, Natural Scene Statistics, and Fourier Analysis
text: Adaptation, Natural Scene Statistics, and Fourier Analysis SNR → center-surround adaptation → translation invariance → Fourier basis → convolution theorem → power spectrum Explain from the relative strengths of input signal and noise why decorrelating filters are appropriate at high SNR while spatial averaging serves a different objective at low SNR. Express translation-invariant image statistics as a correlation function of displacement alone and explain why complex exponentials are the natural basis of convolution operators. Derive the convolution theorem and output power-spectrum equation step by step, then infer the frequency trend of a whitening filter from the approximate natural-image spectrum \(1/|\xi |^{2}\). Design an LNP comparison across illumination levels or stimulus statistics that separates a change in the linear filter, a change in the static nonlinearity, and a mere response-scale change. The central prediction of Atick–Redlich theory is not one fixed filter but a filter that changes with SNR: high SNR permits strong decorrelation, while low SNR favors spatial averaging and denoising. Approximate translation invariance of natural scenes makes covariance depend only on displacement, allowing Fourier modes to diagonalize convolution and covariance. Natural-image power falls approximately with inverse squared spatial frequency. Perfect whitening would boost high frequencies, but optics, photoreceptors, and noise suppress excessive high-frequency gain. Treating the Fourier transform as a table of physically meaningless formulas. Confusing spatial-frequency magnitude, orientation, and phase. Assuming complex numbers introduce an additional biological variable; they are a representational tool. Using the convolution theorem without a normalization or sign convention. Treating \(1/|\xi |^{2}\) as an exact law for every image. Letting perfect whitening amplify high frequencies without bound while ignoring optics and noise.
