Comparing only firing rates in an adaptation experiment and not the filter or nonlinearity. Do not teach the Fourier transform as a formula table. Always explain the physical meaning of spatial frequency for an image and receptive field, and state what amplitude and phase each represent. Signal-to-noise ratio SN \(R = S/N\) One frequency and measurement convention Translation-invariant covariance \(C(\rho _{1}, \rho _{2} ) = C(\rho _{1} - \rho _{2} )\) Stationary field Fourier transform \(\hat{s}(\xi ) = e^{-i2\pi \xi }\cdot x s(x)dx\) Chosen normalization Euler's identity ei\(\theta  = \cos \theta  + i \sin \theta \) Complex representation Convolution theorem \ \(K \ast  s = \hat{K}\) \(\hat{s}\) Linear shift-invariant filtering Power spectrum \(P (\xi ) = E[|\hat{s}(\xi )|2 ]\) Ensemble or time average Perfect-whitening magnitude −1/2 |K̂| ∝ Pin No additional noise or cost adaptation A change in response or model parameters with stimulus statistics or state. signal-to-noise ratio, SNR Signal magnitude or power relative to noise. translation invariance Statistics or an operator that do not depend on absolute position. spatial frequency Sinusoidal cycles per unit distance; the vector also encodes direction. Fourier transform A conversion between position and frequency representations. complex \(\operatorname{exponential} A\) unified representation of sine/cosine amplitude and phase. power spectrum Mean squared amplitude of each frequency component. whitening Making an output spectrum or covariance approximately flat or identity. low-pass Preserving low frequencies while suppressing high frequencies. aliasing Undersampling that makes a high frequency appear as a lower one. Four adjacent receptors all receive common signal value 8, and each has independent noise with standard deviation 2. After averaging the four, what are the signal mean and noise standard deviation? Averaging does not attenuate a signal identical across the four channels. Independent-noise variances add and are then divided by \(4^{2}\). This is the quantitative reason spatial pooling can improve readability at low SNR. The common signal remains 8; the average noise variance is \(4/4=1\), so its standard deviation is 1. A two-dimensional grating is \(\cos(\xi \cdot x)\). Are its equal-luminance stripes parallel or perpendicular to frequency vector \(\xi\)? \(\xi\) points along fastest phase increase, not along the stripes themselves. Confusing those directions rotates an orientation-tuning interpretation by ninety degrees. Equal-luminance lines have constant \(\xi \cdot x\), so motion along a stripe must leave the dot product unchanged. The stripe direction is perpendicular to \(\xi\). If \(y(x)=(K*s)(x)\), how is \(\hat{y}(\xi )\) written in the Fourier domain? The multiplication magnitude determines amplification or attenuation at that frequency, and its phase determines spatial shift. Each frequency mode can therefore be analyzed independently. \(\hat{y}(\xi )=\hat{K}(\xi )\hat{s}(\xi )\): spatial convolution becomes complex multiplication at each frequency. Suppose the natural-image input spectrum is \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(\xi )\propto 1/|\xi |^{2}\). If complete whitening is the sole objective, how should \(|\hat{K}(\xi )|\) vary with \(|\xi |\)? That is the ideal noise-free result. Real retinas are also limited by optical low-pass filtering, receptor noise, and metabolic cost, so gain cannot grow without bound at the highest frequencies. \(|\hat{K}(\xi )|\) should increase approximately linearly with \(|\xi |\), because \(|\hat{K}|^{2}P_{\mathrm{in}}\) must be constant across frequencies. Why should a weaker surround in low light not be summarized as the visual system “no longer caring about edges”? Edges can remain behaviorally important. The change means that current high-frequency evidence is unreliable relative to noise and strong differencing would amplify noise. The system temporarily sacrifices resolution for a more stable estimate; the behavioral target need not have changed. This is the distinction tested in SNR Selects the Filtering Objective: Remove Redundancy or Reduce Noise. Worked example — Comparing Four-Point Averaging with Neighbor Differencing: A flat region has common signal 10 and independent pixel noise of standard deviation 2. Compute the noise standard deviation after averaging four pixels, then for the difference x1-x2. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: A flat region has common signal 10 and independent pixel noise of standard deviation 2. Compute the noise standard deviation after averaging four pixels, then for the difference x1-x2. The four-point average preserves common value 10. Its noise variance is \(2^{2}/4=1\), so standard deviation is 1. Neighbor differencing cancels the common value, \(10-10=0\). Its noise is \(\epsilon _{1}-\epsilon _{2}\), with variance \(2^{2}+2^{2}=8\). The difference-noise standard deviation is \(\sqrt 8\approx 2.83\), larger than that of one pixel. This cost is worthwhile only when the edge signal is strong enough. If both channels contain identical rather than independent noise, differencing cancels it. The result shows why noise correlation structure must be stated. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “SNR Selects the Filtering Objective: Remove Redundancy or Reduce Noise”? At high SNR, reliable high-frequency information lets center-surround differencing reduce redundancy across neighboring channels. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “SNR Selects the Filtering Objective: Remove Redundancy or Reduce Noise”? At low SNR, spatial averaging preserves common signal and lowers independent-noise standard deviation at the cost of spatial resolution. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “SNR Selects the Filtering Objective: Remove Redundancy or Reduce Noise” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? At high SNR, reliable high-frequency information lets center-surround differencing reduce redundancy across neighboring channels. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “How Noise Shrinks When n Neighboring Measurements Are Averaged”? x, s, \(\epsilon\), and y share luminance or voltage units. n and SNR are dimensionless; variance has squared signal units. For \(n=1\), noise is unchanged. As n grows, independent noise falls, but signal bias increases if the signal varies within the window, so an infinitely large window cannot produce infinite performance. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: Why might one visual system strengthen center-surround filtering in bright conditions but behave more like a spatial averager in dim conditions? This section interprets filter shape along an SNR axis. At high SNR, input detail is reliable relative to internal and photon noise. Neighboring pixels are then strongly correlated, and transmitting them unchanged wastes limited output dynamic range on repeated information. An excitatory-center, inhibitory-surround difference kernel suppresses common slow components while retaining edges, reducing output correlations. A strong surround is a normative prediction under specified statistics and costs; it does not alone establish its synaptic implementation. At low SNR, differencing creates another problem: subtracting two channels removes their common signal but imports both independent noise sources into the result. When genuine high-frequency signal is already buried in noise, amplifying high frequencies wastes firing range. Spatial pooling sums or averages nearby measurements. Shared low-frequency structure adds coherently, whereas independent noise adds in variance, raising output SNR. A broad same-sign receptive field is then more useful than a sharp center-surround. Why do Fourier modes “diagonalize” a translation-invariant linear filter? After convolution, each input mode \(e^{i\xi \cdot x}\) remains the same \(\xi\) and is multiplied only by complex number \(\hat{K}(\xi )\); distinct \(\xi\) never mix. In this basis, the operator is represented by diagonal gains, one per mode. This is the distinction tested in From Translation-Invariant Statistics to Fourier Diagonalization. Worked example — Passing a Sinusoid Through a Filter with Amplitude and Phase: The input is \(s(x)=3\cos(2x)\). At \(\xi =2\) the filter response is \(\hat{K}(2)=0.5e^{-i\pi /4}\). Find the output sinusoid's amplitude and phase shift. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: The input is \(s(x)=3\cos(2x)\). At \(\xi =2\) the filter response is \(\hat{K}(2)=0.5e^{-i\pi /4}\). Find the output sinusoid's amplitude and phase shift. The input contains only the conjugate frequency pair \(\xi =+2\) and \(\xi =-2\), with real-space amplitude 3. Multiplying each component by \(\hat{K}\) scales amplitude from 3 to 1.5 because its magnitude is 0.5. The angle \(-\pi /4\) adds phase \(-\pi /4\) to the positive-frequency component, so \(y(x)=1.5\cos(2x-\pi /4)\). A linear translation-invariant filter cannot turn one sinusoid into a new frequency. Obtaining \(\xi =4\) means multiplication was mistaken for a nonlinear square. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “From Translation-Invariant Statistics to Fourier Diagonalization”? Translation-invariant covariance depends only on positional difference, making Fourier modes statistically nonmixing directions. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “From Translation-Invariant Statistics to Fourier Diagonalization”? Frequency vector \(\xi\) is perpendicular to image stripes, and \(|\xi |\) sets spatial oscillation speed. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “From Translation-Invariant Statistics to Fourier Diagonalization” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Frequency vector \(\xi\) is perpendicular to image stripes, and \(|\xi |\) sets spatial oscillation speed. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Deriving the Convolution Theorem Term by Term”? If spatial integral dx' has area units and y and s share units, K must have inverse-area units. Fourier-transform scale units depend on convention but remain consistent on both sides. For a delta-function K, \(\hat{K}=1\) and every frequency passes unchanged. For a broad averaging K, \(\hat{K}\) is concentrated at low frequency, matching the smoothing intuition. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why must an LNP filter's scale convention be fixed before comparing two adaptation conditions? Multiplying k by constant a while dividing the nonlinearity's horizontal axis by a gives identical firing predictions. Without fixing ||k|| or another convention, an apparent gain change can be only parameterization nonuniqueness. This is the distinction tested in Natural-Image Power Spectra, Whitening, and Testable Adaptation. Worked example — Whitening Two Frequencies and Its Noise Cost: Let \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(1)=16\) and \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(4)=1\), and require output signal power 4 at both frequencies. Find both gains. Then assume post-input noise power 1 at each frequency and compute output noise powers. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(1)=16\) and \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(4)=1\), and require output signal power 4 at both frequencies. Find both gains. Then assume post-input noise power 1 at each frequency and compute output noise powers. From \(|K|^{2}P_{\mathrm{in}}=4\), the low-frequency gain is \(|K(1)|=\sqrt{4/16}=0.5\). The high-frequency gain is \(|K(4)|=\sqrt{4/1}=2\), consistent with a fourfold frequency difference and a fourfold gain difference. Noise is also multiplied by squared gain, so low-frequency output noise is 0.25 and high-frequency output noise is 4. Although signal powers are equalized, high-frequency SNR remains worse. Substitution confirms equal signal powers: \(0.5^{2}\times 16=4\) and \(2^{2}\times 1=4\). Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Natural-Image Power Spectra, Whitening, and Testable Adaptation”? Linear filtering yields \(P_{\mathrm{out}}(\xi )=|\hat{K}(\xi )|^{2}P_{\mathrm{in}}(\xi )\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Natural-Image Power Spectra, Whitening, and Testable Adaptation”? For \(P_{\mathrm{in}}\propto 1/|\xi |^{2}\), noise-free whitening gives \(|\hat{K}|\propto |\xi |\), but optics and noise force real filters to roll off at high frequency. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Natural-Image Power Spectra, Whitening, and Testable Adaptation” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Cross-condition LNP comparisons must fix filter scale, estimate each nonlinearity separately, and test parameter swaps on held-out data. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Inferring Whitening Gain from the Input Power Spectrum”? If input and output share signal units, \(|\hat{K}|\) is dimensionless gain. P has \(\mathrm{signal}^{2}\) units, and c has the same units as \(P_{\mathrm{out}}\). As \(|\xi |\to 0\), ideal gain tends to zero, removing the global mean. As \(|\xi |\to \infty\), the formula diverges, exposing its noise-free infinite-bandwidth assumptions; a real system must regularize. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Noise Truncates the Ideal High-Frequency Gain of Natural-Image Whitening”? If natural-image power is approximated by \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(\xi )\propto 1/|\xi |^{2}\) and noise and gain limits are temporarily ignored, flattening \(P_{\mathrm{out}}=|\hat{K}|^{2}P_{\mathrm{in}}\) requires \(|\hat{K}|\propto |\xi |\). Real optics attenuate extreme high-frequency signal without eliminating approximately flat output noise, so a noise-aware filter rolls off at high frequencies. When SNR falls further, the reliable band narrows and favors pooling. All three curves are normalized theoretical sketches, not empirical measurements. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “adaptation” mean in this lecture? adaptation: A change in response or model parameters with stimulus statistics or state. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “signal-to-noise ratio, SNR” mean in this lecture? signal-to-noise ratio, SNR: Signal magnitude or power relative to noise. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “translation invariance” mean in this lecture? translation invariance: Statistics or an operator that do not depend on absolute position. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “spatial frequency” mean in this lecture? spatial frequency: Sinusoidal cycles per unit distance; the vector also encodes direction. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “Fourier transform” mean in this lecture? Fourier transform: A conversion between position and frequency representations. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “complex exponential” mean in this lecture? complex exponential: A unified representation of sine/cosine amplitude and phase. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “power spectrum” mean in this lecture? power spectrum: Mean squared amplitude of each frequency component. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “whitening” mean in this lecture? whitening: Making an output spectrum or covariance approximately flat or identity. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “low-pass” mean in this lecture? low-pass: Preserving low frequencies while suppressing high frequencies. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “Signal-to-noise ratio” be used? Signal-to-noise ratio: SN \(R = S/N\). One frequency and measurement convention This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Translation-invariant covariance” be used? Translation-invariant covariance: \(C(\rho _{1}, \rho _{2} ) = C(\rho _{1} - \rho _{2} )\). Stationary field This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Fourier transform” be used? Fourier transform: \(\hat{s}(\xi ) = e^{-i2\pi \xi }\cdot x s(x)dx\). Chosen normalization This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Euler's identity” be used? Euler's identity: ei\(\theta  = \cos \theta  + i \sin \theta \). Complex representation This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Convolution theorem” be used? Convolution theorem: \ \(K \ast  s = \hat{K}\) \(\hat{s}\). Linear shift-invariant filtering This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Power spectrum” be used? Power spectrum: \(P (\xi ) = E[|\hat{s}(\xi )|2 ]\). Ensemble or time average This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Perfect-whitening magnitude” be used? Perfect-whitening magnitude: −1/2 |K̂| ∝ Pin. No additional noise or cost This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written.

title: Lecture 17: Visual Networks: Cascades, Complex Cells, and Recurrence
subtitle: Visual Networks: Cascades, Complex Cells, and Recurrence
text: Visual Networks: Cascades, Complex Cells, and Recurrence LNP cascade → simple-cell pooling → complex-cell \(STA=0\)→ quadrature energy → task-optimized models → E/I recurrence Distinguish linear selectivity in simple cells from phase invariance in complex cells, and explain why an even-symmetric response can drive the first-order STA toward zero. Derive phase invariance step by step from the two linear outputs of a quadrature pair while stating the amplitude and orientation dependence that remains. Separate task training of an optimized model from evaluation of neural predictivity, and design a comparison that never leaks test neural data. Write the fixed-point equations and nullclines of an E/I rate network and analyze how surround input can produce suppression without raising inhibitory rate. Use local stability to define an inhibition-stabilized network and avoid reducing ISN to “strong inhibition.” Feedforward cascades can construct selectivity and invariance stage by stage, but descriptive blocks do not automatically identify biological mechanisms. Complex cells are approximately invariant to grating phase, so a single linear STA can be zero; a quadrature-pair square-and-sum energy model is a minimal explanation. Surround suppression likewise is not simply “more inhibition”: recurrent E/I dynamics can make excitation and inhibition fall together, with excitation falling more. Nullclines show the fixed-point shift, while Jacobian stability and an unstable E-only subsystem establish an inhibition-stabilized regime. Treating a descriptive LNP cascade automatically as anatomy or mechanism. Concluding from complex-cell \(STA=0\) that there is no stimulus selectivity. Forgetting that squaring changes sign and phase information. Treating task accuracy and neural predictivity as the same metric. Equating surround suppression with a necessary increase in inhibitory firing or conductance. Reading ISN as meaning that inhibitory rate is always higher. Locating a fixed point without checking its stability. State explicitly that “complex-cell \(STA=0\)” does not mean “no stimulus selectivity”; it is a central counterexample in nonlinear system identification. Motion or orientation energy model \(E = (K_{1} \ast  s)2 + (K_{2} \ast  s)2\) Quadrature filters Phase-invariance identity \(\cos 2 \varphi  + \sin 2 \varphi  = 1\) Ideal pair Linear model-to-neuron mapping \(\hat{r} = Bz\) Fixed features z E/I nullclines \(\dot{r}E = 0\), \(\dot{r}I = 0\) Steady state Rate-network fixed point \(r = F (W r + I)\) Chosen nonlinearities Intuitive ISN criterion E-only unstable + feedback I stable Local effective gain matters cascade Several processing stages composed in sequence. simple cell A classical V1 cell type selective for orientation and sensitive to spatial phase. complex cell A classical V1 cell type selective for orientation but more invariant to phase. quadrature pair Matched filters separated by 90° of phase. energy model A nonlinear model that squares and sums quadrature-filter outputs. neural predictivity How well model features predict neural responses. surround suppression A reduction in center response when the receptive-field surround is stimulated. nullcline A phase-plane curve on which one state derivative equals zero. inhibition-stabilized network, ISN A network whose E subnetwork is unstable alone but stabilized by feedback inhibition. A neuron responds identically to filter projections z and -z. Why can the first-order average of spike-triggered stimuli be nearly zero? A zero STA rules out one signed linear direction as a complete account, not selectivity for |z| or \(z^{2}\). STC or an energy feature can detect the latter. Spikes select large projections on both the positive and negative sides. With a symmetric stimulus distribution, the two trigger means point in opposite directions and cancel. If \(L_{1}=A\cos\phi\) and \(L_{2}=A\sin\phi\), does \(L_{1}^{2}+L_{2}^{2}\) depend on phase \(\phi\)? A quadrature pair turns phase into rotation of a two-dimensional vector; the squared sum reads its length and ignores its direction. No. Since \(\cos^{2}\phi +\sin^{2}\phi =1\), the sum of squares is always \(A^{2}\). Must a network with higher classification accuracy predict visual-cortical responses better? Choosing a layer, mapping, or network after inspecting test neural data inflates predictivity through selection bias. The evaluation pipeline must keep these data isolated. No. Task performance constrains only the final behavioral output, while internal representations may differ. Predictivity must be tested separately on held-out neural stimuli. After surround stimulation, both excitatory and inhibitory rates fall. Can recurrent inhibition still contribute to the suppression? A lower I rate does not make inhibition irrelevant. Analyze the recurrent equations, the changed inputs, and the fixed-point shift rather than treating inhibitory firing itself as inhibitory current. Yes. Surround input can first reduce network excitation, causing the inhibitory population to receive less drive. If E falls more, the net outcome remains suppression. Why does the energy model retain orientation tuning after gaining phase invariance? Phase rotates the matched quadrature outputs in their two-dimensional plane. Changing orientation reduces both filter projections' common amplitude A, so \(A^{2}\) still falls with orientation mismatch. This is the distinction tested in From Simple-Cell Pooling to Complex-Cell Energy. Worked example — Equal Energy at Three Phases: Let \(A=4\) and compute L1, L2, and E at \(\phi =0\), \(\pi /4\), and \(\pi /2\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(A=4\) and compute L1, L2, and E at \(\phi =0\), \(\pi /4\), and \(\pi /2\). For \(\phi =0\), \(L_{1}=4\) and \(L_{2}=0\), hence \(E=16\). For \(\phi =\pi /4\), \(L_{1}=L_{2}=4/\sqrt 2\); each square is 8, hence \(E=16\). For \(\phi =\pi /2\), \(L_{1}=0\) and \(L_{2}=4\), hence \(E=16\). Every pair (L1,L2) lies on a circle of radius 4, and the sum of squares is the squared radius. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “From Simple-Cell Pooling to Complex-Cell Energy”? Spatially aligned simple-cell pooling produces orientation selectivity while preserving phase sensitivity. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “From Simple-Cell Pooling to Complex-Cell Energy”? A complex-cell energy model uses the squared sum of a quadrature pair to turn stimulus phase into an ignored two-dimensional angle. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “From Simple-Cell Pooling to Complex-Cell Energy” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Spatially aligned simple-cell pooling produces orientation selectivity while preserving phase sensitivity. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Why Quadrature Energy Is Invariant to Phase”? If linear outputs use drive units of spikes/s, their squared sum has \(drive^{2}\) units. A final output nonlinearity can map it back to firing rate. When \(A=0\), every phase gives \(E=0\). If the second filter has twice the gain of the first, the squared sum varies with \(\phi\) and phase invariance fails. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: How can two filters separated by one-quarter period retain orientation selectivity while discarding grating phase? This section links cascade models to the Hubel–Wiesel construction. If multiple LGN-like center-surround units are arranged along an oblique axis and pooled with same-sign weights, only a light-dark edge matching that arrangement drives many inputs together, producing an elongated simple-cell receptive field. This construction explains the spatial geometry of orientation selectivity but remains sensitive to light-dark position: translating the same grating by half a period reverses the linear projection. The challenge for a complex cell is phase invariance. If it responds strongly to both positive and negative phases of a grating at one orientation, a linear STA averages the two spike-triggered groups toward zero. This section instead uses two filters separated by 90° of spatial phase—a quadrature pair. As input phase changes, their linear outputs carry energy in turn like two coordinates. Squaring and adding reads vector radius rather than angle. Why is it invalid to repeatedly select the most brain-like network layer on test neural stimuli and report its highest correlation on the same data? Repeated layer selection already uses the test responses. The maximum contains positive selection noise and is biased upward. Choose layers and regularization on validation neural data and perform the final evaluation once on an independent test set. This is the distinction tested in Task Optimization and Neural Predictivity Are Two Different Tests. Worked example — A Least-Squares Readout from One Feature: For three training stimuli, the model feature is \(z=[1,2,3]\) and one neuron's responses are \(r=[2,4,5]\). Without an intercept, find scalar weight b and predict the response at \(z=4\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: For three training stimuli, the model feature is \(z=[1,2,3]\) and one neuron's responses are \(r=[2,4,5]\). Without an intercept, find scalar weight b and predict the response at \(z=4\). The one-dimensional normal equation gives \(b=(z^\mathrm{T} r)/(z^\mathrm{T} z)\). \(z^\mathrm{T} r=1\times 2+2\times 4+3\times 5=25\) and \(z^\mathrm{T}z=1+4+9=14\), so \(b=25/14\approx 1.786\). For a new stimulus with \(z=4\), prediction is \(4b=100/14\approx 7.14\). Its reliability must be tested against the actual held-out response. If \(r=2z\) exactly, the formula returns \(b=2\). Here the third point is below 6, so the fitted slope is slightly below 2. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Task Optimization and Neural Predictivity Are Two Different Tests”? Task training determines the representation; a neural readout and held-out evaluation test its alignment with biological responses. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Task Optimization and Neural Predictivity Are Two Different Tests”? Classification performance and neural predictivity answer different questions and must be reported separately. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Task Optimization and Neural Predictivity Are Two Different Tests” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Classification performance and neural predictivity answer different questions and must be reported separately. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Deriving a Neural Readout from a Least-Squares Objective”? The units of Z depend on network activations. B has neural-response-units per feature-unit so that ZB and R both use spikes/s or trial counts. With only a constant column in Z, the model predicts only each neuron's mean response. If \(d\ge N\) without regularization, training error may be tiny while overfitting is severe. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does lower inhibitory-neuron firing after surround not imply that inhibition did not cause surround suppression? A firing rate is the network fixed-point outcome, while inhibitory current also depends on connectivity and presynaptic rate. Surround can first lower E drive and thereby lower I, even though I feedback still determines the fixed point at which E amplification is contained. This is the distinction tested in E/I Recurrence, Nullclines, and Inhibition Stabilization. Worked example — Surround Suppression with Simultaneous Decreases in E and I Rates: Use the derived network. For center only, \(I_{E}=10\) and \(I_{I}=2\). With surround, \(I_{E}\) remains 10 but drive \(I_{I}\) to the inhibitory population rises to 5. Find both fixed points. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Use the derived network. For center only, \(I_{E}=10\) and \(I_{I}=2\). With surround, \(I_{E}\) remains 10 but drive \(I_{I}\) to the inhibitory population rises to 5. Find both fixed points. Center only: \(r_{E}=(10-2)/0.8=10\) and \(r_{I}=r_{E}+2=12\). Surround: \(r_{E}=(10-5)/0.8=6.25\) and \(r_{I}=r_{E}+5=11.25\). Thus E falls from 10 to 6.25 and I from 12 to 11.25. Although the I population receives more external drive, its steady rate falls slightly because recurrent E input falls more. Substitution verifies the surround E equation: \(-6.25+1.2\times 6.25-11.25+10=0\); and I equation: \(-11.25+6.25+5=0\). Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “E/I Recurrence, Nullclines, and Inhibition Stabilization”? Surround suppression is a shift of the full recurrent fixed point and does not require an increase in inhibitory firing rate. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “E/I Recurrence, Nullclines, and Inhibition Stabilization”? Nullcline intersections give steady states; local vector fields or Jacobian eigenvalues determine stability. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “E/I Recurrence, Nullclines, and Inhibition Stabilization” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? An ISN has an unstable E-only subsystem but a stable complete E/I loop; it is not merely a network with qualitatively strong inhibition. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Fixed Point, Surround Shift, and Local Stability in a Linear E/I Network”? For rates in spikes/s, dimensionless weights map presynaptic rates into drive of the same units, and \(I_{E}\),\(I_{I}\) are equivalent rate drives. Jacobian eigenvalues contain \(1/\tau\) and therefore have reciprocal-time units. Setting \(w_{\mathrm{EI}}\) or \(w_{\mathrm{IE}}\) to zero breaks the stabilizing E/I feedback loop. If E gain exceeds leak, the E-only mode runs away, exposing the ISN condition. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “After Surround Input Shifts the I-Nullcline, Both E and I Can Fall at the Stable Intersection”? In a locally linear E/I rate model, a nullcline intersection is a steady state. Increasing surround drive to the I population shifts the I-nullcline upward. Its new intersection with the fixed E-nullcline can have both lower \(r_{E}\) and lower \(r_{I}\), so surround suppression does not require inhibitory firing to rise. The curves are normalized geometric sketches of the course equations. Full stability still requires Jacobian eigenvalues and cannot be inferred from line intersection alone. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “cascade” mean in this lecture? cascade: Several processing stages composed in sequence. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “simple cell” mean in this lecture? simple cell: A classical V1 cell type selective for orientation and sensitive to spatial phase. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “complex cell” mean in this lecture? complex cell: A classical V1 cell type selective for orientation but more invariant to phase. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “quadrature pair” mean in this lecture? quadrature pair: Matched filters separated by 90° of phase. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “energy model” mean in this lecture? energy model: A nonlinear model that squares and sums quadrature-filter outputs. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “neural predictivity” mean in this lecture? neural predictivity: How well model features predict neural responses. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “surround suppression” mean in this lecture? surround suppression: A reduction in center response when the receptive-field surround is stimulated. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “nullcline” mean in this lecture? nullcline: A phase-plane curve on which one state derivative equals zero. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “inhibition-stabilized network, ISN” mean in this lecture? inhibition-stabilized network, ISN: A network whose E subnetwork is unstable alone but stabilized by feedback inhibition. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “Motion or orientation energy model” be used? Motion or orientation energy model: \(E = (K_{1} \ast  s)2 + (K_{2} \ast  s)2\). Quadrature filters This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Phase-invariance identity” be used? Phase-invariance identity: \(\cos 2 \varphi  + \sin 2 \varphi  = 1\). Ideal pair This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Linear model-to-neuron mapping” be used? Linear model-to-neuron mapping: \(\hat{r} = Bz\). Fixed features z This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “E/I nullclines” be used? E/I nullclines: \(\dot{r}E = 0\), \(\dot{r}I = 0\). Steady state This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Rate-network fixed point” be used? Rate-network fixed point: \(r = F (W r + I)\). Chosen nonlinearities This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Intuitive ISN criterion” be used? Intuitive ISN criterion: E-only unstable + feedback I stable. Local effective gain matters This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written.

title: Lecture 18: Motor Systems and Linear Neural Dynamics
subtitle: Motor Systems and Linear Neural Dynamics
text: Motor Systems and Linear Neural Dynamics Brain-body-environment → feedback control → recurrent rate network → eigendecomposition → mode dynamics → effective time constant Draw the brain, body, and environment as a closed-loop dynamical system and distinguish feedforward commands, sensory feedback, state estimates, and external disturbances. Generalize the first-order equation for one neuron to \(\tau dh/dt=-h+Wh+I\), correctly interpreting the direction of \(W_{ij}\) and every matrix shape. When W is diagonalizable, transform population activity into its eigenbasis and derive mutually decoupled mode equations step by step. From eigenvalue \(\lambda _{i}\), derive effective time constant \(\tau /(1-\lambda _{i})\) and interpret \(\lambda _{i}<1\), =1, and >1 as decay, integration, and instability. Find the fixed point under constant input and distinguish long memory near an integrator, a perfect integrator, and runaway positive feedback. Motor control consists of closed-loop dynamics among brain, body, and environment, and neural activity is highly distributed. In a linear recurrent network, transforming individual neuronal activities into eigenmode coordinates decouples the system so each mode behaves like an independent first-order process. Eigenvalue \(\lambda\) sets effective time constant \(\tau /(1-\lambda )\): \(\lambda <1\) decays, \(\lambda \approx 1\) has long memory, \(\lambda =1\) is a perfect integrator, and \(\lambda >1\) grows without bound. Restricting a motor signal to one region and overlooking distributed population activity. Confusing neuronal activity coordinates with eigenmode coordinates. Treating an eigenmode as one neuron. Writing \(V^{-1}WV=D\) without checking the convention that columns of V are right eigenvectors. Using \(\tau /(1-\lambda )\) as a positive decay time when \(\lambda >1\). Assuming \(\lambda =1\) is automatically robust, despite its sensitivity to perturbation. Analyzing neural dynamics without body and environmental feedback. Distinguish individual-neuron activity, population-mode coordinates, and behavioral state; do not turn an eigenmode into one “special neuron.” Linear recurrent rate network \(\tau \) \(\dot{h} = -h + W h + I\) Common \(\tau\) and linearization Diagonalization \(W = V DV -1\) Diagonalizable W Mode coordinates \(\alpha  = V -1 h\) Invertible V Decoupled mode \(\tau \) \(\dot{\alpha }i = -(1 - \lambda _{i} )\alpha _{i} + \beta _{i}\) Eigenbasis Mode time constant \(\tau ef\) \(f = \tau  /(1 - \lambda )\) \(\lambda <1\) for stable decay Perfect integrator \(\lambda  = 1 \Rightarrow  \dot{\alpha } = \beta /\tau \) Exact cancellation of feedback and leak feedforward control Control based mainly on a prior model or command rather than current feedback correction. feedback control Online correction of action from sensory or state error. proprioception Sensory feedback about body position or force. recurrent network A network with feedback loops among its units. eigenmode A population activity pattern associated with an eigenvector of W. change of basis Conversion of the same state between neuronal and modal coordinates. effective time constant A mode's decay or integration timescale after feedback. fixed point A state whose derivative is zero. stability Whether a small perturbation returns to a fixed point. perfect integrator A mode that accumulates input without leak. Under convention \((Wh)_i=\sum _j W_{ij}h_{j}\), does \(W_{ij}\) represent a connection from i to j or from j to i? Some texts use the transposed convention. Expanding the matrix multiplication first prevents reversing the connection diagram. It represents source j to target i, because \(W_{ij}h_{j}\) contributes to output component i. If \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\) and an eigenvalue \(\lambda =0\), what is the mode's effective time constant? \(\lambda =0\) means no recurrent input along that mode, so leak alone sets decay. \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau /(1-\lambda )=20 \mathrm{ms}\), equal to the intrinsic time constant without recurrent feedback. Which continuous-time mode decays more slowly, \(\lambda =0.9\) or \(\lambda =-0.5\)? For this continuous-time equation, the stability boundary for a real eigenvalue is 1, not absolute value 1, because the dynamics contain -I+W. \(\lambda =0.9\) is slower, with \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=10\tau\); \(\lambda =-0.5\) gives \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau /1.5\), so negative feedback accelerates decay beyond the intrinsic rate. Is eigenmode amplitude \(\alpha _{i}\) the firing rate of neuron i? A mode coincides with one neuron coordinate only when W is diagonal in the neuronal basis. Treating modes as neurons misreads distributed dynamics. Usually not. \(\alpha _{i}\) is the coordinate of the population vector along eigenvector \(v_{i}\), and one mode generally combines many neurons. Why does larger proportional gain improve disturbance rejection in a delay-free model but not justify infinite gain in a biological system? The ideal equation omits sensory delay, muscle dynamics, noise, saturation, and energetic cost. High gain amplifies noise and can cause overshoot or oscillation in a delayed loop, so stability must be assessed for the complete loop. This is the distinction tested in Motor Control Is a Brain–Body–Environment Loop. Worked example — Steady Position Error Under a Persistent Velocity Disturbance: For \(dx/dt=-2x+0.6\) and initial \(x(0)=1\), find the fixed point and time constant and compute position at \(t=1 \mathrm{s}\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: For \(dx/dt=-2x+0.6\) and initial \(x(0)=1\), find the fixed point and time constant and compute position at \(t=1 \mathrm{s}\). The fixed point is \(x^{*}=d/k=0.6/2=0.3\). Error \(e=x-0.3\) obeys \(de/dt=-2e\), so \(e(t)=0.7e^{-2t}\) and the time constant is 1/2 s. At \(t=1\), \(x=0.3+0.7e^{-2}\approx 0.3+0.0947=0.3947\). At initial \(x=1\), derivative=\(-2+0.6=-1.4\), so the trajectory must move downward. The computed result has the correct direction. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Motor Control Is a Brain–Body–Environment Loop”? Brain, body, and environment form a closed loop through commands, mechanics, disturbances, and sensory feedback. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Motor Control Is a Brain–Body–Environment Loop”? Feedforward control anticipates; feedback corrects disturbances. Delay, noise, and gain set the stability costs. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Motor Control Is a Brain–Body–Environment Loop” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Brain, body, and environment form a closed loop through commands, mechanics, disturbances, and sensory feedback. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “How Proportional Feedback Rejects a Constant Disturbance”? x has position units and \(dx/dt\), u, and d have position/time units. Thus kx has position/time units and k has units 1/time. As \(k\to 0\), restoring feedback disappears and constant disturbance makes position drift. Increasing k reduces ideal-model error, but an unmodeled delay can destabilize high gain. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: Why is a single command arrow from motor cortex to muscle insufficient to explain stability and correction during real movement? This section embeds the motor system in coupled brain, body, and environment dynamics. Descending pathways change muscle activation; body mechanics convert activation into posture and velocity; gravity, contact, and object reaction forces alter body state; and proprioceptive, visual, and cutaneous signals return the outcome to the nervous system. Every arrow has delay and dynamics. Movement is therefore a time-evolving closed loop, not a static stimulus-response lookup. A feedforward command acts in advance from a goal and internal model and can compensate for known delays, but it is vulnerable to unexpected disturbances and model error. A feedback controller corrects output using sensed state error and resists disturbances, but excessive gain combined with delay can oscillate. Biological control combines both, with spinal cord, brainstem, cerebellum, basal ganglia, and motor cortex contributing on different timescales and representational levels rather than taking over sequentially. For asymmetric W, why can normalized right eigenvectors not justify writing \(\alpha =V^\mathrm{T} h\)? Right eigenvectors of an asymmetric matrix are generally not orthogonal, so \(V^\mathrm{T}V\ne I\). The correct transform is \(\alpha =V^{-1}h\), equivalently using the associated left eigenvectors to read amplitudes. This is the distinction tested in The Recurrent Population Equation and Eigenmode Decomposition. Worked example — Common and Difference Modes in a Two-Neuron Network: Let \(W=[[0.8,0.1],[0.1,0.8]]\) and \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\). Find two normalized eigenvectors and eigenvalues and write the input-free mode equations. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(W=[[0.8,0.1],[0.1,0.8]]\) and \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\). Find two normalized eigenvectors and eigenvalues and write the input-free mode equations. For common pattern \(v_{+}=(1,1)/\sqrt 2\), \(Wv_{+}=(0.9,0.9)/\sqrt 2\), so \(\lambda _{+}=0.9\). For difference pattern \(v_{-}=(1,-1)/\sqrt 2\), \(Wv_{-}=(0.7,-0.7)/\sqrt 2\), so \(\lambda _{-}=0.7\). The mode equations are \(20 \mathrm{ms}\cdot d\alpha _{+}/dt=-0.1\alpha _{+}\) and \(20 \mathrm{ms}\cdot d\alpha _{-}/dt=-0.3\alpha _{-}\). The common mode decays more slowly. Matrix \(\operatorname{trace} 1.6\) equals eigenvalue \(\operatorname{sum} 0.9+0.7\), and determinant 0.63 equals product \(0.9\times 0.7\). Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “The Recurrent Population Equation and Eigenmode Decomposition”? The direction of \(W_{ij}\) follows by expanding \((Wh)_i\); here it is \(j\to i\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “The Recurrent Population Equation and Eigenmode Decomposition”? \(h=V\alpha\) decomposes neuronal-coordinate activity into amplitudes of eigenvector patterns. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “The Recurrent Population Equation and Eigenmode Decomposition” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? \(h=V\alpha\) decomposes neuronal-coordinate activity into amplitudes of eigenvector patterns. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “From the Recurrent Equation to Decoupled Mode Equations”? If V consists of dimensionless normalized patterns, \(\alpha\) and h have firing-rate units; W and \(\lambda\) are dimensionless, \(\tau\) has time units, and Ĩ has the same units as h. For \(W=0\), choose \(V=I\) and \(\lambda _{i}=0\); every neuronal mode decays independently with \(\tau\). If W is already diagonal, the basis change leaves the coordinates unchanged. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does changing \(\lambda\) from 0.98 to 0.999 create drift risk in addition to longer memory? The denominator \(1-\lambda\) shrinks from 0.02 to 0.001, multiplying timescale and constant-input gain by twenty. A tiny persistent bias, low-frequency noise, or connectivity error produces a much larger state displacement. This is the distinction tested in Eigenvalues Control Timescale, Fixed Points, and Integration. Worked example — Extending an Intrinsic 20 ms Time Constant to 1 s of Memory: A mode has \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\), \(\lambda =0.98\), initial amplitude 5, and no input. Find \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and amplitude after 1 s, then compare with \(\lambda =1\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: A mode has \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\), \(\lambda =0.98\), initial amplitude 5, and no input. Find \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and amplitude after 1 s, then compare with \(\lambda =1\). Because \(1-\lambda =0.02\), \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=20 \mathrm{ms}/0.02=1000 \mathrm{ms}=1 \mathrm{s}\). After 1 s, \(\alpha =5e^{-1}\approx 1.84\). Recurrent feedback lengthens but does not eliminate decay. For \(\lambda =1\) without input, \(d\alpha /dt=0\) and the amplitude remains 5 after 1 s. A persistent small bias would be integrated continuously. The incorrect formula \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau /(1+\lambda )\) gives about 10 ms, the opposite of the memory-lengthening effect of positive feedback. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Eigenvalues Control Timescale, Fixed Points, and Integration”? For a real eigenvalue \(\lambda <1\), \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau /(1-\lambda )\); decay slows as the eigenvalue approaches 1. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Eigenvalues Control Timescale, Fixed Points, and Integration”? \(\lambda =1\) removes leak and integrates input; \(\lambda >1\) makes the linear mode grow exponentially. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Eigenvalues Control Timescale, Fixed Points, and Integration” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Approaching 1 increases both memory time and constant-input gain, amplifying bias and connectivity error as well. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Mode Solution, Effective Time Constant, and Fixed Point”? \(\lambda\) is dimensionless, while \(\tau\) and \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) are times. \(\alpha\) and Ĩ share units, so \(\int \widetilde I ds/\tau\) retains the units of \(\alpha\). \(\lambda =0\) gives \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau\). As λ→1^-, both \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and constant gain grow. For \(\lambda >1\), the exponent changes sign and the zero fixed point is unstable. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “In the Eigenbasis, Coupled Neuronal Dynamics Decompose into Independent Modes”? If recurrent matrix W is diagonalizable as \(W=V\Lambda V^{-1}\), activity \(h=V\alpha\) expresses a neuronal-space pattern in eigenmode amplitudes. After left multiplication by \(V^{-1}\), each \(\alpha _{i}\) independently obeys \(\tau \dot{\alpha }_i=-(1-\lambda _{i})\alpha _{i}+\widetilde I_{i}\). Thus \(\lambda _{i}\), rather than one neuron, sets decay, integration, or growth of that population pattern. A basis change is a mathematical coordinate transformation; a mode is not an anatomical neuron. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “feedforward control” mean in this lecture? feedforward control: Control based mainly on a prior model or command rather than current feedback correction. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “feedback control” mean in this lecture? feedback control: Online correction of action from sensory or state error. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “proprioception” mean in this lecture? proprioception: Sensory feedback about body position or force. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “recurrent network” mean in this lecture? recurrent network: A network with feedback loops among its units. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “eigenmode” mean in this lecture? eigenmode: A population activity pattern associated with an eigenvector of W. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “change of basis” mean in this lecture? change of basis: Conversion of the same state between neuronal and modal coordinates. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “effective time constant” mean in this lecture? effective time constant: A mode's decay or integration timescale after feedback. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “fixed point” mean in this lecture? fixed point: A state whose derivative is zero. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “stability” mean in this lecture? stability: Whether a small perturbation returns to a fixed point. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “Linear recurrent rate network” be used? Linear recurrent rate network: \(\tau \) \(\dot{h} = -h + W h + I\). Common \(\tau\) and linearization This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Diagonalization” be used? Diagonalization: \(W = V DV -1\). Diagonalizable W This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Mode coordinates” be used? Mode coordinates: \(\alpha  = V -1 h\). Invertible V This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Decoupled mode” be used? Decoupled mode: \(\tau \) \(\dot{\alpha }i = -(1 - \lambda _{i} )\alpha _{i} + \beta _{i}\). Eigenbasis This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Mode time constant” be used? Mode time constant: \(\tau ef\) \(f = \tau  /(1 - \lambda )\). \(\lambda <1\) for stable decay This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Perfect integrator” be used? Perfect integrator: \(\lambda  = 1 \Rightarrow  \dot{\alpha } = \beta /\tau \). Exact cancellation of feedback and leak This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written.

title: Lecture 19: Population Activity and Principal Component Analysis
subtitle: Population Activity and Principal Component Analysis
text: Population Activity and Principal Component Analysis two-neuron W → common/difference modes → mode regimes → activity-space trajectory → covariance → PCA top-K Starting from the two-neuron recurrent equation, compute by hand the eigenvalues, normalized eigenvectors, and input coordinates of the common and difference modes. Use each mode's time constant to classify stable decay, leaky integration, perfect integration, and unstable growth, then reinterpret the mode coordinates as trajectories in neural activity space. Derive PCA by maximizing the projection variance of centered data, and work through numerical examples of top-K projection, reconstruction, variance explained, and dimensional truncation. Distinguish rigorously between dynamical modes of a recurrent weight matrix and principal components of a covariance matrix, including when they may align and when no such alignment should be expected. Compare eigenvalue-cliff, cumulative-variance, and held-out-performance criteria for choosing dimensionality. The common and difference eigenmodes of a symmetric two-neuron network can be calculated completely by hand: one receives feedback +w0 and the other −w0. If the difference mode decays rapidly, the neural trajectory collapses toward the common-mode line and becomes approximately one-dimensional. PCA does not require W; it finds maximum projected variance from centered activity covariance. Dynamical eigenvectors of W can relate to principal components of C, but they are not generally identical. Equating eigenvectors of W with covariance PCs without additional assumptions. Omitting \(1/\sqrt 2\) when normalizing the common and difference modes. Using the wrong ± sign in the mode time constants. Misreading a low-dimensional trajectory as activity in only a few neurons. Applying PCA without centering the data. Treating maximum variance as maximum causal or behavioral relevance. Treating the eigenvalue cliff as an objectively unique dimensionality cutoff. PCA orders directions by variance; it does not automatically discover causal dynamics and can mix signal, noise, and condition structure. common and difference modes \(\xi \pm  = (1, \pm 1)T / 2\) symmetric two-neuron W orthonormal mode coordinates \(\alpha  = V\) Th \(V^\mathrm{T}V=I\) mode time constants \(\tau \pm  = \tau  /(1 \mp  w_{0} )\) \(|w_{0}|<1\) for stability of both modes activity covariance \(C = E[\delta h\delta hT ]\) centered data PC1 v1 = arg \(\max v\) T Cv \(\Vert v\Vert =1 C\) symmetric positive semidefinite PC score and projection pk = vkT \((h - \bar{h})\) orthonormal PCs cumulative variance explained ∑ ∑ VarFrac\((K) = \lambda _{k} / \lambda _{j} k\le K j\) sorted eigenvalues common mode An eigenmode in which both neurons change in the same direction. difference mode An eigenmode in which the two neurons change in opposite directions. neural activity space A state space whose coordinates are the activities of individual neurons. mode space A state space whose coordinates are dynamical eigenmode amplitudes. principal component analysis, PCA A linear method that orders orthogonal directions by the covariance variance they capture. principal component A covariance eigenvector together with the score obtained by projecting data onto it. projection The component of a vector along a specified basis direction. reconstruction An approximation of the original data formed from retained components. scree plot A plot of eigenvalue against component index. variance explained The fraction of the total eigenvalue sum retained by selected components. What is the result of multiplying \(W=[[0,0.6],[0.6,0]]\) by \((1,1)^\mathrm{T}\)? Multiply row by row: the first row gives \(0\times 1+0.6\times 1\) and the second gives \(0.6\times 1+0\times 1\). If this calculation is unfamiliar, return to the common/difference-mode module and check each component. The result is \((0.6,0.6)^\mathrm{T}\), so \((1,1)^\mathrm{T}\) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 0.6. For \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(\lambda =0.8\), what is the effective time constant of \(\tau d\alpha /dt=-(1-\lambda )\alpha\)? The coefficient \(1-\lambda\) sets the decay rate: the smaller this gap, the longer the time constant. Do not mistake \(\lambda\) itself for a time constant measured in milliseconds. \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=20/(1-0.8)=100 \mathrm{ms}\). Why must each neuron's mean activity be subtracted before computing the covariance? Without centering, the second moment h \(h^\mathrm{T}\) contains both the mean outer product and trial-to-trial variation, so PC1 may primarily track mean activity. Centering makes covariance describe joint fluctuations around the mean firing pattern instead of mistaking the mean response direction for the direction of greatest variability. Does a nearly one-dimensional trajectory mean that only one neuron is active? Dimension counts independent, variable population coordinates; it does not count nonzero neurons. Return to the activity-space reconstruction to see how both neurons participate in the common mode. No. It means that the joint activity of many neurons varies mainly along one population direction, which usually contains nonzero components from multiple neurons. If the PCA eigenvalues are 9, 3, 1, and 1, what cumulative variance is explained by retaining the first two PCs? The denominator of cumulative variance explained must contain every eigenvalue. Dividing only by the retained eigenvalues would incorrectly give 100%. \((9+3)/(9+3+1+1)=12/14\), or approximately 85.7%. If \(I_{1}=1\) and \(I_{2}=-1\), which mode is driven directly? \(\beta _{+}=(1-1)/\sqrt 2=0\) and \(\beta _{-}=(1-(-1))/\sqrt 2=\sqrt 2\), so only the difference mode is driven directly; the neurons tend to change in opposite directions. This is the distinction tested in Symmetric two-neuron network: natural coordinates for coupled equations. Worked example — Transform a population state into mode coordinates: Given \(h=(3,1)^\mathrm{T}\) and \(I=(2,2)^\mathrm{T}\), calculate \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), then verify that \(\alpha\) reconstructs h without loss. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Given \(h=(3,1)^\mathrm{T}\) and \(I=(2,2)^\mathrm{T}\), calculate \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), then verify that \(\alpha\) reconstructs h without loss. Compute \(\alpha _{+}=(3+1)/\sqrt 2=2\sqrt 2\) and \(\alpha _{-}=(3-1)/\sqrt 2=\sqrt 2\). Compute \(\beta _{+}=(2+2)/\sqrt 2=2\sqrt 2\) and \(\beta _{-}=(2-2)/\sqrt 2=0\), so the input drives only the common mode. Reconstruct \(\alpha +\xi _{+}+\alpha -\xi _{-}\): the first component is \((2\sqrt 2+\sqrt 2)/\sqrt 2=3\) and the second is \((2\sqrt 2-\sqrt 2)/\sqrt 2=1\). The squared coordinates sum to \(8+2=10\), matching the original vector's squared length \(3^{2}+1^{2}=10\). An orthogonal transform preserves length, providing an arithmetic check. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Symmetric two-neuron network: natural coordinates for coupled equations”? \(\lambda _{+}=w_{0}\) corresponds to the normalized common vector \((1,1)^\mathrm{T}/\sqrt 2\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Symmetric two-neuron network: natural coordinates for coupled equations”? \(\lambda _{-}=-w_{0}\) corresponds to the normalized difference vector \((1,-1)^\mathrm{T}/\sqrt 2\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Symmetric two-neuron network: natural coordinates for coupled equations” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? \(\lambda _{+}=w_{0}\) corresponds to the normalized common vector \((1,1)^\mathrm{T}/\sqrt 2\). The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Complete solution of the common/difference eigensystem”? \(V^\mathrm{T}h\) has shape \((2\times 2)(2\times 1)=2\times 1\), and every term in the mode ODE has units of a rate coordinate. At \(w_{0}=0\) the original neurons are uncoupled and the two basis directions decay at the same rate. The eigenbasis is then not unique: common/difference coordinates remain valid but are no longer the only choice. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: Why does replacing h1 and h2 with common and opposing changes decouple the originally coupled network? This lesson gives \(W=[[0,w_{0}],[w_{0},0]]\) and the rate equations \(\tau dh_{1}/dt=-h_{1}+w_{0}h_{2}+I_{1}\) and \(\tau dh_{2}/dt=-h_{2}+w_{0}h_{1}+I_{2}\). Zeros on the diagonal mean that this teaching example has no self-coupling, while equal off-diagonal entries make the reciprocal coupling symmetric. That symmetry suggests testing \(h_{1}=h_{2}\) and \(h_{1}=-h_{2}\): exchanging the neurons leaves the first pattern unchanged and changes only the sign of the second. Set \(\det(W-\lambda I)=\lambda ^{2}-w_{0}^{2}=0\) to obtain \(\lambda _{+}=w_{0}\) and \(\lambda _{-}=-w_{0}\). Substituting \(\lambda _{+}\) gives \(h_{2}=h_{1}\), so a common eigenvector is \((1,1)^\mathrm{T}\). Substituting \(\lambda _{-}\) gives \(h_{2}=-h_{1}\), so a difference eigenvector is \((1,-1)^\mathrm{T}\). Dividing each by \(\sqrt 2\) produces unit vectors with zero dot product, an orthonormal basis V. Normalization preserves direction and lets coordinates be computed directly by dot products. At \(w_{0}=-0.9\), which mode is slowest, and what is its time constant in units of \(\tau\)? The difference mode is slowest because \(\tau _{-}=\tau /(1-0.9)=10\tau\); the common mode has \(\tau _{+}=\tau /(1+0.9)\approx 0.526\tau\). Negative coupling near -1 preserves the opposing-change pattern. This is the distinction tested in Coupling strength sets time constants, integration, and stability. Worked example — Compare the speeds of the two modes: Let the single-cell time constant be \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(w_{0}=0.8\). Remove the input, calculate both mode time constants, and predict the fraction remaining after 100 ms. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let the single-cell time constant be \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(w_{0}=0.8\). Remove the input, calculate both mode time constants, and predict the fraction remaining after 100 ms. \(\tau _{+}=20/(1-0.8)=100 \mathrm{ms}\); \(\tau _{-}=20/(1+0.8)=11.11 \mathrm{ms}\). After 100 ms, the common-mode amplitude fraction is \(e^{-100/100}=e^{-1}\approx 0.368\). The difference-mode fraction is \(e^{-100/11.11}=e^{-9}\approx 0.000123\), so it has nearly vanished. Setting w0 to 0 should return both time constants to 20 ms. One long and one short time constant here agrees with the direction of positive reciprocal feedback. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Coupling strength sets time constants, integration, and stability”? \(\tau _{+}=\tau /(1-w_{0})\) and \(\tau _{-}=\tau /(1+w_{0})\); the signs cannot be collapsed into a common denominator. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Coupling strength sets time constants, integration, and stability”? Only \(|w_{0}|<1\) makes both modes stable; \(w_{0}=\pm 1\) produces a perfect integrator in one mode. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Coupling strength sets time constants, integration, and stability” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Only \(|w_{0}|<1\) makes both modes stable; \(w_{0}=\pm 1\) produces a perfect integrator in one mode. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Read the effective time constant from the mode coefficient”? Because the denominator is dimensionless, \(\tau /(1\mp w_{0})\) retains the time unit of \(\tau\). A unitless 'time constant' signals that \(\tau\) was omitted. As w0→1^-, \(\tau +\to \infty\). Beyond 1 the formula becomes negative; this is not a negative physical time but a sign that the exponent now describes growth. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. If a constant input \(\beta _{-}=1\) acts at every moment, must \(\alpha _{-}\) approach zero? No. A stable difference mode approaches the nonzero fixed point \(\alpha _{-}* = \beta _{-}/(1+w_{0})\), so the trajectory can remain away from the common axis. Low-dimensional conclusions depend on input structure. This is the distinction tested in Activity-space and mode-space views of the same trajectory. Worked example — How quickly does the trajectory enter the low-dimensional manifold?: Let \(\alpha +(0)=4\), \(\alpha -(0)=2\), \(\tau _{+}=200 \mathrm{ms}\), and \(\tau _{-}=20 \mathrm{ms}\). Find both amplitudes and the difference-mode energy fraction after 100 ms. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(\alpha +(0)=4\), \(\alpha -(0)=2\), \(\tau _{+}=200 \mathrm{ms}\), and \(\tau _{-}=20 \mathrm{ms}\). Find both amplitudes and the difference-mode energy fraction after 100 ms. \(\alpha +(100)=4e^{-0.5}\approx 2.426\). \(\alpha -(100)=2e^{-5}\approx 0.0135\). The difference fraction is \(0.0135^{2}/(2.426^{2}+0.0135^{2})\approx 0.000031\), or about 0.0031%. Swapping 20 ms and 200 ms reverses the fast/slow conclusion; first check which denominator is closer to zero. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Activity-space and mode-space views of the same trajectory”? Activity coordinates and mode coordinates are reversible representations of the same state. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Activity-space and mode-space views of the same trajectory”? After the fast mode decays, the slow mode dominates the trajectory and produces approximate low dimensionality. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Activity-space and mode-space views of the same trajectory” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The error from discarding a mode is quantified by the square of that mode's coordinate. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Why the loss of a fast mode yields a nearly one-dimensional trajectory”? \(\alpha \pm\) and h share the same units, while \(\xi \pm\) is dimensionless, so both terms in the reconstruction have compatible units. If \(\tau _{-}=\tau _{+}\), both modes decay at the same relative rate, so timescale separation does not automatically collapse the initial two-dimensional structure to one dimension. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is chiefly mixed in if \(E[hh^\mathrm{T}]\) is computed without centering? The mean outer-product term \(\bar{h}\) \(\bar{h}^\mathrm{T}\) is included, so the leading direction may represent the mean firing pattern rather than trial or temporal fluctuations. This is the distinction tested in PCA: from projection variance to covariance eigenvectors. Worked example — Compute the PC of a two-dimensional covariance by hand: Given \(C=[[5,4],[4,5]]\), find both eigenvectors and eigenvalues, then interpret the long axis of the data cloud. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Given \(C=[[5,4],[4,5]]\), find both eigenvectors and eigenvalues, then interpret the long axis of the data cloud. For common vector \((1,1)^\mathrm{T}\), \(C(1,1)^\mathrm{T}=(9,9)^\mathrm{T}\), so the eigenvalue is 9. For difference vector \((1,-1)^\mathrm{T}\), \(C(1,-1)^\mathrm{T}=(1,-1)^\mathrm{T}\), so the eigenvalue is 1. After normalization, PC1=\((1,1)^\mathrm{T}/\sqrt 2\) and PC2=\((1,-1)^\mathrm{T}/\sqrt 2\); the variance of PC1 is 9 times that of PC2. The trace of C is 10, equal to the eigenvalue \(\operatorname{sum} 9+1\), which checks the arithmetic. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “PCA: from projection variance to covariance eigenvectors”? PCA must be applied to centered activity: \(C=E[\delta h\delta h^\mathrm{T}]\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “PCA: from projection variance to covariance eigenvectors”? Under a unit-norm constraint, projected variance is \(v^\mathrm{T}Cv\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “PCA: from projection variance to covariance eigenvectors” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Maximum variance is not the same as maximum causal or behavioral relevance. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Rayleigh-quotient derivation of PC1”? If h is a firing rate, C and \(\lambda\) have units of \(\mathrm{rate}^{2}\); v is dimensionless and projection p retains the rate unit. If every sample is identical, centering gives \(C=0\). Variance is zero in every direction and the PC directions are not unique. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does \(V_{K}^\mathrm{T}V_{K}=I\) not imply \(V_{\mathrm{KV},K}^\mathrm{T}=I\)? When \(K<N\), \(V_{K}\) is not square. \(V_{K}^\mathrm{T}V_{K}\) is the identity in K-space, while \(V_{\mathrm{KV},K}^\mathrm{T}\) is the N-space projector onto a K-dimensional subspace. This is the distinction tested in Top-K PCA, orthogonal projection, and the boundary between reversible and approximate representations. Worked example — Top-2 reconstruction of a three-dimensional state: Let \(\operatorname{mean}=0\), with PCs equal to coordinate axes \(v_{1}=(1,0,0)\), \(v_{2}=(0,1,0)\), \(v_{3}=(0,0,1)\), and sample \(h=(4,2,1)\). Retain \(K=2\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(\operatorname{mean}=0\), with PCs equal to coordinate axes \(v_{1}=(1,0,0)\), \(v_{2}=(0,1,0)\), \(v_{3}=(0,0,1)\), and sample \(h=(4,2,1)\). Retain \(K=2\). The scores are \(p_{1}=4\), \(p_{2}=2\), and \(p_{3}=1\). Keeping the first two terms gives \(\hat{h}=4v_{1}+2v_{2}=(4,2,0)\). The residual is \(h-\hat{h}=(0,0,1)\), with squared error 1. The original squared norm is 21, the reconstruction has 20, and the residual has 1, satisfying the orthogonal Pythagorean relation \(21=20+1\). Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Top-K PCA, orthogonal projection, and the boundary between reversible and approximate representations”? \(V_{K}\) is N×K, scores are K×1, and reconstruction returns to N×1 neuron space. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Top-K PCA, orthogonal projection, and the boundary between reversible and approximate representations”? A complete orthogonal basis transform is lossless; dimensions are discarded only by projection with \(K<N\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Top-K PCA, orthogonal projection, and the boundary between reversible and approximate representations” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? \(V_{K}\) is N×K, scores are K×1, and reconstruction returns to N×1 neuron space. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Top-K reconstruction and error”? \(V_{\mathrm{KV},K}^\mathrm{T}\) has shape N×N and acts on N×1 centered activity. \(V_{K}^\mathrm{T}V_{K}=I_{K}\), but \(V_{\mathrm{KV},K}^\mathrm{T}\) is generally not \(I_{N}\). At \(K=N\), residual and error are zero; at \(K=0\), reconstruction is only the mean and error equals total variance. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does '95% variance explained' not guarantee retention of 95% of behavioral information? Variance measures activity amplitude, whereas behavioral information depends on condition distributions and the decoder. A low-variance direction may reliably distinguish choices, so the two percentages are not generally equivalent. This is the distinction tested in Choosing dimensionality with the eigenvalue cliff and cumulative variance. Worked example — Different cutoffs produce different values of K: The eigenvalues are \([9,3,1,1]\). Find the smallest K under cumulative-variance thresholds of 80% and 95%. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: The eigenvalues are \([9,3,1,1]\). Find the smallest K under cumulative-variance thresholds of 80% and 95%. Total variance is 14; \(F(1)=9/14\approx 64.3\)%. \(F(2)=12/14\approx 85.7\)%, so an 80% threshold selects \(K=2\). \(F(3)=13/14\approx 92.9\)% and \(F(4)=100\)%, so a 95% threshold selects \(K=4\). Cumulative variance should never decrease and must equal 1 at \(K=N\). Violating either condition usually signals an error in sorting or the denominator. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Choosing dimensionality with the eigenvalue cliff and cumulative variance”? A scree-plot elbow is a heuristic and usually has no unique location. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Choosing dimensionality with the eigenvalue cliff and cumulative variance”? Cumulative variance \(F(K)\) is the partial sum of sorted eigenvalues divided by their total sum. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Choosing dimensionality with the eigenvalue cliff and cumulative variance” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Cumulative variance \(F(K)\) is the partial sum of sorted eigenvalues divided by their total sum. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Complementarity of cumulative variance and residual error”? Numerator and denominator both have units of \(\mathrm{rate}^{2}\), so the ratio is unitless. K is an integer index, not a continuous parameter. If \(\lambda _{1}=\cdots =\lambda _{N}\), the spectrum has no cliff and \(F(K)=K/N\). Any low-dimensional cutoff then reflects an external tolerance rather than a natural turning point in the data. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Scree-plot cliff and cumulative variance”? Read the two curves in principal-component order: beyond the cliff, each eigenvalue contributes little additional variance, while cumulative variance continues to rise monotonically.
