The elbow suggests candidate dimensionalities but does not determine a unique cutoff; the plotted coordinates illustrate the normalized relation and are not empirical data. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “common mode” mean in this lecture? common mode: An eigenmode in which both neurons change in the same direction. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “difference mode” mean in this lecture? difference mode: An eigenmode in which the two neurons change in opposite directions. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “neural activity space” mean in this lecture? neural activity space: A state space whose coordinates are the activities of individual neurons. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “mode space” mean in this lecture? mode space: A state space whose coordinates are dynamical eigenmode amplitudes. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “principal component analysis, PCA” mean in this lecture? principal component analysis, PCA: A linear method that orders orthogonal directions by the covariance variance they capture. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “principal component” mean in this lecture? principal component: A covariance eigenvector together with the score obtained by projecting data onto it. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “projection” mean in this lecture? projection: The component of a vector along a specified basis direction. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “reconstruction” mean in this lecture? reconstruction: An approximation of the original data formed from retained components. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “scree plot” mean in this lecture? scree plot: A plot of eigenvalue against component index. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “common and difference modes” be used? common and difference modes: \(\xi \pm  = (1, \pm 1)T / 2\). symmetric two-neuron W This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “orthonormal mode coordinates” be used? orthonormal mode coordinates: \(\alpha  = V\) Th. \(V^\mathrm{T}V=I\) This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “mode time constants” be used? mode time constants: \(\tau \pm  = \tau  /(1 \mp  w_{0} )\). \(|w_{0}|<1\) for stability of both modes This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “activity covariance” be used? activity covariance: \(C = E[\delta h\delta hT ]\). centered data This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “PC1” be used? PC1: v1 = arg \(\max v\) T Cv \(\Vert v\Vert =1\). C symmetric positive semidefinite This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “PC score and projection” be used? PC score and projection: pk = vkT \((h - \bar{h})\). orthonormal PCs This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “cumulative variance explained” be used? cumulative variance explained: ∑ ∑ VarFrac\((K) = \lambda _{k} / \lambda _{j} k\le K j\). sorted eigenvalues This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written.

title: Lecture 20: Central Pattern Generators and Oscillations
subtitle: Central Pattern Generators and Oscillations
text: Central Pattern Generators and Oscillations pacemaker vs follower → half-center → complex eigenvalues → Morris–Lecar → nullclines/limit cycle → release vs escape Use synaptic-block logic to distinguish a cell-intrinsic pacemaker, a follower, and a network-generated half-center rhythm, while stating the limits of this experimental diagnosis. Solve for the complex eigenvalues of a two-neuron rotation matrix, using the real and imaginary parts to assess envelope stability and oscillation frequency, respectively. Explain every term in the Morris–Lecar voltage and recovery equations, then reconstruct the relaxation cycle from nullclines, fixed points, and fast–slow separation. Distinguish intrinsic release from intrinsic escape in a reciprocally inhibitory half-center, identifying whose intrinsic transition triggers each phase switch. Transfer the phase-plane geometry of a conductance model to a firing-rate model with adaptation while respecting the difference in model level. Whether rhythm persists after synaptic block can distinguish candidate intrinsic-pacemaker and network-generated mechanisms. Complex eigenvalues in a linear two-neuron system produce only damped or growing oscillatory components; a stable autonomous limit cycle requires nonlinearity. Fast voltage and slow recovery nullclines in Morris–Lecar generate a relaxation oscillation, while a mutually inhibitory half-center can alternate through intrinsic release or escape. Calling every rhythmic activity pattern a CPG. Assuming complex eigenvalues automatically imply sustained oscillation. Ignoring the real part of the full eigenvalue. Treating a nullcline as a trajectory. Assuming a fixed point is stable merely because a nullcline intersection exists. Distinguishing release from escape by superficial firing order rather than the intrinsic transition that triggers the switch. Excluding sensory feedback from real locomotor rhythms. Avoid classifying all rhythmic activity as a CPG, and do not conflate a damped linear oscillation with an autonomous nonlinear oscillator. complex mode \(\lambda  = a \pm  ib\) a controls the envelope; b controls frequency Euler decomposition e(a+ib)t = eat (cos bt + i sin bt) complex representation two-dimensional conductance model \(\dot{V} = F (V, N )\), \(\dot{N} = G(V, N )\) fast–slow variables V-nullcline \(F (V, N ) = 0\) \(dV/dt=0\) N-nullcline \(G(V, N ) = 0\) \(dN/dt=0\) sharp synaptic-threshold approximation \(S_{\infty } (V ) = H(V - VT )\) idealized switch central pattern generator, CPG A neural circuit that can generate a rhythmic motor pattern without periodic sensory drive. pacemaker neuron A neuron that oscillates spontaneously through intrinsic dynamics. half-center oscillator A network oscillator in which two mutually inhibitory units alternate activity. complex eigenvalue An eigenvalue that encodes both an exponential envelope and oscillatory phase. Morris-Lecar model A reduced, conductance-based neuron model with two variables. phase plane The trajectories and nullclines in a two-dimensional state space. relaxation oscillation A limit cycle that alternates slow drift with fast jumps. intrinsic release Removal of inhibition when the active neuron terminates its activity. intrinsic escape A transition in which the inhibited neuron recovers first and escapes inhibition. limit cycle A closed periodic orbit that attracts nearby trajectories. A neuron's linear mode has eigenvalue -2+6i s^-1. Does its amplitude grow or decay over time? Read the real part first to determine the envelope and the imaginary part second to determine oscillation. If you equated a complex eigenvalue with a sustained rhythm, review linear complex modes. The amplitude decays as \(e^{-2t}\); 6 rad/s specifies only the angular frequency of rotation. What does an intersection of the V-nullcline and N-nullcline represent? Stability still depends on the nearby vector field; an intersection alone does not tell you whether the point is stable, a saddle, or unstable. It simultaneously satisfies \(dV/dt=0\) and \(dN/dt=0\), so it is a fixed point of the two-dimensional system. After synapses are blocked, one cell continues at approximately its original rhythm. Which candidate mechanism does this most directly support? This is supporting evidence, not a logical proof; the diagnosis assumes a complete block that does not alter intrinsic currents. It supports a cell-intrinsic pacemaker mechanism in that cell, although drug side effects and residual coupling must still be controlled. What is the central criterion for distinguishing release from escape? Do not look only at which cell spikes first. Track the intrinsic variable and nullcline crossing that trigger the transition. Ask whether the active cell stops and lifts inhibition, or the inhibited cell recovers intrinsically, crosses a threshold, and escapes inhibition. If both cells stop alternating after the block but continue to oscillate at different frequencies, is this a purely network-generated rhythm? No. Coordinated alternation depends on network coupling, but each cell retains intrinsic oscillatory capacity; the full mechanism is coupled intrinsic oscillators. This is the distinction tested in Sources of rhythm: pacemaker, follower, and network half-center. Worked example — Diagnose a candidate network from block results: In the intact preparation, cells A/B alternate at 2 Hz. After the block, A still oscillates at 1.8 Hz and B fires constantly. Give the minimal mechanism and the next control. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: In the intact preparation, cells A/B alternate at 2 Hz. After the block, A still oscillates at 1.8 Hz and B fires constantly. Give the minimal mechanism and the next control. Because A's rhythm is approximately preserved, first classify A as an intrinsic-pacemaker candidate. B loses its modulation, consistent with a follower candidate. The intact alternation could arise from periodic drive from A to B or from more complex inhibition. Next inject periodic current into B to verify that it can follow, measure synaptic current to confirm a complete block, and check whether the drug altered A's waveform. 1.8 Hz is close to but not identical to 2 Hz, reasonably suggesting that removing coupling changed the pacemaker frequency slightly rather than requiring exact equality. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Sources of rhythm: pacemaker, follower, and network half-center”? Persistence of intrinsic rhythm after a block supports a pacemaker; loss of alternation supports network dependence. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Sources of rhythm: pacemaker, follower, and network half-center”? A synaptic-block result requires checks for block completeness and side effects on intrinsic currents. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Sources of rhythm: pacemaker, follower, and network half-center” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Persistence of intrinsic rhythm after a block supports a pacemaker; loss of alternation supports network dependence. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Compare mechanistic hypotheses with intervention outcomes”? Measure frequency in Hz and period in s, with \(f=1/T\); when comparing after a block, use a sufficiently long recording window. If both cells combine intrinsic oscillation with reciprocal inhibition, the block reveals a mixed mechanism rather than forcing the system into one category. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: How does persistence or loss of rhythm after synaptic block narrow the mechanisms, and why is it not sufficient proof by itself? This section distinguish two origins. A cell-intrinsic pacemaker continues to generate a rhythm from its own voltage-gated currents even without periodic synaptic input; a follower does not oscillate on its own and simply tracks synaptic drive from a pacemaker. The second origin is a network-generated rhythm: individual cells may remain tonic or silent in isolation, but reciprocal inhibition makes the pair alternate activity as a half-center oscillator. Respiration and alternating muscles during walking are the functional examples used in the course. Synaptic block is an intervention, not a labeling exercise. If neuron 1 retains its rhythm after the block while neuron 2 becomes tonic or silent, the result is consistent with 1 as pacemaker and 2 as follower. If the pair alternates naturally but both lose rhythmicity under the block, the result supports a network-generated candidate. The key observation is each cell's time series in intact and blocked conditions, not a comparison of average frequency across different animals. What happens if the full eigenvalues are \(0.2\pm 5i s^{-1}\)? The trajectory rotates while its envelope grows as \(e^{0.2t}\), producing an outward spiral. The linear model is unstable; whether a limit cycle subsequently forms depends on nonlinear saturation. This is the distinction tested in Complex modes and damped oscillation in a linear two-neuron system. Worked example — Read the waveform from the full eigenvalue: Given \(\tau =0.2 \mathrm{s}\) and \(w_{0}=4\), find the envelope time constant, angular frequency, frequency in Hz, and amplitude fraction after one period. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Given \(\tau =0.2 \mathrm{s}\) and \(w_{0}=4\), find the envelope time constant, angular frequency, frequency in Hz, and amplitude fraction after one period. The full eigenvalues are \((-1\pm 4i)/0.2=-5\pm 20i s^{-1}\). The envelope time constant is \(1/5=0.2 \mathrm{s}\); \(f=20/(2\pi )\approx 3.18 \mathrm{Hz}\) and the period is ≈0.314 s. After one period, the amplitude fraction is \(e^{-0.314/0.2}=e^{-1.57}\approx 0.208\). The period comes from the imaginary part and the envelope from the real part; using \(|\lambda |\) for both gives inconsistent results. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Complex modes and damped oscillation in a linear two-neuron system”? The full-system eigenvalues are \((-1\pm iw0)/\tau\); the ±iw0 eigenvalues of W alone are insufficient. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Complex modes and damped oscillation in a linear two-neuron system”? The real part determines the envelope, and the imaginary part determines angular frequency. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Complex modes and damped oscillation in a linear two-neuron system” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The real part determines the envelope, and the imaginary part determines angular frequency. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Solve the complex modes and recover a real oscillation”? \(\omega\) has units rad/s and f has units Hz; the exponent in \(e^{-t/\tau }\) must be dimensionless. When \(w_{0}=0\), \(\omega =0\) and the system only decays exponentially without oscillating; as \(\tau \to \infty\), both decay and rotation slow in this model. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why is a nullcline not the neuron's actual trajectory? A nullcline is only the set of points where one derivative is instantaneously zero. The other variable usually continues to change, so the state crosses or moves nearby; only an intersection of both nullclines can remain stationary. This is the distinction tested in Morris–Lecar current balance, nullclines, and fixed points. Worked example — Use signs to determine motion at a phase-plane point: At a point above the V-nullcline, substitution gives \(dV/dt<0\); the same point lies below the N-nullcline. Determine its initial direction of motion. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: At a point above the V-nullcline, substitution gives \(dV/dt<0\); the same point lies below the N-nullcline. Determine its initial direction of motion. \(dV/dt<0\) means that V moves leftward. Below the N-nullcline, \(N<N_{\infty }(V)\), so \(dN/dt>0\) and N moves upward. The combined vector points up and left. If the trajectory crosses a nullcline at the next moment, reassess the signs. Only the corresponding derivative is zero on a nullcline. Merely being 'above the V-nullcline' does not establish the sign of dV; the problem supplies the test-point sign. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Morris–Lecar current balance, nullclines, and fixed points”? The V equation balances leak, Ca, K, and external currents. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Morris–Lecar current balance, nullclines, and fixed points”? The V-nullcline satisfies \(dV/dt=0\); the N-nullcline satisfies \(N=N_{\infty }(V)\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Morris–Lecar current balance, nullclines, and fixed points” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Nullcline intersections are fixed points; their stability still requires the vector field. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Derive both nullclines from current balance”? Conductance×voltage has units of current, as does C dV/dt. Both sides of the recovery equation describe dimensionless change per unit time. If \(g_{K}=0\), the formula that isolates N on the V-nullcline is invalid, and N no longer feeds back onto voltage; the two-dimensional oscillator mechanism changes accordingly. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why can two mutually inhibitory cells generate a network rhythm even when neither oscillates in isolation? Inhibition switches each partner's effective nullcline between active and inactive conditions. Slow recovery makes the cells reach their transitions in turn, so coupling creates periodic state switching. This is the distinction tested in Relaxation cycles and phase geometry of a reciprocally inhibitory half-center. Worked example — Predict the effect of increasing the recovery time constant: Keep the nullcline shapes fixed and increase \(\tau N\) from 100 ms to 300 ms. Predict the main changes in period and fast-jump duration. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Keep the nullcline shapes fixed and increase \(\tau N\) from 100 ms to 300 ms. Predict the main changes in period and fast-jump duration. Slow motion along the branches becomes about three times slower because \(dN/dt\) is reduced. Because the cycle spends most of its time on the slow branches, its period lengthens substantially, approximately in proportion to \(\tau N\). Fast V jumps are governed mainly by C and the conductances, so their duration should not also increase threefold. If the parameter change alters fixed-point stability or branch range, the simple proportional prediction fails; the problem explicitly holds the shapes fixed. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Relaxation cycles and phase geometry of a reciprocally inhibitory half-center”? A relaxation cycle has four stages: slow motion on the low branch, an upward jump, slow motion on the high branch, and a downward jump. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Relaxation cycles and phase geometry of a reciprocally inhibitory half-center”? Slow recovery largely determines period; fast jumps determine the waveform edges. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Relaxation cycles and phase geometry of a reciprocally inhibitory half-center” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? A half-center rhythm requires cooperation between intrinsic recovery and synaptic switching. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “The sign sequence around a four-stage trajectory”? The phase-plane axes are mV and dimensionless N. Elapsed time cannot be inferred from geometric distance alone. If fast–slow separation disappears, a cycle may remain, but the approximation of slow branch motion and fast fold jumps becomes less accurate. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. If the active cell falls below VT and its partner jumps 20 ms later, does that delay refute release? No. Release requires only that removal of inhibition be the upstream trigger. The partner still takes finite time to leave its low state according to its own membrane and recovery dynamics. This is the distinction tested in Intrinsic release and intrinsic escape: what triggers the phase switch?. Worked example — Infer the switch mechanism from event times: A is active. At \(t=500 \mathrm{ms}\), B suddenly depolarizes while inhibition remains strong; at \(t=507 \mathrm{ms}\), A is inhibited; at \(t=512 \mathrm{ms}\), A falls below VT. Which mechanism dominates? Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: A is active. At \(t=500 \mathrm{ms}\), B suddenly depolarizes while inhibition remains strong; at \(t=507 \mathrm{ms}\), A is inhibited; at \(t=512 \mathrm{ms}\), A falls below VT. Which mechanism dominates? B depolarizes before A falls below VT, so B did not wait for inhibition to shut off before rising. B then inhibits A, consistent with the inhibited cell actively escaping its low state. Classify the event as escape-dominant and test whether manipulating B's recovery variable changes the 500 ms latency. Confirm that synaptic conductance was still high when B depolarized; A's spikes alone may underestimate the actual conductance offset. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Intrinsic release and intrinsic escape: what triggers the phase switch?”? A sharp \(S_{\infty }\) threshold approximates the synapse as an on/off switch. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Intrinsic release and intrinsic escape: what triggers the phase switch?”? Release is triggered by intrinsic termination of the active cell. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Intrinsic release and intrinsic escape: what triggers the phase switch?” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? A sharp \(S_{\infty }\) threshold approximates the synapse as an on/off switch. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Distinguish release from escape by threshold-crossing order”? The synaptic term \(gS(V-Es)\) has units of current; Heaviside S merely selects whether the conductance is on. If synaptic activation is graded rather than sharp, there is no unique on/off time. Compare the rise in conductance with the timing of intrinsic transitions. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why are two linear rate variables h1 and h2 usually insufficient for a stable half-center limit cycle? A linear system can only decay, rotate neutrally, or grow; it lacks a slow state and amplitude regulation. Adaptation or recovery plus nonlinear F supplies phase switching and a bounded cycle. This is the distinction tested in From a conductance oscillator to a rate–adaptation half-center. Worked example — Predict rhythm from a parameter change: The model initially has \(\tau _{h}=20 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(\tau a=400 \mathrm{ms}\). Double only \(\tau a\) to 800 ms, keeping all else fixed and assuming the cycle persists. Predict frequency and phase relation. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: The model initially has \(\tau _{h}=20 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(\tau a=400 \mathrm{ms}\). Double only \(\tau a\) to 800 ms, keeping all else fixed and assuming the cycle persists. Predict frequency and phase relation. Both slow adaptation and recovery become slower, so the active phase generally lengthens. Because the two cells remain structurally symmetric, they should stay approximately in antiphase rather than acquire a fixed phase bias. The period is governed mainly by the slow process and should increase, so frequency decreases, though it need not be exactly halved. Because \(\tau _{h}\) is unchanged, the edge of each fast rate transition should not stretch by the same factor as the plateau. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “From a conductance oscillator to a rate–adaptation half-center”? A rate–adaptation model needs at least fast activity, slow recovery, reciprocal inhibition, and a nonlinearity. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “From a conductance oscillator to a rate–adaptation half-center”? Accumulating adaptation can trigger release; recovery during low activity can support escape. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “From a conductance oscillator to a rate–adaptation half-center” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Accumulating adaptation can trigger release; recovery during low activity can support escape. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Feedback chain of a minimal rate half-center”? If h and the output of F are in Hz, every term is in Hz and division by \(\tau\) gives Hz/s. The quantities a, I, and w h must be addable. When \(b=0\), activity no longer builds adaptation. Pure reciprocal inhibition without another slow process usually loses stable alternation. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Morris–Lecar nullclines and the relaxation cycle”? The intersection of the two nullclines is a candidate equilibrium. Here it is unstable, so the trajectory moves slowly along the outer attracting branches of the V-nullcline and jumps rapidly to the other branch near each fold. Long portions of the loop represent slow recovery, whereas nearly horizontal crossings represent fast voltage transitions. The curves are a normalized schematic of the mechanisms. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “central pattern generator, CPG” mean in this lecture? central pattern generator, CPG: A neural circuit that can generate a rhythmic motor pattern without periodic sensory drive. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “pacemaker neuron” mean in this lecture? pacemaker neuron: A neuron that oscillates spontaneously through intrinsic dynamics. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “half-center oscillator” mean in this lecture? half-center oscillator: A network oscillator in which two mutually inhibitory units alternate activity. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “complex eigenvalue” mean in this lecture? complex eigenvalue: An eigenvalue that encodes both an exponential envelope and oscillatory phase. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “Morris-Lecar model” mean in this lecture? Morris-Lecar model: A reduced, conductance-based neuron model with two variables. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “phase plane” mean in this lecture? phase plane: The trajectories and nullclines in a two-dimensional state space. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “relaxation oscillation” mean in this lecture? relaxation oscillation: A limit cycle that alternates slow drift with fast jumps. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “intrinsic release” mean in this lecture? intrinsic release: Removal of inhibition when the active neuron terminates its activity. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “intrinsic escape” mean in this lecture? intrinsic escape: A transition in which the inhibited neuron recovers first and escapes inhibition. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “complex mode” be used? complex mode: \(\lambda  = a \pm  ib\). a controls the envelope; b controls frequency This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Euler decomposition” be used? Euler decomposition: e(a+ib)t = eat (cos bt + i sin bt). complex representation This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “two-dimensional conductance model” be used? two-dimensional conductance model: \(\dot{V} = F (V, N )\), \(\dot{N} = G(V, N )\). fast–slow variables This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “V-nullcline” be used? V-nullcline: \(F (V, N ) = 0\). \(dV/dt=0\) This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “N-nullcline” be used? N-nullcline: \(G(V, N ) = 0\). \(dN/dt=0\) This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “sharp synaptic-threshold approximation” be used? sharp synaptic-threshold approximation: \(S_{\infty } (V ) = H(V - VT )\). idealized switch This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written.

title: Lecture 21: Oculomotor Integrator, Degeneracy, and Sloppy Models

title: Lecture 22: Motor Cortex Latent Dynamics and Brain–Machine Interfaces
subtitle: Motor Cortex Latent Dynamics and Brain–Machine Interfaces
text: Motor Cortex Latent Dynamics and Brain–Machine Interfaces center-out tuning → PCA low dimension → latent vs activity space → GPFA → preparatory trajectories → output-null readout Distinguish three levels of description—single-neuron directional tuning, low-dimensional population trajectories, and latent dynamics—and explain how all three can hold simultaneously. Explain each component of GPFA from high-dimensional neural activity to low-dimensional factors, including the observation model, temporal covariance, matrix shapes, and non-identifiability. Use a delayed-reach timeline to explain how preparatory states enter movement-potent and output-null subspaces without misrepresenting graphical correlations as causal conclusions. Compute the null space and rank–nullity of a linear readout by hand, construct a simple decoder, and apply the results to closed-loop BMI and cross-day alignment. Connect PCA/GPFA, linear readout, closed-loop feedback, and cross-day alignment into a testable BMI analysis pipeline. Directional tuning is a classic description of motor cortex, whereas the modern population view asks whether low-dimensional trajectories generate movement dynamics. GPFA embeds smooth latent factors into noisy neural activity with a Gaussian observation model and explicitly models temporal covariance. A preparatory state can vary within the null space of muscle readout U without causing movement. BMI decodes neural or latent state into device commands and uses feedback and cross-day latent alignment to improve stability. Conflating a single-neuron tuning curve with a latent trajectory. Using PCA components, GPFA factors, dynamical modes, and decoder axes interchangeably. Assuming that a K-dimensional model means only K neurons matter. Ignoring non-identifiability of \(C-\alpha\) scale and rotation. Inferring \(r=0\) from \(Ur=0\). Ignoring user feedback and learning in a feedforward BMI account. Describing cross-day latent stability as absolute invariance. Tuning curves, principal components, latent factors, dynamical modes, and decoder axes must be distinguished explicitly. They may be related, but they are not interchangeable. GPFA observation model rt |αt ∼ N (Cαt + d, Σ) Gaussian approximation GP temporal covariance ′ 2 \(K(t, t' ) = \sigma s_{2} e-(t-t ) /(2\tau  ) + \sigma n_{2} \delta tt'\) 2 stationary smooth kernel linear motor readout \(m = Ur\) local approximation output-null space Null(U ) = {r: U r = 0} linear algebra rank–nullity dim N ull\((U ) = N - \operatorname{rank}(U )\) U: M×N latent decoder \(\hat{v} = B\alpha \) aligned latent coordinates center-out reach task A reaching paradigm from a central location to multiple radial targets. direction tuning Variation of the mean response with reach direction. latent factor A low-dimensional hidden variable that explains shared population variability. embedding A mapping from latent coordinates into high-dimensional activity. Gaussian-process factor analysis, GPFA A latent-factor model with a temporal Gaussian-process prior. preparatory activity A target-dependent population state before movement. output-null space Neural directions that do not change the current readout. output-potent space Directions that change muscle or device output. brain-machine interface, BMI A system that controls an external device from neural activity. closed-loop control Online control that includes sensory or device feedback. If 100 neurons are recorded and 6 latent factors are retained, what is the shape of the GPFA loading matrix C? Check matrix multiplication from output dimension back to input dimension; do not mix trials or time bins into the neuron axis of C. C is \(100\times 6\); it maps a \(6\times 1\) latent vector to a \(100\times 1\) mean neural-activity vector. Does a directional tuning curve prove that the neuron directly encodes force in one muscle? A causal encoding claim additionally requires control of confounders and tests of perturbations and decoder generalization. No. Tuning establishes a statistical association between firing rate and reach direction; it may arise from input, shared dynamics, task covariates, or a readout. If U is \(2\times 5\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(U)=2\), what is the dimension of its linear output-null space? Null-space dimension is input dimension minus rank, not output dimension minus rank. By rank–nullity, the dimension is \(5-2=3\). As \(\tau\) in a GP kernel increases, do neighboring latent values usually become smoother or more abrupt? Substitute both limits into the kernel: with very large \(\tau\), the exponential approaches 1; with very small \(\tau\), covariance at a nonzero lag falls rapidly. Smoother. A fixed temporal separation becomes smaller relative to \(\tau\), making kernel covariance closer to its maximum. Why should a cross-day decoder not require exact correspondence of individual neuron identities every day? Cross-day stability is a hypothesis about population structure. It must be tested on held-out days and cannot be confirmed by an attractive two-dimensional plot. Electrode drift changes which units are visible. If the stable computation lies in a latent subspace, align each day's latent coordinates before decoding. Why does a PC explaining 70% of neural variance not necessarily explain 70% of behavioral variance? Behavior depends on a separate readout map, which may ignore high-variance directions or amplify low-variance directions; there is no fixed ratio between the two variances. This is the distinction tested in Center-out tuning and low-dimensional population trajectories. Worked example — Compute tuning at four directions: A neuron has \(b=20 \mathrm{Hz}\), \(k=8 \mathrm{Hz}\), and \(\theta _{\mathrm{pref}}=0\). Find the predicted rates at \(\theta =0\), \(\pi /2\), \(\pi\), and \(3\pi /2\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: A neuron has \(b=20 \mathrm{Hz}\), \(k=8 \mathrm{Hz}\), and \(\theta _{\mathrm{pref}}=0\). Find the predicted rates at \(\theta =0\), \(\pi /2\), \(\pi\), and \(3\pi /2\). At \(\theta =0\), \(\cos 0=1\), giving 28 Hz. At \(\pi /2\) and \(3\pi /2\), the cosine is 0, giving 20 Hz in both cases. At \(\pi\), cos\(\pi =-1\), giving 12 Hz. The maximum and minimum are symmetric around the 20 Hz baseline, and their mean remains 20 Hz. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Center-out tuning and low-dimensional population trajectories”? Directional tuning is a statistical condition average, not a unique neural code. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Center-out tuning and low-dimensional population trajectories”? Single-cell tuning can be a coordinate projection of a low-dimensional population trajectory. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Center-out tuning and low-dimensional population trajectories” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Directional tuning is a statistical condition average, not a unique neural code. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Directional tuning as a linear projection of a two-dimensional movement vector”? The direction vectors in the dot product are dimensionless; multiplying by k yields Hz, which can be added to baseline b. When \(k=0\), every direction gives b. At \(\theta =\theta _{\mathrm{pref}}\) the rate is b+k, and in the opposite direction it is b-k. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: Why can the same center-out data support directional tuning curves and also be viewed as projections of a low-dimensional dynamical system? A center-out task begins at a central location and reaches toward multiple radial targets, making direction, speed, and time from the go cue well structured. For one neuron, mean directional tuning can be described by \(r(\theta )=b+k \cos(\theta -\theta _{\mathrm{pref}})\), where \(\theta _{\mathrm{pref}}\) is preferred direction and k is modulation depth. This formula summarizes a condition average; it does not mean the neuron 'knows' the angle or guarantee that other movement variables have been excluded. Stack all neuronal rates at one moment into \(r(t)\), so each reach condition traces an N-dimensional trajectory. If most variance lies on a few PCs, the trajectory is close to a low-dimensional subspace. A single-neuron curve is the shadow of the high-dimensional trajectory on one coordinate axis. Multiple phase-shifted shadows can arise from one rotating or curved population trajectory, so tuning and dynamics are compatible observations. If one latent factor is multiplied everywhere by 2 without changing C, is it still the same GPFA model? No; the predicted mean changes. It is an equivalent coordinate reparameterization only if the corresponding column of C is also divided by 2. This is the distinction tested in Latent space, activity space, and the GPFA observation model. Worked example — Reconstruct two neurons from one factor: Let \(C=(2,-1)^\mathrm{T} \mathrm{Hz}\), \(d=(10,20)^\mathrm{T} \mathrm{Hz}\), and \(\alpha =3\) at one moment. Find the predicted rates. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(C=(2,-1)^\mathrm{T} \mathrm{Hz}\), \(d=(10,20)^\mathrm{T} \mathrm{Hz}\), and \(\alpha =3\) at one moment. Find the predicted rates. The first neuron's mean is \(2\times 3+10=16 \mathrm{Hz}\). The second neuron's mean is \(-1\times 3+20=17 \mathrm{Hz}\). A negative loading means that as the latent increases, the second neuron falls below baseline; it does not imply a negative firing rate. Setting \(\alpha\) to 0 should recover the baseline \((10,20)^\mathrm{T} \mathrm{Hz}\). Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Latent space, activity space, and the GPFA observation model”? C is N×K and links latent space with neural activity space. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Latent space, activity space, and the GPFA observation model”? \(\Sigma\) describes residuals conditional on the latent state; it is not the covariance of the raw data. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Latent space, activity space, and the GPFA observation model” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? \(\Sigma\) describes residuals conditional on the latent state; it is not the covariance of the raw data. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Shapes in the observation model and reparameterizing its conditional mean”? \(C\alpha\) and d must share the units of r. If \(\alpha\) is dimensionless, entries of C have units of rate or count. \(\Sigma\) uses squared observation units. When \(K=N\) and C is invertible, there is no dimensionality reduction. If all latent factors share an identical kernel, an orthogonal rotation can preserve the prior form; different kernels generally preclude arbitrary rotation. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does a smooth kernel not prove that the true cortical trajectory is intrinsically smooth? Some smoothness comes from the prior. Compare held-out data, alternative kernels, and temporal resolutions to determine whether the data support that time scale. This is the distinction tested in GP temporal kernels, parameter fitting, and delayed-reach trajectories. Worked example — Compare correlation strength at two time lags: Ignore \(\sigma n\) and set \(\sigma s^{2}=1\) and \(\tau =100 \mathrm{ms}\). Approximate the covariance for \(\Delta t=100 \mathrm{ms}\) and 200 ms. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Ignore \(\sigma n\) and set \(\sigma s^{2}=1\) and \(\tau =100 \mathrm{ms}\). Approximate the covariance for \(\Delta t=100 \mathrm{ms}\) and 200 ms. At \(\Delta t=100\), the exponent is -1/2 and \(K=e^{-1/2}\approx 0.607\). At \(\Delta t=200\), the exponent is \(-4/2=-2\) and \(K=e^{-2}\approx 0.135\). The second lag is twice as long, but covariance falls by more than a factor of four because distance is squared. At \(\Delta t=0\) the value should be 1; the kernel decreases monotonically as \(|\Delta t|\) grows. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “GP temporal kernels, parameter fitting, and delayed-reach trajectories”? \(\tau\) is a temporal correlation scale, not trial duration. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “GP temporal kernels, parameter fitting, and delayed-reach trajectories”? A kernel family is a modeling assumption that must be tested with held-out data. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “GP temporal kernels, parameter fitting, and delayed-reach trajectories” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Target, go, and movement events must delimit the epochs of a delayed-reach trajectory. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Two limits of the squared-exponential kernel”? The numerator and denominator of the exponent both have units of time squared, so their ratio is dimensionless; K retains units of latent variance. As \(\tau \to \infty\), the factor is nearly constant within a finite window. As \(\tau \to 0\), between-bin covariance vanishes and the smooth prior degenerates. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. If the downstream readout changes to \(U'\), must the original output-null vector remain null? No. The null space depends on the particular readout. One neural direction may be irrelevant to one output yet affect another muscle group or cognitive variable. This is the distinction tested in Preparatory activity, linear readouts, and output-null space. Worked example — Compute an output-null vector: Let \(U=[1,2]\) and \(r=(2,-1)^\mathrm{T}\). Find m and give one potent vector. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(U=[1,2]\) and \(r=(2,-1)^\mathrm{T}\). Find m and give one potent vector. \(m=1\times 2+2\times (-1)=0\), so r is a nonzero null vector. Choose rpotent=\((1,0)^\mathrm{T}\), giving \(m=1\). Adding the two vectors gives \((3,-1)^\mathrm{T}\), whose output remains \(3+2\times (-1)=1\). A null vector of U has zero dot product with the row vector (1,2), so the two are geometrically orthogonal. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Preparatory activity, linear readouts, and output-null space”? \(Ur=0\) can hold with \(r\ne 0\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Preparatory activity, linear readouts, and output-null space”? Null-space size is determined by input dimensionality and rank. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Preparatory activity, linear readouts, and output-null space” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? \(Ur=0\) can hold with \(r\ne 0\). The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Rank–nullity and the potent/null decomposition”? If r is in Hz and m in command units, U has units of command units/Hz; the zero vector carries the corresponding output units. If U has full column rank and \(N\le M\), its null space contains only the zero vector. If N≫M, the null space has at least N-M dimensions. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why can an improvement in closed-loop performance not be attributed entirely to more accurate decoder parameters? The participant changes neural strategy in response to feedback, and the decoder may update online. Performance comes from joint adaptation, so one side must be frozen or otherwise controlled to separate the causes. This is the distinction tested in Closed-loop BMI and cross-day latent alignment. Worked example — Swap the axes of a two-dimensional latent space: On day 2, latent coordinates are swapped relative to day 1: \(\alpha _{2}=(3,1)^\mathrm{T}\), whereas the reference order is \((1,3)^\mathrm{T}\). Give the alignment and compute the prediction for \(B=[2,-1]\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: On day 2, latent coordinates are swapped relative to day 1: \(\alpha _{2}=(3,1)^\mathrm{T}\), whereas the reference order is \((1,3)^\mathrm{T}\). Give the alignment and compute the prediction for \(B=[2,-1]\). Use \(A=[[0,1],[1,0]]\) to swap the coordinates, giving \(\widetilde{\alpha }=(1,3)^\mathrm{T}\). Apply B: \(\hat{v}=2\times 1-1\times 3=-1\). Without alignment, the result is \(2\times 3-1\times 1=5\), showing how a coordinate-convention change can seriously disrupt the decoder. A is a permutation matrix, so \(A^\mathrm{T} A=I\) and latent-vector length is unchanged. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Closed-loop BMI and cross-day latent alignment”? A closed-loop BMI is a joint brain–decoder–feedback system. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Closed-loop BMI and cross-day latent alignment”? Cross-day alignment aligns population coordinates rather than demanding stable unit identity. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Closed-loop BMI and cross-day latent alignment” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Cross-day alignment aligns population coordinates rather than demanding stable unit identity. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Mapping chain of a cross-day latent decoder”? If velocity is in cm/s and the latent is dimensionless, B is in cm/s; squared error is in \(\mathrm{cm}^{2}/s^{2}\). \(A_{d}=I\) means that no rotation is required. If latent subspaces do not overlap at all, linear alignment should not be expected to recover an accurate decoder. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “From population activity to closed-loop BMI”? Observed activity is first compressed by GPFA into daily latent coordinates, then \(A_{d}\) aligns those coordinates to a shared space and passes them to shared decoder B. Decoder output changes cursor feedback, which in turn changes subsequent neural activity. Cross-day stability therefore means that a low-dimensional mapping is transferable; it does not require each neuron's loading to remain fixed. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “center-out reach task” mean in this lecture? center-out reach task: A reaching paradigm from a central location to multiple radial targets. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “direction tuning” mean in this lecture? direction tuning: Variation of the mean response with reach direction. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “latent factor” mean in this lecture? latent factor: A low-dimensional hidden variable that explains shared population variability. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “embedding” mean in this lecture? embedding: A mapping from latent coordinates into high-dimensional activity. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “Gaussian-process factor analysis, GPFA” mean in this lecture? Gaussian-process factor analysis, GPFA: A latent-factor model with a temporal Gaussian-process prior. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “preparatory activity” mean in this lecture? preparatory activity: A target-dependent population state before movement. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “output-null space” mean in this lecture? output-null space: Neural directions that do not change the current readout. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “output-potent space” mean in this lecture? output-potent space: Directions that change muscle or device output. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “brain-machine interface, BMI” mean in this lecture? brain-machine interface, BMI: A system that controls an external device from neural activity. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “GPFA observation model” be used? GPFA observation model: rt |αt ∼ N (Cαt + d, Σ). Gaussian approximation This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. GP temporal covariance: ′ 2 \(K(t, t' ) = \sigma s_{2} e-(t-t ) /(2\tau  ) + \sigma n_{2} \delta tt'\) 2. stationary smooth kernel This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. title: Lecture 23: Short-Term Memory and Perceptual Decisions
subtitle: Short-Term Memory and Perceptual Decisions
text: Short-Term Memory and Perceptual Decisions cognition/decoupling → DMS/Romo → persistent activity → long recurrent mode → drift-diffusion → psychometric/chronometric/LIP Organize decision-making, working memory, and long-term learning around the working definition that current brain state is not determined solely by current input, while recognizing that this is not an exhaustive definition. Reconstruct DMS and Romo parametric working-memory tasks through sample, delay, comparison, and choice, specifying what information must be retained during the delay. Derive the effective time constant of graded persistent activity from a recurrent eigenmode and classify leaky, perfectly persistent, and unstable regimes. Explain the evidence, noise, bias, bounds, and reaction time of a leaky drift-diffusion process, and predict its psychometric and chronometric curves. Use the Wong–Wang phase plane to distinguish fixed points, separatrices, and stochastic choice while keeping model predictions separate from correlations in LIP. This lecture provisionally defines cognition as a brain state not determined solely by present input. Short-term memory can preserve a past sample in persistent population modes without immediately modifying synapses. Perceptual decisions can be described behaviorally by noisy evidence accumulation and bounds; LIP ramps are correlated neural variables, not automatic proof of mechanism. A reduced Wong–Wang attractor model uses two-dimensional nonlinear nullclines to connect integration, competition, and discrete choice. Treating the working definition of cognition as a complete philosophical or psychological definition. Assuming that STM requires immediate synaptic plasticity. Conflating persistent single-cell activity with a stable population mode. Treating the DDM decision variable as a directly observed neuron. Fitting only the psychometric function and not testing the chronometric function. Equating an LIP correlation directly with a causal accumulator. Conflating a descriptive DDM with a biophysical attractor model at the same explanatory level. Distinguish working-memory content, neural correlates, persistent modes, and synaptic memory; also distinguish a descriptive DDM from a biophysical attractor model. persistent memory mode \(\tau ef\) \(f = \tau  /(1 - \lambda )\) \(\lambda <1\) but close to 1 leaky evidence accumulator \(\tau a\) \(\dot{a} = -a + e(t) + \gamma (t)\) white or colored noise specified decision bias \(a(0) = b\) initial-condition interpretation absorbing decision bounds \(a = \pm B\) first-passage rule psychometric function \(P (\mathrm{choice}|c)\) signed stimulus strength chronometric function \(E[RT |c]\) state whether nondecision time is included Wong–Wang nullclines \(G_{1} = 0\), \(G_{2} = 0 2D\) reduced dynamics cognition This lecture's working definition: a brain state partly decoupled from present input and shaped by past events or future goals. short-term memory The ability to retain recently encountered information briefly. working memory Information retained for use in a current computation. delayed match-to-sample A sample–delay–test memory task. persistent activity Neural activity that remains after the stimulus ends. drift-diffusion model, DDM A decision model that accumulates noisy evidence to bounds. psychometric curve Choice or accuracy as a function of stimulus strength. chronometric curve Reaction time as a function of stimulus strength. separatrix A boundary separating different attractor basins. attractor A state or set toward which nearby states converge under the dynamics. DMS needs only a memory that the sample was seen. What additional information must the Romo task preserve? A one-bit 'sample occurred' label cannot explain graded comparison errors between nearby frequencies. The Romo parametric task must retain the continuous or graded value of the first vibration frequency so it can be compared with the second. For a recurrent mode with \(\lambda =0.9\) and \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\), what is the effective time constant? First compute the eigenvalue gap \(1-\lambda\), then divide the intrinsic time constant by it; \(\lambda\) has no time units. \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=20/(1-0.9)=200 \mathrm{ms}\). If only decision bound B is increased, how do accuracy and reaction time usually change in a DDM? A farther bound permits more evidence collection but requires a longer first-passage time. With other parameters fixed and informative trials, accuracy usually increases and reaction time lengthens. Both LIP firing rate and the model decision variable ramp. Is that enough to conclude that LIP implements a DDM? The claim additionally requires trial-level covariation, perturbations, parameter-linked predictions, and comparison with alternative models. No. Similar temporal shapes are correlational and can arise from common input, urgency, condition averaging, or other dynamics. What happens when a phase-plane trajectory lies exactly on a separatrix? A separatrix is not a broad third choice region; it is the boundary between attractor basins. In an ideal deterministic system it follows the boundary toward a saddle; a minute noise fluctuation or bias pushes it into one of the two choice basins. Why does continued brain activity with the eyes closed not by itself prove cognition in this lecture's sense? Persistent activity may be spontaneous fluctuation or an unmeasured input. It must carry task-relevant history and predict later behavior. This is the distinction tested in A working definition of cognition: internal state beyond current input. Worked example — Identify history dependence: Two trial groups share a current comparison stimulus of 20 Hz. The first sample is 10 Hz in one group and 30 Hz in the other. Animals predominantly choose 'comparison larger' and 'comparison smaller,' respectively. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Two trial groups share a current comparison stimulus of 20 Hz. The first sample is 10 Hz in one group and 30 Hz in the other. Animals predominantly choose 'comparison larger' and 'comparison smaller,' respectively. Because the current comparison is identical, a current-input-only model predicts the same choice distribution. Different sample histories change both the correct relation and actual choice. The internal state must carry at least the sample's relation to 20 Hz to explain the difference. First rule out confounds if motor cues or rewards also differ systematically between the groups. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “A working definition of cognition: internal state beyond current input”? The working definition emphasizes a history-dependent internal state. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “A working definition of cognition: internal state beyond current input”? The key experimental control holds current input fixed while varying the past. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “A working definition of cognition: internal state beyond current input” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The working definition emphasizes a history-dependent internal state. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Express 'current input is insufficient' with conditional probability”? These are probabilities, dimensionless and between 0 and 1; the conditioning variables themselves may have different units. If a history effect vanishes after all observable current inputs are included, no additional cognitive state is needed to explain that effect. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: How can the course's definition of cognition become a testable state dependence rather than an abstract label? This lecture adopts a working definition: cognition makes brain state or behavior incompletely determined by present sensory input. The same current stimulus can produce different responses under different memories, goals, or beliefs; conversely, an internal decision variable can keep evolving while the outside world is unchanged. This definition is useful for modeling, but it is not a complete philosophical definition of consciousness, language, or intelligence. A test presents the same current input after different histories. If sample identity, previous reward, or instruction changes delay activity and choice, the system requires a history-dependent state. Control current stimulus, movement preparation, and arousal; otherwise an apparent internal state may simply be an omitted external or bodily variable. Why does monotonic delay-period firing with f1 not by itself prove that this is the memory used for behavior? The correlated signal could be a passive readout. Functional evidence is stronger when its trial fluctuations, selective perturbation, or downstream coupling affect comparison behavior. This is the distinction tested in Timelines of DMS and Romo parametric working memory. Worked example — Make a comparison from noisy memory: The internal memory value is \(m_{1}=18 \mathrm{Hz}\), the comparison estimate is \(m_{2}=22 \mathrm{Hz}\), and the rule is to choose 'second is larger' when \(m_{2}-m_{1}>0\). Ignoring decision noise, find the choice variable. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: The internal memory value is \(m_{1}=18 \mathrm{Hz}\), the comparison estimate is \(m_{2}=22 \mathrm{Hz}\), and the rule is to choose 'second is larger' when \(m_{2}-m_{1}>0\). Ignoring decision noise, find the choice variable. Compute \(d=m_{2}-m_{1}=22-18=4 \mathrm{Hz}\). Since \(d>0\), the result lies on the 'second is larger' side. If memory error overestimates m1 beyond 22 Hz, the choice reverses, showing that an error need not arise from comparison sensation. Swapping the two estimates should produce -4 Hz and the opposite choice. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Timelines of DMS and Romo parametric working memory”? DMS can be supported by categorical or identity memory. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Timelines of DMS and Romo parametric working memory”? The Romo task must preserve a comparable magnitude for f1. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Timelines of DMS and Romo parametric working memory” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The Romo task must preserve a comparable magnitude for f1. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Why does increasing \(\lambda\) from 0.99 to 1.01 not simply lengthen memory a little? It crosses the stability boundary. The linear mode changes from slow decay to exponential growth and needs another nonlinearity to limit amplitude. This is the distinction tested in Persistent activity and a recurrent mode near one. Worked example — Predict drift during a delay: Let \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\), \(\lambda =0.99\), and \(\alpha _{0}=10\) after the sample. Find \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and estimate the amplitude after 1 s. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\), \(\lambda =0.99\), and \(\alpha _{0}=10\) after the sample. Find \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and estimate the amplitude after 1 s. \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=20/(1-0.99)=2000 \mathrm{ms}=2 \mathrm{s}\). After 1 s, \(\alpha =10e^{-1/2}\approx 6.07\). Although \(\lambda\) is very close to 1, a 1 s delay still loses about 39%, so 'near one' does not mean perfect memory. After one \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=2 \mathrm{s}\), the amplitude should fall to \(e^{-1}\approx 36.8\)% of its initial value. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Persistent activity and a recurrent mode near one”? The eigenvalue gap \(1-\lambda\) amplifies \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Persistent activity and a recurrent mode near one”? \(\lambda =1\) is the ideal persistence boundary, not a necessary condition for every memory network. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Persistent activity and a recurrent mode near one” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Directions outside the memory mode must also be stable. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Derive the effective time constant from a recurrent eigenvalue”? The exponent must be dimensionless, as \((1-\lambda )t/\tau\) is. For \(\lambda =0\), \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau\). As λ→1^-, \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) diverges. When \(\lambda >1\), the formula becomes negative, indicating growth rather than a decay time constant. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why do identical coherence values yield different choices and RTs? Each trial has a different noise path, which changes both the first-passage time and which boundary is reached first. This is the distinction tested in Leaky drift-diffusion: evidence, noise, and first passage. Worked example — Determine a deterministic first-passage time: Let \(\tau a=1 \mathrm{s}\), \(b=0\), \(\mu =2\), and \(B=1\). Ignoring noise, find the time to +B. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(\tau a=1 \mathrm{s}\), \(b=0\), \(\mu =2\), and \(B=1\). Ignoring noise, find the time to +B. The solution is \(a(t)=2(1-e^{-t})\). Set \(a=1\) to get \(1=2(1-e^{-t})\), hence \(e^{-t}=1/2\). Taking the natural logarithm gives \(t=\ln 2\approx 0.693 \mathrm{s}\). The steady state 2 exceeds bound 1, so the trajectory must cross. If \(\mu \le 1\) and \(b=0\), a deterministic leaky trajectory never reaches +B. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Leaky drift-diffusion: evidence, noise, and first passage”? This lecture's accumulator includes leak and must be distinguished from a perfect DDM. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Leaky drift-diffusion: evidence, noise, and first passage”? Choice and decision time are determined jointly by the first boundary crossing. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Leaky drift-diffusion: evidence, noise, and first passage” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? This lecture's accumulator includes leak and must be distinguished from a perfect DDM. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “A leaky accumulator under constant evidence”? \(da/dt\) has units of state/time; dividing every state term on the right by \(\tau a\) gives the same units. The no-leak limit requires \(\tau a\to \infty\) together with appropriate input scaling. As \(t\to \infty\), \(a\to \mu\); if \(|\mu |<B\), a deterministic trajectory never reaches a boundary. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why can mean LIP ramp slopes alone not distinguish accumulation from averaged discrete steps? Both forms of single-trial dynamics can yield similar smooth curves when different onset or choice times are averaged, requiring single-trial model comparison. This is the distinction tested in Psychometric and chronometric functions and LIP ramping. Worked example — Identify bias from simplified psychometric data: At signed coherences -10, 0, and +10%, the probabilities of a right choice are 0.15, 0.65, and 0.93. Does the pattern suggest a rightward bias? Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: At signed coherences -10, 0, and +10%, the probabilities of a right choice are 0.15, 0.65, and 0.93. Does the pattern suggest a rightward bias? An unbiased model generally predicts about 0.5 at 0 coherence. The observed 0.65 exceeds 0.5, suggesting a starting-point or choice-rule bias toward the right. A confidence interval and lapse model are still needed; one proportion cannot identify the source of bias. At strong evidence on the two sides, probabilities approach 0 and 1 respectively, so the sign convention for direction is consistent. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Psychometric and chronometric functions and LIP ramping”? Psychometric and chronometric functions should be interpreted jointly. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Psychometric and chronometric functions and LIP ramping”? A condition-averaged ramp does not uniquely imply a single-trial ramp. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Psychometric and chronometric functions and LIP ramping” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? A condition-averaged ramp does not uniquely imply a single-trial ramp. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Why do two choice attractors generally require a saddle or basin boundary between them? Distinct basins of attraction in a continuous dynamical system must be separated by a boundary that flows to neither attractor. In two dimensions, that boundary is commonly the stable manifold of a saddle. This is the distinction tested in Wong–Wang choice attractors and phase-plane boundaries. Worked example — Classify two points from their Jacobians: Point A has Jacobian eigenvalues -2 and -0.5 s^-1; point B has +1 and -3 s^-1. Classify them. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Point A has Jacobian eigenvalues -2 and -0.5 s^-1; point B has +1 and -3 s^-1. Classify them. Both real parts at A are negative, so every small perturbation decays. At B, one direction grows and the other decays. A is therefore a local attractor and B a saddle; B's stable manifold can form a separatrix. The eigenvalue units match the given s^-1; positive and negative signs denote growth and decay, respectively. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Wong–Wang choice attractors and phase-plane boundaries”? Nullcline intersections are fixed points; their stability requires a separate test. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Wong–Wang choice attractors and phase-plane boundaries”? A separatrix is the boundary between choice basins. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Wong–Wang choice attractors and phase-plane boundaries” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Evidence biases one attractor by changing input and geometry. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Classify fixed-point stability from the local Jacobian”? The derivative \(G_{i}/\partial S_{j}\) has units 1/time, matching a local exponential growth or decay rate. Recovery slows as an eigenvalue's real part approaches 0; a positive eigenvalue destabilizes the fixed point. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “First-passage paths in drift–diffusion”? Each path begins at bias b, accumulates noisy evidence step by step, and stops the first time it reaches +B or −B. The endpoint determines choice and the horizontal coordinate determines decision time. Under identical task parameters, noise can carry the two trajectories to different boundaries; a trajectory must not be averaged further after crossing before a decision is assigned. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “cognition” mean in this lecture? cognition: This lecture's working definition: a brain state partly decoupled from present input and shaped by past events or future goals. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “short-term memory” mean in this lecture? short-term memory: The ability to retain recently encountered information briefly. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “working memory” mean in this lecture? working memory: Information retained for use in a current computation. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “delayed match-to-sample” mean in this lecture? delayed match-to-sample: A sample–delay–test memory task. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “persistent activity” mean in this lecture? persistent activity: Neural activity that remains after the stimulus ends. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “drift-diffusion model, DDM” mean in this lecture? drift-diffusion model, DDM: A decision model that accumulates noisy evidence to bounds. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “psychometric curve” mean in this lecture? psychometric curve: Choice or accuracy as a function of stimulus strength. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “chronometric curve” mean in this lecture? chronometric curve: Reaction time as a function of stimulus strength. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “separatrix” mean in this lecture? separatrix: A boundary separating different attractor basins. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “leaky evidence accumulator” be used? leaky evidence accumulator: \(\tau a\) \(\dot{a} = -a + e(t) + \gamma (t)\). white or colored noise specified This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “decision bias” be used? decision bias: \(a(0) = b\). initial-condition interpretation This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “absorbing decision bounds” be used? absorbing decision bounds: \(a = \pm B\). first-passage rule This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written.
