Wong–Wang nullclines: \(G_{1} = 0\), \(G_{2} = 0\). 2D reduced dynamics This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written.

title: Lecture 24: Learning from Rewards
subtitle: Learning from Rewards
text: Learning from Rewards stimulus/action/reward → three-factor plasticity → reward baseline/covariance → matching law → Rescorla–Wagner → TD/RPE Organize stimulus, action, reward, and synaptic eligibility into a three-factor learning rule, explaining why naive reward-gated Hebbian learning remains excessively strong. Derive the reward-baseline covariance update and matching equilibrium, stating assumptions such as stationary reward and the choice rule at each step. Derive Rescorla–Wagner learning from squared prediction error and use blocking to explain why an already predicted reward produces no further learning. Express delayed reward as a temporal-difference error and distinguish state value, action value, reward-prediction error, and dopamine response. Read dopamine timelines for early reward, cue transfer, and omission while preserving the evidential boundary for alternatives such as salience. Learned decisions must connect stimulus/action activity to delayed reward. A simple reward-gated Hebbian rule keeps strengthening when reward is common; subtracting the expected-reward baseline turns it into a covariance rule. Under a specified choice model and assumptions, the stationary covariance condition produces matching behavior. Rescorla–Wagner learns cue value from current reward-prediction error, while TD extends error to future value. Dopamine cue-transfer and omission patterns resemble RPE, though dopamine signals may also mix salience and movement. Failing to subtract a baseline from reward-gated Hebbian learning, so every rewarded coactivity continues to strengthen. Treating matching as an unconditional law of rational optimality. Explaining blocking by claiming that S2 did not coincide with reward. Conflating RPE, value, and salience. Omitting \(\gamma\) or next value from TD error. Treating dopamine as the only third factor in all reward learning. Prematurely treating this lecture's simplified Q concept as a complete Q-learning algorithm. Lecture 24 is a biological and reward-learning bridge; Lecture 25 introduces MDP/RL systematically. Do not let Bellman equations or Q-learning obscure this lecture's plasticity and dopamine logic. reward-baseline three-factor update ∆\(w = \eta e(R - \bar{R})\) eligibility e defined covariance learning E[∆w] = \(\eta \operatorname{Cov}(e, R)\) stationary average matching law \(CA /CB \approx  RA /RB\) specific foraging assumptions linear value predictor \(V = w_{\mathrm{T}} x\) features x Rescorla–Wagner update ∆\(w = \eta x(R - V )\) immediate or represented reward TD/RPE \(\delta  = R + \gamma V_{\mathrm{next}} - V\) Markov or state representation implicit state–action value \(Q(s, a) = E[G|s, a]\) policy and future behavior specified reward learning Adjustment of stimulus–action associations by outcomes. eligibility \(\operatorname{trace} A\) variable marking recent pre/post or action activity for modification by a later reward. reward baseline Expected reward used to compute a signal above or below expectation. matching law Approximate matching of choice proportions to obtained-reward proportions. value Expected discounted future reward from the current state or cue. Rescorla-Wagner rule A rule that updates cue value using reward-prediction error. blocking Failure of a new cue to learn because an existing predictor leaves zero error. temporal-difference error, TD error Reward plus discounted next value minus current value. reward-prediction error, RPE The difference between an actual or updated target and predicted value. Q value Expected return conditioned on a state–action pair. If reward is always 1 and the naive update is \(\Delta w=\eta Rxy\), with x and y often positive, what happens? A baseline, prediction error, normalization, or another stabilizing mechanism is needed. The weight keeps increasing whenever the activities coincide; correctly predicting the reward supplies no natural stopping point. For \(R=0\), baseline \(b=0.4\), eligibility \(e=2\), and \(\eta =0.1\), what is the covariance update? Failing to receive reward is negative relative to a positive baseline, so the eligible connection weakens on this trial. \(\Delta w=0.1\times (0-0.4)\times 2=-0.08\). At a matching equilibrium, what do the choice-conditioned expected rewards of two selected actions generally satisfy? This condition depends on the relevant stochastic-choice and learning assumptions and need not hold exactly in every environment. Their marginal or choice-conditioned expected rewards are equal; otherwise choice probability continues moving toward the action with higher return. In blocking, an old cue already predicts reward completely and a new cue is presented beside it. Why does the new cue acquire little learning? This is the key prediction that separates an error-correcting rule from pure reward-gated coactivity. The total prediction is already close to reward, so prediction error is nearly zero; even though the new cue is active, it receives almost no update signal. After a cue predicts reward, does a smaller dopamine response at reward time mean that the reward has lost value? Keep the time series for value, received reward, and prediction error separate. No. The cue now predicts value, so RPE transfers to the cue; at reward time, outcome matches prediction and \(\delta\) is nearly zero. Why should a dopamine pulse without preceding eligibility not selectively strengthen one stimulus–action synapse? The third factor broadcasts the outcome, but local eligibility identifies the synapse that participated in the action; without eligibility, there is no correct credit address. This is the distinction tested in Learned choice and three-factor synaptic credit. Worked example — Eligibility under delayed reward: At the action, \(e_{0}=1\). With no new coactivity, \(\tau e=2 \mathrm{s}\); after 1 s, \(M=0.6\) and \(\eta =0.1\). Find the instantaneous update magnitude \(\eta Me\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: At the action, \(e_{0}=1\). With no new coactivity, \(\tau e=2 \mathrm{s}\); after 1 s, \(M=0.6\) and \(\eta =0.1\). Find the instantaneous update magnitude \(\eta Me\). The trace decays to \(e=e^{-1/2}\approx 0.607\). Multiplying by the third factor gives \(Me\approx 0.364\). After multiplying by \(\eta\), the update magnitude is approximately 0.0364. With a delay of 0, the update would be 0.06; the smaller delayed update is consistent with trace decay. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Learned choice and three-factor synaptic credit”? Eligibility identifies candidate synapses; the third factor specifies the sign of the outcome. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Learned choice and three-factor synaptic credit”? A naive nonnegative reward gate lacks error-driven stopping and weakening. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Learned choice and three-factor synaptic credit” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Eligibility identifies candidate synapses; the third factor specifies the sign of the outcome. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “A three-factor update with an eligibility trace”? If x and y are treated as rates, the trace equation must normalize them consistently; \(\eta\) balances units on the two sides of the weight derivative. As \(\tau e\to 0\), a delayed outcome can barely credit the earlier action. When \(b=R\), \(M=0\) and updating stops. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: When reward arrives, how can learning modify only the connections that participated in the preceding choice? A foraging animal selects an action from a sensory cue and receives reward. Learning must establish the stimulus–action–outcome relation rather than strengthen every recently active synapse. Let x be a presynaptic stimulus feature and y postsynaptic or action activity, so xy creates eligibility. A third factor M arrives after the outcome, giving update \(\Delta w=\eta Mxy\). An eligibility trace can bridge the delay from action to reward. If M is simply the nonnegative reward R, every rewarded coactivity grows. A mastered action continues to strengthen, and the common offset of frequent reward contaminates credit; weights stop only through saturation rather than a correct equilibrium. If \(R=0\), an unrewarded choice merely receives no update and the wrong association cannot actively weaken. Why does an underestimated baseline produce systematic positive drift? The mean of R-b becomes positive. If mean eligibility is also positive, an offset update appears that is unrelated to genuine reward–eligibility covariance. This is the distinction tested in Reward baseline, covariance rule, and equilibrium. Worked example — Compute a covariance update over four trials: For four trials, \(R=[1,0,1,0]\), \(e=[2,1,0,1]\), \(b=0.5\), and \(\eta =0.1\). Find the average update. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: For four trials, \(R=[1,0,1,0]\), \(e=[2,1,0,1]\), \(b=0.5\), and \(\eta =0.1\). Find the average update. Across trials, (R-b)e is 1, -0.5, 0, and -0.5. The average of the four terms is 0. After multiplying by \(\eta\), the average \(\Delta w\) is 0 even though individual trials have positive and negative updates. \(E[R]=0.5\) matches the stated baseline. Direct calculation gives \(E[Re]=0.5\) and \(E[R]E[e]=0.5\), so the covariance is again zero. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Reward baseline, covariance rule, and equilibrium”? An average baseline turns expected updating into reward–eligibility covariance. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Reward baseline, covariance rule, and equilibrium”? A state-dependent baseline can reduce error in heterogeneous environments. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Reward baseline, covariance rule, and equilibrium” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? A state-dependent baseline can reduce error in heterogeneous environments. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “From a baseline update to covariance”? R-b has the same units as R; \(\eta e\) must convert it into a dimensionless or otherwise specified weight change. If e is constant, covariance is zero. If b is not \(E[R]\), the update also contains a baseline-mismatch term. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does a matching curve not prove that the animal explicitly computes RA/RB? A long-run ratio can emerge automatically from local prediction-error updates and stochastic choice; the behavioral equality does not uniquely identify the internal algorithm. This is the distinction tested in Matching law and choice allocation in fly foraging. Worked example — Check matching: Across 100 choices, A is selected 60 times and earns 30 rewards; B is selected 40 times and earns 20 rewards. Check the conditional returns and both ratios. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Across 100 choices, A is selected 60 times and earns 30 rewards; B is selected 40 times and earns 20 rewards. Check the conditional returns and both ratios. \(qA=30/60=0.5\) reward/choice. \(qB=20/40=0.5\) reward/choice. The choice ratio is \(60/40=1.5\) and the reward ratio is \(30/20=1.5\). Total rewards are 50 and total choices 100, giving an overall reward rate of 0.5, consistent with both conditional rates. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Matching law and choice allocation in fly foraging”? Matching relates long-run choice allocation to obtained-reward allocation. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Matching law and choice allocation in fly foraging”? Equal choice-conditioned return is the core equilibrium condition. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Matching law and choice allocation in fly foraging” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? A local learner can generate a ratio law without an explicit division neuron; interpret the update sign together with the direction convention of the choice readout. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Derive the matching ratio from equal marginal returns”? Both ratios are dimensionless, and the observation window must be the same. When \(RB=0\) or \(CB=0\), the ratio form is undefined. Retain the cross-multiplied equation and discuss boundary behavior. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. If reward is unchanged but the prediction from old cue A is removed, why does B begin learning again? The total prediction falls and positive prediction error returns. Because B is active, it now receives an update—the logic of unblocking. This is the distinction tested in Rescorla–Wagner, blocking, and the temporal-difference bridge. Worked example — Demonstrate blocking numerically: Reward is \(R=1\). After A-alone training, \(wA=0.9\) and novel B has \(wB=0\). On a compound trial, \(xA=xB=1\) and \(\eta =0.2\). Find both weight updates. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Reward is \(R=1\). After A-alone training, \(wA=0.9\) and novel B has \(wB=0\). On a compound trial, \(xA=xB=1\) and \(\eta =0.2\). Find both weight updates. Total \(V=0.9+0=0.9\). The error \(R-V=0.1\). A and B are both active, so each update is \(0.2\times 0.1=0.02\); B acquires only a small increment. If wA were exactly 1, the error would be 0 and neither weight would change. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Rescorla–Wagner, blocking, and the temporal-difference bridge”? The negative gradient gives a prediction-error × feature update. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Rescorla–Wagner, blocking, and the temporal-difference bridge”? Blocking occurs because the total prediction from the compound cue already equals reward. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Rescorla–Wagner, blocking, and the temporal-difference bridge” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The negative gradient gives a prediction-error × feature update. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Derive Rescorla–Wagner from squared error”? \(w^\mathrm{T} x\) must have units compatible with subtraction from R, and loss has squared-value units. When \(V=R\), the update is zero. When \(x_{i}=0\), that cue's weight does not change on this trial. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does equal state value not imply that two actions are equally good? V is a policy-weighted average. One action may have high Q and another low Q while producing the same aggregate V under a particular policy. This is the distinction tested in Temporal features, state–action value, and choice. Worked example — Make a softmax choice from two Q values: In one state, \(QA=2\), \(QB=1\), and inverse temperature \(\beta =\ln 3\). Find \(P(A)=\exp(\beta QA)/[\exp(\beta QA)+\exp(\beta QB)]\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: In one state, \(QA=2\), \(QB=1\), and inverse temperature \(\beta =\ln 3\). Find \(P(A)=\exp(\beta QA)/[\exp(\beta QA)+\exp(\beta QB)]\). Factor out \(\exp(\beta QB)\), giving \(P(A)=\exp(\beta )/(\exp(\beta )+1)\). Because \(\beta =\ln 3\), \(\exp(\beta )=3\). \(P(A)=3/(3+1)=0.75\) and \(P(B)=0.25\). The two probabilities sum to 1; if \(QA=QB\), each should be 0.5. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Temporal features, state–action value, and choice”? Temporal features represent different time positions after a cue. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Temporal features, state–action value, and choice”? Q includes an explicit action condition absent from V. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Temporal features, state–action value, and choice” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Q includes an explicit action condition absent from V. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Why does an omission dip support prediction error more strongly than merely observing no burst at reward time? It is a negative signal below baseline timed to the expected reward. A purely nonnegative reward detector cannot naturally generate this timed negative response. This is the distinction tested in Dopamine RPE timelines and the boundary with action selection. Worked example — Compute an omission error: Before the reward deadline, \(V_{\mathrm{current}}=0.8\); afterward \(V_{\mathrm{next}}=0\), with \(R=0\) and \(\gamma =0.95\). Find \(\delta\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Before the reward deadline, \(V_{\mathrm{current}}=0.8\); afterward \(V_{\mathrm{next}}=0\), with \(R=0\) and \(\gamma =0.95\). Find \(\delta\). Substitute \(\delta =0+0.95\times 0-0.8\). The result is \(\delta =-0.8\). The negative sign means that the outcome was worse than predicted, not that a negative physical reward was received. If reward arrives as expected with \(R=0.8\) and next value 0, then \(\delta =0\), consistent with correct prediction. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Dopamine RPE timelines and the boundary with action selection”? RPE is jointly determined by actual reward and successive value predictions. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Dopamine RPE timelines and the boundary with action selection”? Cue transfer and an omission dip require a temporal state representation. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Dopamine RPE timelines and the boundary with action selection” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Effects of dopamine perturbation on learning and performance must be separated. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Signs of TD error for three events”? R can be added to \(\gamma V\), and \(\delta\) retains value units. When \(\gamma =0\), only immediate reward is learned. With perfect prediction, \(\delta\) approaches zero for every event other than transition surprises. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “TD error transfers from reward to a predictive cue”? Compare the same trial row by row. Before learning, only unexpected reward produces positive \(\delta\). After the cue–reward relation is learned, positive \(\delta\) moves earlier to the cue and is nearly zero when reward arrives on time. If reward is omitted at the deadline, negative \(\delta\) appears then. This pattern of signs supports prediction error rather than a pure reward response. Check the labeled axes, nodes, or event order before mapping the schematic back to the model claim. What does “reward learning” mean in this lecture? reward learning: Adjustment of stimulus–action associations by outcomes. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “eligibility trace” mean in this lecture? eligibility trace: A variable marking recent pre/post or action activity for modification by a later reward. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “reward baseline” mean in this lecture? reward baseline: Expected reward used to compute a signal above or below expectation. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “matching law” mean in this lecture? matching law: Approximate matching of choice proportions to obtained-reward proportions. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “value” mean in this lecture? value: Expected discounted future reward from the current state or cue. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “Rescorla-Wagner rule” mean in this lecture? Rescorla-Wagner rule: A rule that updates cue value using reward-prediction error. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “blocking” mean in this lecture? blocking: Failure of a new cue to learn because an existing predictor leaves zero error. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “temporal-difference error, TD error” mean in this lecture? temporal-difference error, TD error: Reward plus discounted next value minus current value. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “reward-prediction error, RPE” mean in this lecture? reward-prediction error, RPE: The difference between an actual or updated target and predicted value. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. Under which conditions should “reward-baseline three-factor update” be used? reward-baseline three-factor update: ∆\(w = \eta e(R - \bar{R})\). eligibility e defined This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “covariance learning” be used? covariance learning: E[∆w] = \(\eta \operatorname{Cov}(e, R)\). stationary average This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “matching law” be used? matching law: \(CA /CB \approx  RA /RB\). specific foraging assumptions This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “linear value predictor” be used? linear value predictor: \(V = w_{\mathrm{T}} x\). features x This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “Rescorla–Wagner update” be used? Rescorla–Wagner update: ∆\(w = \eta x(R - V )\). immediate or represented reward This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “TD/RPE” be used? TD/RPE: \(\delta  = R + \gamma V_{\mathrm{next}} - V\). Markov or state representation implicit This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written. Under which conditions should “state–action value” be used? state–action value: \(Q(s, a) = E[G|s, a]\). policy and future behavior specified This condition keeps the operation's dimensions and interpretation well defined; without it, the formula cannot be applied as written.

title: Lecture 25: Reinforcement Learning: MDPs, Bellman Equations, and Q-Learning
subtitle: Reinforcement Learning: MDPs, Bellman Equations, and Q-Learning
text: Reinforcement Learning: MDPs, Bellman Equations, and Q-Learning agent/state/action/reward → Markov property → discounted return → V/Q/policy → Bellman backup → Q-learning/exploration Define an MDP completely in terms of agent, state, action, reward, and a transition distribution, and use counterexamples to test whether a state satisfies the Markov property. Derive discounted return, \(V_{\pi }\), and \(Q_{\pi }\) from a reward sequence, computing both a finite chain and an infinite geometric series by hand. Derive the Bellman expectation and optimality equations by splitting return after its first step, making explicit that the maximum ranges over actions in the next state. Carry out tabular Q-learning and ε-greedy exploration update by update, distinguishing the behavior policy, target, and off-policy update. Compare model-free learning, model-based learning, generative representations, and replay while rigorously separating algorithmic variables from hippocampal evidence. The central MDP claim is not that the environment has no history, but that the chosen state representation makes the future conditionally independent of earlier history given current state and action. Discounted return decomposes recursively into immediate reward plus \(\gamma\) times future return, yielding the Bellman optimality equation. Q-learning uses a sampled Bellman error for an off-policy bootstrap update. Model-based RL also learns a transition/reward model and can improve sample efficiency with simulated experience or replay. Equating the Markov property with an environment that has no history. Confusing \(V_{\pi }\), \(Q_{\pi }\), \(V^{*}\), and \(Q^{*}\). Omitting the transition expectation from the Bellman equation. Using the behavior action in a Q-learning target and inadvertently writing SARSA. Assuming that the random branch of ε-greedy samples only nongreedy actions without stating that convention. Equating model-free learning with an absence of internal representation. Equating hippocampal replay directly with an exact Bellman backup. Q-learning is not a synonym for every TD-learning method, and hippocampal replay is not directly equivalent to an exact Bellman backup; evidence and inference must be distinguished explicitly. MDP transition/reward model \(p(s', r|s, a)\) Markov state discounted return Gt = \(\gamma \) k Rt+k+1 \(k\ge 0\) \(0\le \gamma <1\) or a finite episode state value \(V_{\pi } (s) = E_{\pi } [G_{t} |s_{t} = s]\) policy \(\pi\) state-action value \(Q_{\pi } (s, a) = E_{\pi } [G_{t} |s_{t} = s, a_{t} = a]\) first action fixed Bellman optimality \(Q\ast  = E[R + \gamma  \max Q\ast  ]\) optimal continuation tabular Q-learning Q ← Q + α(R + γ max Q′ − Q) sampled transition ε-greedy exploration \(\pi \epsilon  = (1 - \epsilon )\)greedy \(+ \epsilon \mathrm{random}\) finite action set reinforcement learning A framework that learns a policy or value through interaction and rewards. agent A learner that selects actions and updates an internal policy or model. state An environment representation used to predict the future and select an action. Markov property The conditional independence of the future from earlier history given the current state and action. policy A mapping from states to action probabilities. return The discounted sum of future rewards. Bellman equation A recursive self-consistency relation for value. Q-learning A model-free, off-policy TD control algorithm. exploration-exploitation The tradeoff between gathering new information and selecting the currently best action. model-based reinforcement learning A reinforcement-learning approach that learns or uses an environment model for planning. replay A neural or computational process that reinstates or simulates state sequences offline. At the same maze location, available routes differ depending on whether a door is open. Is location alone a Markov state? The Markov property requires the next transition and reward to be independent of earlier history once current state and action are given. Usually not. Include the door state or sufficient history to predict it. If every step forever gives reward=1 and \(\gamma =0.9\), what is the return? This sum is bounded only when \(\gamma <1\) or the episode is finite. The infinite geometric sum is \(1/(1-0.9)=10\). Which variable does the maximum in the Bellman optimality equation range over? Do not maximize again over the already executed current action or over the random reward itself. It maximizes Q over the available next action \(a'\) in the next state \(s'\). Given \(Q=2\), \(R=1\), \(\gamma =0.9\), \(\max Q_{\mathrm{next}}=4\), and \(\alpha =0.5\), what is Q after one update? The update moves an \(\alpha\) fraction toward the target; it does not replace Q directly with reward. The target is 4.6, TD error is 2.6, and new \(Q=2+0.5\times 2.6=3.3\). Hippocampal replay resembles simulated experience. Does that prove that every replay event performs Q-learning? Replay may supply sequences for offline updating or planning, but a reinstated sequence alone cannot distinguish Q-learning, a model-based backup, memory consolidation, or another computation. No. Reinstated content is compatible with planning, but the particular update rule, target, and causal role require further experiments. Why might adding the trial number to state improve training prediction but still be a poor representation? It may memorize samples without capturing generalizable, future-relevant structure and will perform poorly in held-out contexts. This is the distinction tested in MDPs and Markov states: compressing history into a predictive state. Worked example — Repair a non-Markov state: An agent is at the same room location x. If it previously collected a key, opening the door gives 10; otherwise hitting the door gives 0. Give a minimal state extension. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: An agent is at the same room location x. If it previously collected a key, opening the door gives 10; otherwise hitting the door gives 0. Give a minimal state extension. With original state x alone, the same x/action pair has two rewards that depend on history. Add a binary variable \(k\in {0,1}\) indicating whether the key is held. With new state \(s=(x,k)\), the outcome of opening the door is predictable from current s and the action. There is no need to retain the entire route, only the key information that affects the future. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “MDPs and Markov states: compressing history into a predictive state”? The Markov property permits stochastic transitions but requires conditional independence from history. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “MDPs and Markov states: compressing history into a predictive state”? State aliasing incorrectly averages distinct futures. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “MDPs and Markov states: compressing history into a predictive state” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The Markov property permits stochastic transitions but requires conditional independence from history. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “The Markov condition and factorization of trajectory probability”? Discrete probabilities are dimensionless, and trajectory probability is a product of dimensionless factors. In a deterministic environment the transition factor is 0 or 1. Under partial observation, the Markov equality generally fails. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: What information must enter the state so that a one-step transition model no longer depends on earlier history? An MDP is defined by states, actions, reward, and the transition–reward distribution \(p(s',r|s,a)\). The Markov property says that, conditioned on current s and a, the next outcome does not change with earlier trajectory. It does not require a deterministic environment: one s,a pair may lead randomly to several \(s'\) values, provided the probabilities are determined fully by current state. State representation is a modeling choice. Location may be insufficient in a Tolman maze because door status, food depletion, or latent context changes the future. Omitting such variables aliases states, causing Q values to average conflicting outcomes and making learning appear unstable. Including the complete history always restores prediction but sacrifices compression and generalization. The goal is a state that is sufficient without being excessive. Why does a in \(Q_{\pi }(s,a)\) fix only the first step? The definition conditions on \(a_{t}=a\). Future actions are sampled from \(\pi\) beginning in the next state, so Q evaluates 'take a first, then follow \(\pi\).' This is the distinction tested in Discounted return, \(V_{\pi }\), and \(Q_{\pi }\). Worked example — A finite three-step return: Future rewards are 2, 0, and 4, after which the episode terminates; \(\gamma =0.5\). Find Gt. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Future rewards are 2, 0, and 4, after which the episode terminates; \(\gamma =0.5\). Find Gt. The first term is 2. The second term is \(0.5\times 0=0\). The third term is \(0.5^{2}\times 4=1\). The return is less than the undiscounted total 6, and the final reward has weight 0.25. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Discounted return, \(V_{\pi }\), and \(Q_{\pi }\)”? Return is the discounted sum of future rewards. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Discounted return, \(V_{\pi }\), and \(Q_{\pi }\)”? V fixes the state; Q additionally fixes the first action. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Discounted return, \(V_{\pi }\), and \(Q_{\pi }\)” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? V fixes the state; Q additionally fixes the first action. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Sum an infinite reward stream”? Powers of \(\gamma\) are dimensionless, so every term and the sum retain reward units. For \(\gamma =0\), \(G=r\). As γ→1^-, a continuing constant-positive return diverges. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why can the maximum not be moved outside the expectation while fixing the same \(a'\)? Different random next states can have different best actions. Averaging first would force one action across states and change the optimal-continuation problem. This is the distinction tested in Bellman recursion: from the entire future to a one-step backup. Worked example — A Bellman backup with two possible next states: After an action, with probability 0.5 the agent receives \(R=1\) and reaches s1, where maxQ\((s_{1})=4\); with probability 0.5 it receives \(R=3\) and reaches s2, where maxQ\((s_{2})=2\). Let \(\gamma =0.9\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: After an action, with probability 0.5 the agent receives \(R=1\) and reaches s1, where maxQ\((s_{1})=4\); with probability 0.5 it receives \(R=3\) and reaches s2, where maxQ\((s_{2})=2\). Let \(\gamma =0.9\). The s1 target is \(1+0.9\times 4=4.6\). The s2 target is \(3+0.9\times 2=4.8\). Probability averaging gives \(Q^{*}=0.5\times 4.6+0.5\times 4.8=4.7\). The target lies between the two outcome targets, 4.6 and 4.8. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Bellman recursion: from the entire future to a one-step backup”? Bellman recursion follows from the one-step decomposition of Gt. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Bellman recursion: from the entire future to a one-step backup”? The optimal maximum ranges over the next action separately for each next state. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Bellman recursion: from the entire future to a one-step backup” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? A tabular contraction guarantee does not automatically extend to arbitrary function approximation. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “The Bellman optimality equation”? Q and R share value units, and \(\gamma\) is dimensionless. At a terminal state, future \(\max Q\) is 0. When \(\gamma =0\), \(Q^{*}\) equals expected immediate reward only. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why can the random branch of ε-greedy still select the greedy action? The random branch samples uniformly from all actions, including the greedy action, so total greedy probability exceeds \(1-\epsilon\). This is the distinction tested in Tabular Q-learning and exploration. Worked example — Two consecutive updates: Initially \(Q=0\), with \(\gamma =0.5\) and \(\alpha =0.5\). The first transition has \(R=2\) and next maxQ=4; the second visit to the same entry has \(R=0\) and next maxQ=2. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Initially \(Q=0\), with \(\gamma =0.5\) and \(\alpha =0.5\). The first transition has \(R=2\) and next maxQ=4; the second visit to the same entry has \(R=0\) and next maxQ=2. The first target is \(2+2=4\), so new \(Q=0+0.5\times 4=2\). The second target is \(0+1=1\), and error=\(1-2=-1\). New \(Q=2+0.5\times (-1)=1.5\). The second target is below the old value, so Q falls but moves only halfway. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Tabular Q-learning and exploration”? Q-learning uses a sampled Bellman target to update one state–action entry. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Tabular Q-learning and exploration”? The behavior policy can explore while the target policy remains greedy. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Tabular Q-learning and exploration” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Q-learning uses a sampled Bellman target to update one state–action entry. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Error structure of one Q-learning update”? The convex coefficients sum to 1, so new Q retains value units. With \(\alpha =0\) there is no learning; with \(\alpha =1\) the current estimate is replaced completely by this sampled target. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why is immediate sensitivity to revaluation not sufficient proof of a complete internal map? Other rules, instructions, or direct cues can also alter choice rapidly; constrain the explanation with multiple novel transitions and control conditions. This is the distinction tested in Tolman mazes, latent state, and generative maps. Worked example — Plan after a one-step revaluation: In state s, action A deterministically reaches terminal state s1 with reward 5; B reaches terminal state s2 with reward 3. Outcome devaluation then informs the agent that reward at s1 has changed to -1, while transitions are unchanged. Compare model-based and cached model-free choice. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: In state s, action A deterministically reaches terminal state s1 with reward 5; B reaches terminal state s2 with reward 3. Outcome devaluation then informs the agent that reward at s1 has changed to -1, while transitions are unchanged. Compare model-based and cached model-free choice. The model-based learner changes \(r(s,A,s_{1})\) in its reward model from 5 to -1. It updates the outcome model rather than treating a derived value as an environmental parameter. Both next states are terminal, so continuation value is 0. Replanning gives \(Q_{\mathrm{MB}}(s,A)=-1\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{MB}}(s,B)=3\). The agent can switch to B without executing A again. Cached \(Q_{\mathrm{MF}}(s,A)\), which has received no new prediction error, may remain 5 and temporarily favor A. Terminal continuation is 0, so the new Q ranking must match the updated immediate rewards. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Tolman mazes, latent state, and generative maps”? A generative model can simulate a future before it is experienced. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Tolman mazes, latent state, and generative maps”? Model-based learning is flexible but computationally costly; model-free learning is fast but updates with delay. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Tolman mazes, latent state, and generative maps” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Model-based learning is flexible but computationally costly; model-free learning is fast but updates with delay. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Why is more replay not always better? If the learned model has systematic error, repeated simulation amplifies its bias; coverage, priority, and model uncertainty must be balanced. This is the distinction tested in Simulated experience, hippocampal replay, and sample efficiency. Worked example — One real backup followed by two simulated backups: One Q estimate starts at 0 with \(\alpha =0.5\) and \(\gamma =0\). A real reward is 2; the model then simulates rewards 2 and 0. Update in order. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: One Q estimate starts at 0 with \(\alpha =0.5\) and \(\gamma =0\). A real reward is 2; the model then simulates rewards 2 and 0. Update in order. Real update: \(Q=0+0.5\times (2-0)=1\). Simulated reward 2: \(Q=1+0.5\times (2-1)=1.5\). Simulated reward 0: \(Q=1.5+0.5\times (0-1.5)=0.75\). The mean reward of the three samples is 4/3. With constant \(\alpha\), recent samples receive more weight, so the result is not a simple average. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Simulated experience, hippocampal replay, and sample efficiency”? Simulated transitions can repeatedly drive value backups. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Simulated experience, hippocampal replay, and sample efficiency”? Evidence of a replay sequence does not specify the downstream learning rule. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Simulated experience, hippocampal replay, and sample efficiency” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Prioritized replay increases efficiency and changes the sample distribution. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “A Dyna-style chain of real and simulated updates”? Real and simulated rewards must use the same value units to share one Q table. With zero simulated updates, the algorithm reduces to ordinary model-free sampling. If the model is entirely wrong, additional simulation can amplify bias. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “The agent–environment loop and a one-step Bellman backup”? In the forward interaction, policy maps \(s_{t}\) to \(a_{t}\), after which the environment samples r and \(s_{t+1}\). The backup then uses \(r+\gamma \max_{a'}Q(s_{t+1},a')\) to update current \(Q(s_{t},a_{t})\). A dashed path carries \(s_{t+1}\) into the next cycle, showing that the Markov transition and value backup are connected steps pointing in opposite directions. This is the meaning used in this lecture, not every possible use of the term. What does “agent” mean in this lecture? agent: A learner that selects actions and updates an internal policy or model. title: Lecture 26: Hopfield Associative Memory
subtitle: Hopfield Associative Memory
text: Hopfield Associative Memory Hebbian assembly → binary asynchronous dynamics → energy → stored attractors/basins → spurious mixtures → signal+crosstalk From Hebbian cell assemblies to the binary Hopfield abstraction, distinguish the biological hypothesis, state variable, encoding rule, and retrieval dynamics. Execute asynchronous sign updates by hand, compute overlap, and explain how symmetric weights and a zero diagonal support energy descent. Derive the energy change from flipping one neuron and the local field for a \(P=1\) stored pattern, identifying aligned, antialigned, and spurious attractors. Separate a multi-pattern local field into signal and crosstalk, estimating variance, error probability, and loading \(\alpha =P/N\). Explain why \(\alpha c\approx 0.138\) applies only under the assumptions of the classic dense, unbiased, random Hopfield model, and compare sparse stochastic and global-inhibition variants. The Hopfield model abstracts explicit memory as attractor dynamics: recurrent updates drive a partial cue toward a stored pattern. Symmetric weights and asynchronous single-neuron updates ensure that Ising energy cannot increase. For \(P=1\), Hebbian weights make both the target and its sign-reversed pattern fixed points. For \(P>1\), the other memories produce crosstalk noise; as loading \(\alpha =P/N\) rises, retrieval errors increase, and stable retrieval disappears near \(\alpha \approx 0.138\) in the classic dense random model. Applying an energy proof for asynchronous dynamics to synchronous dynamics. Forgetting that W must be symmetric and \(W_{ii}=0\). Calling only \(\xi\) an attractor for \(P=1\) while overlooking \(-\xi\) and the spurious states implied by global sign symmetry. Conflating overlap with exact bit accuracy. Failing to check how crosstalk variance scales with N and P. Treating the Gaussian approximation as an exact finite-N law. Treating 0.138N as the memory capacity of the brain. Failing to state that a 'memory capacity of 0.138N' refers only to the stable-retrieval criterion of the classic dense random-pattern Hopfield model, not to a conclusion about biological memory capacity. binary neuron state \(S_{i} \in  {-1, +1}\) classic dense model asynchronous update \(S_{i} \leftarrow  \operatorname{sgn}(h_{i} )\) one neuron at a time Hopfield energy \(1\sum  E=- W_{ij} S_{i} S_{j} 2\) ij symmetric W Hebbian storage rule \(W_{ij} = N -1 \xi _{i} \xi _{j}\) µ \(W_{ii}=0\) pattern overlap mµ = N −1 \(\xi \) i Si \(i \pm 1\) patterns retrieval field decomposition h = signal + crosstalk random-pattern analysis loading ratio \(\alpha  = P /N P\) memories, N neurons classic capacity threshold \(\alpha c \approx  0.138\) dense unbiased random Hopfield associative memory The recovery of a stored pattern from a partial or noisy cue. cell assembly A group of neurons that are coactive and linked by Hebbian connections. basin of attraction The set of initial states that converge to the same attractor. pattern completion The reconstruction of a complete memory from an incomplete cue. asynchronous update An update scheme that changes only one unit at each step. Ising energy A Lyapunov function for a symmetric binary network. overlap The normalized dot product between the current state and a stored pattern. crosstalk Interference from other stored patterns during retrieval of a target pattern. spurious attractor A stable state that does not correspond to any single stored pattern. spin glass A regime dominated by many disordered metastable states. temperature A scale parameter for noise in stochastic updates. How do asynchronous and synchronous updates differ? The classic proof that energy cannot increase depends on asynchronous single-unit updating. An asynchronous update changes one neuron at a time and immediately uses the new state; a synchronous update changes all neurons simultaneously. With symmetric W and \(W_{ii}=0\), how does energy change when one unit flips to follow the sign of its local field? Only pair terms involving that unit change, and symmetry combines their two halves. \(\Delta E=-\Delta S_{i}\) hi. If the update aligns with hi, then \(\Delta E\le 0\). Why is \(-\xi\) also usually an attractor when \(P=1\)? The classic unbiased model has global sign symmetry. The weights contain products \(\xi _{i}\xi _{j}\) and are unchanged by a global sign flip; at \(-\xi\), the local field again aligns with the current state. For \(N=1000\) and \(P=100\), what is loading \(\alpha\)? The critical value is not a hard guarantee for every instance and applies only under the specified dense random assumptions. \(\alpha =P/N=0.1\), below the classic value near 0.138, although finite N still permits errors. Why is an odd mixture called a spurious memory? Energy minima include more than the intended memories. It is formed by the component-wise majority of several stored patterns and may be stable even though it is not any single training pattern. Why does \(m>0\) not guarantee successful retrieval? It measures only similarity at the start. The basin also depends on memory load, the particular crosstalk, update order, and network parameters. This is the distinction tested in Explicit memory, Hebbian assemblies, and pattern completion. Worked example — Compute overlap for a noisy cue: A 100-bit pattern has 20 flipped bits. Find its overlap with the original pattern. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: A 100-bit pattern has 20 flipped bits. Find its overlap with the original pattern. Each of the 80 matching bits contributes +1, totaling 80. Each of the 20 flipped bits contributes -1, totaling -20. The total 60 divided by \(N=100\) gives \(m=0.6\). Check equivalently with \(1-2f=1-0.4=0.6\). Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Explicit memory, Hebbian assemblies, and pattern completion”? A cell assembly supplies a hypothesis for pattern completion. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Explicit memory, Hebbian assemblies, and pattern completion”? The Hopfield outer-product rule is an abstract encoding rule. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Explicit memory, Hebbian assemblies, and pattern completion” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? A cell assembly supplies a hypothesis for pattern completion. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “How overlap responds to cue corruption”? Both terms are dimensionless fractions, so overlap is dimensionless. For \(f=0\), \(m=1\); for \(f=0.5\), \(m=0\); and for \(f=1\), \(m=-1\). These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. What is the best response to the guiding question: How can a shared-activity cell assembly yield a testable encoding–cue–retrieval chain? The Hebbian assembly hypothesis proposes that cells jointly active in an experience develop stronger mutual connections. Encoding changes the connections, a partial cue reactivates some members, and recurrent excitation recruits the missing members to complete the pattern. An engram is a cellular ensemble causally involved in memory storage and expression; activation correlation alone is insufficient for that label. The Hopfield abstraction represents an assembly by binary pattern \(\xi\) and sets \(W_{ij}=(1/N)\sum \mu \xi _{i}^{\mu }\xi _{j}^{\mu }\), with \(W_{ii}=0\). Same-sign pairs receive positive weights and opposite-sign pairs negative weights. Real synapses obey Dale's law and constraints from sparse connectivity and spiking; the classic dense matrix first illustrates a computational principle. Why does updating every neuron once not guarantee a fixed point? After an early unit is updated, later unit changes can alter its local field, so another complete sweep without changes is required. This is the distinction tested in Binary asynchronous dynamics and stored random patterns. Worked example — Compute one update by hand: Let \(h_{i}=-0.7\) and current \(S_{i}=+1\), with the rule that \(\operatorname{sgn}(0)\) retains the current value. What are the new state and flip indicator? Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(h_{i}=-0.7\) and current \(S_{i}=+1\), with the rule that \(\operatorname{sgn}(0)\) retains the current value. What are the new state and flip indicator? Because \(h_{i}\) is negative, \(\operatorname{sgn}(h_{i})=-1\). \(S_{i}\) changes from +1 to -1. \(\Delta S_{i}=-1-(+1)=-2\), so a flip occurs. The new state has the same sign as the negative local field. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Binary asynchronous dynamics and stored random patterns”? An asynchronous update immediately writes back one unit. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Binary asynchronous dynamics and stored random patterns”? Convergence requires a fixed-state check, not a preset number of sweeps. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Binary asynchronous dynamics and stored random patterns” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Convergence requires a fixed-state check, not a preset number of sweeps. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “One asynchronous update of three units”? If weights are dimensionless, h is dimensionless and the sign operation is valid. If S2 were not written back immediately on the first step, subsequent fields would differ, demonstrating the importance of the update convention. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does the derivation of \(\Delta E\) fail when W is asymmetric? Pair terms with i as the first and second index cannot be combined into the same local field, so one scalar energy need not decline under updating. This is the distinction tested in Energy descent and the \(P=1\) stored attractor. Worked example — A finite-N field for \(P=1\): Let \(N=5\) and pattern \(\xi =(1,-1,1,-1,1)\), with the network in \(\xi\). Find the local field of unit1. Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(N=5\) and pattern \(\xi =(1,-1,1,-1,1)\), with the network in \(\xi\). Find the local field of unit1. \(W_{ij}=\xi _{1}\xi _{j}/5\). \(h_{1}=\sum _{j\ne 1}(\xi _{1}\xi _{j}/5)\xi _{j}=(\xi _{1}/5)\sum _{j\ne 1}\xi _{j}^{2}\). The four terms \(\xi _{j}^{2}=1\), so \(h_{1}=4/5=0.8\), aligned with \(\xi _{1}\). This agrees with the general expression \((N-1)\xi _{1}/N=4/5\). Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Energy descent and the \(P=1\) stored attractor”? Symmetric asynchronous dynamics makes energy nonincreasing. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Energy descent and the \(P=1\) stored attractor”? For \(P=1\), \(\xi\) and \(-\xi\) are both stable because of global sign symmetry. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Energy descent and the \(P=1\) stored attractor” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Energy descent does not guarantee retrieval of the desired memory. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Energy change from a single-unit flip”? \(\Delta S\) is dimensionless, so multiplying it by h gives energy units. When \(h_{i}=0\), \(\Delta E=0\); flipping a tie can move among equal-energy states. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does low mixture energy not make it a correct memory? Correctness is defined by the training target and behavioral identity; energy determines dynamical stability and does not know which patterns were designated as memories. This is the distinction tested in Spurious mixtures and the signal-plus-crosstalk decomposition. Worked example — A majority bit from three patterns: At one unit, three patterns have bits (+1,+1,-1). Find the odd-mixture bit. What if they are (+1,-1,-1)? Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: At one unit, three patterns have bits (+1,+1,-1). Find the odd-mixture bit. What if they are (+1,-1,-1)? The first sum is +1, so its sign is +1. The second sum is -1, so its sign is -1. A sum of three ±1 values can never be 0, so no tie rule is needed. Each result is the majority sign of the three bits. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Spurious mixtures and the signal-plus-crosstalk decomposition”? A local field separates into target-aligned signal and crosstalk from multiple memories. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Spurious mixtures and the signal-plus-crosstalk decomposition”? An odd component-wise majority can form a spurious attractor. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Spurious mixtures and the signal-plus-crosstalk decomposition” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? A local field separates into target-aligned signal and crosstalk from multiple memories. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Signal and crosstalk in the local field”? The 1/N normalization keeps signal of order one rather than allowing growth with N. When \(P=1\) the crosstalk sum is empty. As \(N\to \infty\) with fixed P, random crosstalk weakens. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does \(\alpha =0.1\) below 0.138 still not guarantee success for every cue? The threshold is a large-N typical statistic under a particular retrieval criterion. Finite patterns, poor cues, basin differences, and random instances can still fail. This is the distinction tested in Gaussian crosstalk, loading, and classic capacity. Worked example — A rough Gaussian bit-error estimate: Let \(\alpha =0.25\), \(\mathrm{signal}=1\), and noise standard deviation \(\sqrt \alpha =0.5\). An error requires \(\mathrm{noise}<-1\), equivalent to standard \(\operatorname{normal} Z<-2\). Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let \(\alpha =0.25\), \(\mathrm{signal}=1\), and noise standard deviation \(\sqrt \alpha =0.5\). An error requires \(\mathrm{noise}<-1\), equivalent to standard \(\operatorname{normal} Z<-2\). The standardized threshold is \(-1/0.5=-2\). The standard-normal tail is \(\Phi (-2)\approx 0.0228\). This is a single-step independent-noise approximation, not the final capacity criterion. As \(\alpha\) grows, the absolute threshold decreases and left-tail probability should rise. Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Gaussian crosstalk, loading, and classic capacity”? Crosstalk variance is approximately the loading \(\alpha\). The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Gaussian crosstalk, loading, and classic capacity”? The Gaussian tail gives an error tendency; the complete critical value requires self-consistency. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Gaussian crosstalk, loading, and classic capacity” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? The Gaussian tail gives an error tendency; the complete critical value requires self-consistency. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “Order of magnitude of crosstalk variance”? Variance has units of dimensionless field squared because classic weights and states are dimensionless. With fixed P and \(N\to \infty\), \(\alpha \to 0\). If P and N grow proportionally, noise remains of order one. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Why does an uncentered 0/1 Hebbian rule produce a global positive bias? Only jointly active bits contribute positively, while inactivity supplies no canceling term. Across many patterns, most weights become positive and drive excessive activity. This is the distinction tested in Sparse stochastic associative memory and global inhibition. Worked example — Center sparse bits: Let sparsity \(a=0.1\). What are the centered values of an active bit and an inactive bit, and what is their product? Which result or conclusion follows from these stated inputs? Worked setup: Let sparsity \(a=0.1\). What are the centered values of an active bit and an inactive bit, and what is their product? Active: \(1-a=0.9\). Inactive: \(0-a=-0.1\). Their product is \(0.9\times (-0.1)=-0.09\), so a pair with different activity contributes a negative association. The mean centered value is \(0.1\times 0.9+0.9\times (-0.1)=0\). Which statement gives the core conclusion developed in “Sparse stochastic associative memory and global inhibition”? Sparse patterns require mean subtraction or threshold control. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. Which statement gives the important constraint or comparison developed in “Sparse stochastic associative memory and global inhibition”? Global inhibition stabilizes population activity. The module's worked example and checks support the same conclusion. When applying “Sparse stochastic associative memory and global inhibition” to a new experiment or dataset, which principle must still hold? Capacity comparisons must use the same information and error metrics. The variables may change in a new setting, but the model must still satisfy this constraint. Which units check correctly constrains the derivation “A sparse Hebbian covariance rule with this lesson's global inhibition”? The normalization \(a(1-a)\) is dimensionless. The global and Hebbian terms must share weight units, and the logistic argument (h-u)/T must be dimensionless. For \(a=0\) or 1, variance is zero and the formula is undefined. As \(T\to 0\), the logistic rule approaches a hard threshold. These checks test both dimensional consistency and limiting behavior. Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “Hopfield basins: descent does not guarantee correct recall”? With symmetric weights, a zero diagonal, and asynchronous updates, both paths make E nonincreasing, but the cue's basin determines the endpoint. A cue near the target can complete to \(\xi ^{\mu }\), whereas crosstalk may draw an ambiguous cue into a mixture. Low energy therefore guarantees stability, not correct recall. title: Lecture 27: Systems Consolidation and Generalization
subtitle: Systems Consolidation and Generalization
text: Systems Consolidation and Generalization Recent versus remote memory → hippocampal replay → Teacher–Student–Notebook → pattern separation and completion → memory error → generalization error Distinguish changes over time in memory's anatomical dependence from changes in its psychological character, and interpret patient E.P. and recent-versus-remote evidence cautiously. Define the Teacher, Student, and Notebook and their information flows one by one, separating environmental generation, one-shot storage, replay, and slow cortical learning. Explain how pattern separation, pattern completion, and Hebbian Student↔Notebook links support rapid encoding and replay from a partial cue. Calculate memory error and population generalization error by hand in a linear Teacher/Student model, and identify overfitting to noise. Use predictability and SNR to reason about the Go-CLS stopping condition and lesion predictions without presenting formal-model outputs as established biological facts. Systems consolidation changes both the anatomical dependence and the psychological character of memory: recent memories tend to be more vivid and episodic, whereas remote memories tend to be more gist-like and semantic. In the Teacher–Student–Notebook framework, the environment or Teacher is a generative source, the neocortical Student slowly learns predictive structure, and the hippocampal Notebook rapidly stores and replays one-shot episodes. Continuous standard transfer can also write unpredictable noise into the Student and thereby impair generalization. Go-CLS instead controls transfer according to signal predictability/SNR and stops at the optimum, so unpredictable episodic detail remains hippocampus-dependent. A single case such as patient E.P. cannot establish every mechanism of consolidation. Recent memory is not absolutely equivalent to hippocampal storage, nor is remote memory absolutely equivalent to neocortical storage. A correlation with replay does not by itself demonstrate causal synaptic transfer. Teacher, Student, and Notebook are formal roles rather than one-to-one anatomical labels. Memory error and generalization error are distinct metrics. Lower training error does not necessarily mean that consolidation is better. Go-CLS predictions are not established facts. Can remote-memory findings from a patient such as E.P. alone prove that all remote episodic memories are independent of the hippocampus? It should be treated as important evidence, not an exhaustive law. No. A single case, lesion extent, memory age, semanticization, and related factors limit any universal conclusion. Does the Teacher represent the hippocampus in the Teacher–Student–Notebook framework? The framework names computational roles: the Teacher supplies the training world, the Student learns generalizable regularities, and the Notebook preserves sample-specific information. These names must not be treated as direct brain-region labels. No. The Teacher is the environment or generative process that produces inputs and targets; the Notebook is the abstraction of rapid hippocampal memory. Do pattern separation and pattern completion conflict? They act at different stages of memory. Separation reduces storage interference between similar events, whereas completion uses an incomplete cue to recover the correct event from an existing attractor. No. Encoding maps similar episodes to distinguishable codes, and retrieval reconstructs the corresponding complete code from a partial cue.
